It is a tradition of wrestling, questioning, lamenting, and arguing with God — and it repeatedly presents this wrestling as a sign of faithfulness, not faithlessness.

The book of Job is perhaps the most sustained act of theological deconstruction in all of Scripture. Job's friends represent the received theology of their day: suffering is the result of sin, prosperity is the reward of righteousness, and God's justice operates according to a simple and comprehensible moral calculus. Job — sitting in ash, covered in sores, having lost everything — deconstructs this theology not out of academic curiosity but out of lived experience. The theology he inherited does not match the reality he is enduring, and he refuses to pretend otherwise.

The remarkable thing about the book of Job is its conclusion. God does not validate the theology of Job's friends — the safe, systematic, institutional theology. God rebukes them. "You have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has," God says (Job 42:7). The one who questioned, protested, and demanded answers is commended. The ones who defended the received orthodoxy are corrected. If this is not a biblical endorsement of deconstruction, it is difficult to know what would count as one.

Ecclesiastes pushes further. The Teacher systematically dismantles every source of meaning that conventional wisdom offers — wealth, pleasure, achievement, even wisdom itself — and arrives at a place of profound uncertainty. "Meaningless, meaningless, everything is meaningless" is not a statement of atheism. It is a statement of radical honesty about the limits of human understanding. The book remains in the canon not despite its skepticism but because of it — because the tradition recognized that honest doubt is more faithful than dishonest certainty.

The Psalms of lament — roughly a third of the entire Psalter — are acts of deconstruction in liturgical form. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Psalm 22). "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13). "Why do you stand far off, O Lord? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble?" (Psalm 10). These are not the words of people whose faith is secure and undisturbed. They are the words of people whose experience has shattered their assumptions about God, and who insist on bringing that shattered experience into God's presence rather than pretending it away.

The biblical tradition does not demand unquestioning assent. It demands honest encounter — and honest encounter inevitably involves questioning what one thought one knew.

Why People Deconstruct

The catalysts for deconstruction are various, but they tend to cluster around a few recurring experiences. First, there is the experience of suffering that does not fit the theological framework one was given. When a child dies, when a faithful person is diagnosed with terminal illness, when natural disaster destroys a community — the pieties about God's plan and everything happening for a reason ring hollow, and the person of faith is forced to either suppress their honest response or begin examining the theology that produced those pieties.

Second, there is the experience of moral injury within the church itself. When a person witnesses abuse being covered up, when they see marginalized people being excluded in the name of God, when they discover that the leaders they trusted were hypocrites or predators — the institution's claim to moral authority collapses, and with it the unexamined authority of everything the institution taught. If they lied about this, the reasoning goes, what else did they lie about?

Third, there is the experience of intellectual growth. A person raised in a tradition that insists on young-earth creationism goes to college and encounters the evidence for evolution. A person raised to believe that the Bible was dictated word-for-word by God takes a course in biblical criticism and discovers the complex, human, historically situated process by which the texts were actually produced. A person raised to believe that Christianity has always been monolithic discovers the dizzying diversity of the early church. These intellectual encounters do not necessarily destroy faith, but they make it impossible to maintain faith in the particular form in which it was received.

Fourth, there is the experience of encountering the Other. A person raised to believe that LGBTQ+ people are disordered or sinful develops a close friendship with a gay person and discovers that the theology they inherited does not match the person they know. A person raised in a tradition that demonizes other religions meets a Muslim or Hindu or Buddhist whose spiritual life is manifestly deep, authentic, and morally serious. These encounters do not require the abandonment of Christian conviction, but they demand a more nuanced and generous theology than the one that was handed down.

How to Deconstruct Without Losing Everything

The fear that drives the church's hostility toward deconstruction is not entirely unfounded. Some people do lose their faith in the process. Some deconstruction does become destruction. The question is whether this outcome is inevitable or whether it is often the result of conditions the church itself creates.

When a person begins to question and the church responds with hostility — labeling them as dangerous, withdrawing community, treating doubt as a contagion — the church is creating the very conditions that make deconversion more likely. The message is clear: you cannot question and belong. And so people who need to question are forced to choose between intellectual honesty and communal belonging, and many understandably choose honesty.

Healthy deconstruction requires several things the church is often unwilling to provide. It requires safety — the assurance that questioning will not result in exile. It requires companionship — the presence of others who have walked a similar path and can testify that the road, while painful, is not fatal. It requires theological resources — the awareness that the Christian tradition itself contains rich veins of questioning, doubt, mystery, and intellectual rigor that can sustain a person through the process. And it requires patience — the recognition that deconstruction is not a weekend project but a long, slow, often circuitous journey that cannot be rushed to a tidy conclusion.

The mystics knew this. John of the Cross wrote about the "dark night of the soul" — the experience of spiritual emptiness and disorientation that is not the absence of God but a deeper encounter with God beyond the categories and concepts that once felt sufficient. Meister Eckhart prayed to "God to rid me of God" — the God of his projections and assumptions, so that the living God might be encountered on God's own terms. The contemplative tradition has always understood that the dismantling of one's image of God is not the loss of God but the precondition for a more authentic encounter.

What Reconstruction Looks Like

Reconstruction — the process of building a new faith on the other side of deconstruction — does not look like a return to the old faith with minor modifications. It looks like something genuinely new, though it often incorporates elements of the old in transformed ways.

Reconstructed faith tends to be more comfortable with mystery and less insistent on certainty. It holds doctrines more loosely, not because it takes them less seriously but because it has learned the difference between the reality to which doctrines point and the doctrines themselves. It is more focused on orthopraxy (right practice) than orthodoxy (right belief), not because belief does not matter but because it has learned that belief without practice is empty.

Reconstructed faith tends to be more ecumenical and less tribal. Having discovered that one's own tradition does not have a monopoly on truth, one becomes more willing to learn from other traditions — other Christian traditions, and sometimes other religious traditions entirely. This is not syncretism. It is the recognition that the God who is greater than any human comprehension might be encountered in places one's tradition did not anticipate.

Reconstructed faith tends to be more oriented toward justice and less oriented toward personal piety as an end in itself. The process of deconstruction often involves a confrontation with the ways one's tradition has caused harm — to women, to people of color, to LGBTQ+ people, to indigenous communities — and this confrontation tends to produce a faith that takes the biblical mandate for justice with a seriousness that the pre-deconstructed faith may have lacked.

Reconstructed faith tends to be more honest about the Bible. It can read Scripture with love and seriousness without needing it to be inerrant in a modernist sense. It can hold the tensions and contradictions within the text without needing to resolve them through harmonization. It can acknowledge that the Bible was written by human beings in specific historical contexts while still finding it revelatory, weighty, and authoritative in a way that is deeper than the brittle authority of fundamentalist literalism.

The faith that emerges from honest deconstruction is not a lesser faith. It is a faith that has been tested in the fire and has survived — not unchanged, but refined.

A Word to the Church

The church stands at a crossroads in its response to deconstruction. It can continue to treat questioning as a threat, circling the wagons, demanding loyalty, and expelling those who cannot affirm every item on an increasingly detailed statement of faith. This strategy will produce a smaller, more homogeneous, more rigid institution that feels safe to its remaining members and utterly alien to everyone else.

Or the church can do what Jesus did: welcome the questions, sit with the doubters, honor the struggle, and trust that the truth does not need to be protected from examination — that if it is true, it can survive any question a human being might bring to it. This does not mean the church must abandon its convictions. It means the church must hold its convictions with enough confidence to submit them to honest scrutiny, and with enough humility to acknowledge that its understanding of those convictions may need to grow.

The tradition that produced the book of Job, the Psalms of lament, and Ecclesiastes is a tradition that has always had room for those who question. The question is whether the contemporary church will honor that tradition or betray it in the name of protecting an institutional stability that is already crumbling regardless.

Deconstruction is not the enemy of faith. It may be faith's most demanding and most necessary expression.
excerpt: Deconstruction has become a dirty word in many churches. But the impulse to question inherited beliefs is as old as Scripture itself — and it may be the only path to a faith worth keeping.

title: The Rise of the Nones
body:
When survey researchers ask Americans about their religious affiliation and a respondent checks the box marked "none," the institutional church tends to hear one thing: atheist. This is a profound misunderstanding, and it has led the church to misdiagnose one of the most significant religious shifts in American history. The "nones" — those who claim no religious affiliation — are now approximately 28 to 30 percent of the American population, making them the largest single "religious" category in the country, surpassing Catholics, white evangelicals, and every other identifiable group. And the church, by and large, has no idea who these people are.

The term itself emerged from survey methodology. The General Social Survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago since 1972, asks respondents, "What is your religious preference?" and offers a list of options including Protestant, Catholic, Jewish, and other affiliations. Those who answer "none" are the "nones." When the survey began, they constituted about 5 percent of the population. Their growth since then has been steady, accelerating, and shows no signs of reversing.

But a box on a survey is not an identity, and the assumption that all nones are the same — that they are all secular humanists, or scientific materialists, or village atheists — is flatly contradicted by every study that has examined the category in any depth. The nones are theologically, philosophically, and spiritually diverse. And understanding them requires the church to abandon some of its most comfortable assumptions about what unaffiliation means.

Who the Nones Actually Are

The Pew Research Center's detailed analysis of the religiously unaffiliated breaks the category into three subgroups. The first is atheists, who constitute roughly 4 percent of the overall population. The second is agnostics, who constitute roughly 5 percent. The third — and by far the largest — is the category Pew labels "nothing in particular," which constitutes roughly 20 percent of the population. This last group is the one the church most consistently misunderstands.

People who identify as "nothing in particular" are not, for the most part, committed secularists who have reached a considered philosophical conclusion that God does not exist. Many of them believe in God. Many pray. A significant number describe religion as "somewhat important" or even "very important" in their lives. What they have rejected is not the divine but the institutional — not God but the church, the mosque, the synagogue, the organized religious structure that they associate with hypocrisy, judgment, exclusion, or irrelevance.

Ryan Burge, a political scientist and Baptist pastor whose work on the nones has become foundational in the field, stresses this point in his book The Nones: the unaffiliated are not a monolith. They are not all Richard Dawkins. Many of them are your neighbors who believe in God, pray occasionally, celebrate Christmas, and simply don't see the point of going to church. This is not a comfortable observation for church leaders, because it suggests that the church's problem is not primarily theological (people rejecting God) but institutional (people rejecting the church).

Demographics of Disaffiliation

The demographic profile of the nones challenges several popular narratives about who is leaving organized religion and why. The growth of the nones has been most dramatic among younger Americans — roughly 40 percent of millennials and a similar percentage of Gen Z identify as religiously unaffiliated — but it is not exclusively a young person's phenomenon. The percentage of nones among Gen X has grown significantly, and even among baby boomers, the number has roughly doubled since the turn of the millennium.

The gender gap is notable. Men are more likely than women to identify as nones, though the gap has narrowed in recent years as women — particularly younger women — have disaffiliated at increasing rates. The racial composition of the nones is disproportionately white, though the growth rate among Hispanic and Black Americans has accelerated. Education is a factor, but not in the direction many assume: the nones include both college graduates and those without college degrees, and the growth has been roughly parallel across educational levels.

Geographically, the nones are concentrated in the Pacific Northwest, the Northeast, and urban areas generally, but they are growing in every region of the country, including the South and the rural Midwest. There is no part of America where the church is not losing ground.

Perhaps the most significant demographic finding is this: the nones are not primarily converts from devout households who experienced dramatic crises of faith. Most of them were raised in homes where religion was already nominal — where their parents attended church sporadically, identified as Christian loosely, and practiced their faith inconsistently. The nones, in many cases, are simply the honest children of nominally religious parents. They are making explicit what was already implicit in the previous generation's relationship to organized religion.

What the Nones Believe

The belief structure of the nones is genuinely complex, and it resists the tidy categories that both religious institutions and militant secularists would like to impose on it. The Pew Research Center has found that among nones who are not atheists or agnostics — the "nothing in particular" group — a majority believe in God or some higher power, about a third say they pray at least monthly, and roughly a quarter say religion is somewhat important in their lives.

Many nones hold what sociologists of religion call "believing without belonging" — a phrase coined by Grace Davie to describe the phenomenon of privatized religious belief detached from institutional participation. They may believe in an afterlife, in the power of prayer, in some form of cosmic justice or moral order — but they hold these beliefs privately and do not see institutional religion as necessary or even helpful for sustaining them.

Others occupy a space that might be described as spiritual eclecticism. They draw on multiple traditions without exclusive commitment to any one. A none might practice yoga, read Buddhist texts, find wisdom in the Sermon on the Mount, and consult an astrologer — not because they lack intellectual seriousness but because they have concluded that no single tradition has a monopoly on truth and that wisdom can be found in many wells. The church tends to dismiss this as shallow cafeteria-style spirituality, but that dismissal often reveals more about the church's anxiety than about the actual depth of these practices.

A smaller but significant subset of the nones are genuinely secular — people for whom religion in any form holds no appeal and for whom meaning, morality, and community are constructed without reference to the transcendent. This group is growing, particularly among younger Americans, and it represents a genuine departure from the historically religious character of American public life. But it remains a minority within the broader none category.

The nones are not a void. They are a population with real spiritual needs, real moral commitments, and real reasons for rejecting the institutions that claim to serve those needs.

Sociological Factors: Why Now

The rise of the nones is not simply a matter of individuals making private theological decisions. It is a sociological phenomenon driven by structural changes in American life. Several factors converge to explain why the trend has accelerated so dramatically in the past two decades.

First, the social penalty for non-affiliation has largely disappeared. In mid-twentieth-century America, church membership was a social expectation — a marker of respectability, community standing, and moral seriousness. To be unaffiliated was to be suspect. That social pressure has dissipated. In most American communities today, there is no social cost to being a none. This does not mean that people are leaving because religion was always superficial for them. It means that the people for whom it was primarily a social convention now feel free to say so.

Second, the political alignment of organized religion — particularly white evangelical Christianity — with the Republican Party has created what sociologists call a "backlash effect." Michael Hout and Claude Fischer, in their influential 2002 study, argued that the rise of the Religious Right in the 1980s and 1990s created a negative association between religion and conservative politics that drove politically moderate and liberal Americans away from religious affiliation. People who might otherwise have remained nominally religious chose to disaffiliate because they did not want to be associated with a political movement they found repugnant.

Third, the abuse scandals that have rocked virtually every branch of organized Christianity have undermined institutional credibility. The Catholic Church's abuse crisis, the Southern Baptist Convention's abuse crisis, and the steady stream of revelations about abuse in independent and charismatic churches have collectively communicated a message that is devastating for institutional religion: the people who claim to speak for God cannot be trusted with the vulnerable.

Fourth, the internet has democratized information about religion in ways that undermine institutional authority. A person raised in a fundamentalist church who encounters persuasive biblical scholarship online, or who discovers that the history of Christianity is far more complex and contested than their pastor presented, or who connects with communities of former believers and discovers that their doubts are shared — that person has access to resources and relationships that simply did not exist a generation ago. The church's ability to control the narrative about itself has been fundamentally compromised.

What the Church Gets Wrong About Reaching the Nones

The institutional church's response to the rise of the nones has been, with some exceptions, characterized by strategic thinking that misidentifies the problem. The assumption, usually unstated, is that the nones are people who do not understand the church's message and who could be won back with better communication, more relevant programming, or more attractive worship experiences. This assumption leads to a set of strategies that are, at best, ineffective and, at worst, counterproductive.

The first mistake is treating the nones as a marketing problem. The logic goes: if we can just make our services more engaging, our music more contemporary, our facilities more inviting, our sermons more relevant, people will come. This approach assumes that the nones have rejected the church's packaging but would accept its product if it were better presented. But the nones, by and large, have not rejected the packaging. They have rejected — or at least become deeply skeptical of — the institution itself, its credibility, its moral authority, and its alignment with values they find important.

The second mistake is assuming that the nones are ignorant of Christianity and need to be educated. In fact, many nones — particularly those raised in Christian households — are quite knowledgeable about Christianity. They have not failed to hear the church's message. They have heard it, evaluated it, and found it wanting — not necessarily the message of Jesus, but the message of the institution that claims to represent Jesus.

The third mistake is approaching the nones apologetically — in the philosophical sense, offering arguments for the existence of God, the reliability of the Bible, or the historical evidence for the resurrection. These arguments have their place, but they are largely irrelevant to a population whose objections are not primarily intellectual but moral and institutional. A person who left the church because it covered up sexual abuse does not need a better argument for the resurrection. They need to see an institution that tells the truth and protects the vulnerable.

The fourth mistake is assuming that the nones will "come back" when they get older, get married, or have children. This assumption is based on historical patterns that no longer hold. Previous generations did tend to return to church during the family-formation years. The current generation is not following that pattern. Nones who marry tend to marry other nones, and nones who have children tend to raise them without organized religion. The pipeline that once returned lapsed Christians to the pews has been broken.

What the Nones Might Actually Respond To

If the nones are not a marketing problem, an education problem, or an apologetics problem, what are they? They are, above all, a credibility problem. The church has lost credibility with a significant portion of the population, and credibility cannot be restored through better programming or more persuasive arguments. It can only be restored through changed behavior sustained over time.

The nones respond to authenticity — not the curated authenticity of a pastor sharing a carefully calibrated vulnerability from the stage, but the genuine authenticity of a community that acknowledges its failures, welcomes doubt, practices generosity without strings, and treats every human being with dignity regardless of their beliefs, identity, or behavior.

The nones respond to justice. They care about the poor, the marginalized, the planet. They are drawn to communities that show up for the vulnerable — not as a recruitment strategy but as a fundamental expression of what they believe. A church that is visibly, consistently, and sacrificially committed to justice will earn the respect of nones even if it does not earn their membership.

The nones respond to honesty about complexity. They live in a world of irreducible complexity — moral, intellectual, spiritual — and they are drawn to communities that can hold that complexity without collapsing it into simple answers. A church that can say "this is hard" and "we are not certain" and "we are still learning" is a church that speaks the language the nones actually speak.

The rise of the nones is not a verdict on God. It is a verdict on the church. And verdicts, unlike sentences, can be appealed — but only if the institution is willing to change the behavior that produced them.

The church cannot reach the nones by becoming something it is not. But it might reach them by becoming what it claims to be — a community shaped by the radical love, disarming honesty, and costly justice of the one it calls Lord. The nones are not waiting for a better church service. They are waiting for a better church. Whether the institution can become one remains the open question of American religion in the twenty-first century.
excerpt: They are the fastest-growing 'religious' group in America, and most of them are not atheists. Understanding the 'nones' requires abandoning nearly everything the church assumes about unbelief.

title: Exvangelical: When Leaving Isn't Losing Faith
body:
The hashtag appeared on Twitter in 2016, coined by Blake Chastain, a podcaster and writer from the American Midwest. #Exvangelical. It was not a theological treatise or a manifesto. It was a naming — an attempt to give language to an experience that millions of people were living but that had no public vocabulary. Within months, it had become a movement, or at least the outline of one: a sprawling, decentralized community of people who had left evangelicalism and were trying to figure out who they were on the other side.

The timing was not accidental. The year 2016, with the election of Donald Trump and the overwhelming support he received from white evangelical voters, was a catalytic event for many who had been quietly uncomfortable with the direction of American evangelicalism. For some, it was the final confirmation of suspicions they had held for years. For others, it was a sudden, disorienting rupture — the moment when the gap between the Jesus they had been taught to follow and the political movement that bore his name became too wide to bridge.

But the exvangelical movement did not begin in 2016. It began in living rooms and therapist's offices and late-night conversations, years and sometimes decades before a hashtag gave it a name. It began every time a person raised in the evangelical world looked at what that world had become and said, quietly or loudly, "I cannot do this anymore."

Who Exvangelicals Are

The first and most important thing to understand about exvangelicals is what they are not. They are not, as a group, atheists. They are not angry people who want to destroy Christianity. They are not victims of secular culture who were seduced away from the truth. They are, overwhelmingly, people who took their faith seriously — often more seriously than the institutions they left — and who found that the version of Christianity they were given could not sustain the weight of their honest experience.

Many exvangelicals remain Christians. They have moved to mainline Protestant churches, to Catholic or Orthodox traditions, to progressive evangelical communities, or to non-denominational churches that share none of the cultural markers of the evangelicalism they left. They still pray. They still read Scripture. They still follow Jesus. What they have left is not Christianity but a particular cultural expression of Christianity that they found to be toxic, dishonest, or untenable.

Others have moved to a more ambiguous spiritual space — still believing in God, still shaped by the moral and spiritual formation of their evangelical upbringing, but no longer able to identify with any particular tradition. They are, in sociological terms, "spiritual but not religious," though that phrase does not capture the specificity of their experience. They are not people who never had a religion. They are people who had one — intensely, formatively, all-consumingly — and who had to walk away from it for the sake of their integrity, their mental health, or both.

A smaller number have left religious belief entirely. For them, the process of examining evangelicalism led to the conclusion that the entire framework — not just the evangelical version, but the theistic worldview itself — could not be sustained. These are the genuine deconverts, and their experience deserves respect rather than the contemptuous dismissal it often receives from the communities they left.

The Distinction That Matters

The evangelical establishment has a strong institutional incentive to collapse the distinction between leaving evangelicalism and leaving Christianity. If every departure can be framed as apostasy, then the institution is absolved of responsibility. The problem is not with us, the logic goes; the problem is with people who lack the faith to endure. This framing protects the institution but bears almost no relationship to the actual experience of most exvangelicals.

Leaving evangelicalism is not the same as leaving Christianity, any more than leaving a particular marriage is the same as rejecting the concept of love. Evangelicalism is a specific cultural, theological, and political tradition within the broader Christian family. It has distinctive beliefs (biblical inerrancy, penal substitutionary atonement, the necessity of personal conversion), distinctive practices (altar calls, quiet times, accountability groups), and distinctive cultural markers (Christian music, purity culture, political conservatism). A person can reject every one of these distinctive features and still be a follower of Jesus. The conflation of evangelicalism with Christianity is itself a form of the tribalism that drives people away.

This distinction matters practically as well as theologically. When a person leaves evangelicalism and the community responds as though they have left God, the community inflicts a wound that is both unnecessary and deeply damaging. The person who is already grieving the loss of their community is told that their grief is a sign of spiritual failure. The person who is trying to preserve their faith in a new form is told that any form other than the one they left is no faith at all. This response does not protect faith. It destroys it.

Common Catalysts

The catalysts that precipitate an exvangelical departure are varied, but several recur with striking frequency across the literature, the podcasts, and the personal testimonies that constitute the movement's archive.

The Trump era crystallized a dissonance that many had felt for years. When 81 percent of white evangelicals voted for a candidate whose personal life, business practices, and rhetorical style represented the antithesis of the values evangelicalism claimed to hold — when evangelical leaders who had spent decades insisting on "character" in political leaders suddenly discovered that character was negotiable — the hypocrisy was too flagrant to ignore. For many exvangelicals, the question was not "How can Christians support this?" but rather "What does it say about the movement that this support was so easy and so enthusiastic?"

The church's posture toward LGBTQ+ people has been another major catalyst. A generation of evangelicals grew up being taught that homosexuality was a uniquely grievous sin, that LGBTQ+ people were threats to the family and to civilization, and that the church's opposition to LGBTQ+ rights was a matter of unwavering biblical fidelity. Then they met actual LGBTQ+ people — or discovered that they themselves were LGBTQ+ — and found that the theology they had been given could not account for the full, complex, dignified humanity of the people it condemned. The choice between their theology and their conscience was not a choice between faith and the world. It was a choice between a theology of exclusion and the inclusive love they believed Jesus actually embodied.

Abuse — sexual, spiritual, and emotional — has driven countless departures. The revelations about Ravi Zacharias, Bill Hybels, Mark Driscoll, Jerry Falwell Jr., and the broader SBC abuse crisis created a cascading loss of trust that extended far beyond the specific perpetrators. If the most celebrated leaders of the movement were predators, and if the institutional structures of the movement protected them rather than their victims, then the movement's claim to moral authority was not merely damaged but forfeit.

Racial justice has been an increasingly significant catalyst, particularly for exvangelicals of color but also for white evangelicals whose commitment to racial equity brought them into conflict with their communities. The evangelical church's response to the Black Lives Matter movement, to police violence against Black Americans, and to the broader conversation about systemic racism revealed a fault line that many could no longer straddle. A tradition that could not say "Black lives matter" without qualification had, for many, revealed something fundamental about its moral priorities.

The exvangelical departure is not a rejection of faith. It is an insistence that faith must be more than the cultural and political package in which it was delivered.

Where They Go

The geography of exvangelical life after departure is varied and often surprising. Some find homes in traditions they never expected. The migration of former evangelicals to the Episcopal Church, the ELCA, the United Church of Christ, and other mainline traditions has been well documented. These churches offer liturgical depth, intellectual freedom, social justice commitments, and a theological tradition that does not demand the sacrificium intellectus — the sacrifice of the intellect — that evangelicalism so often requires.

Others have found their way to the Catholic Church or to Eastern Orthodoxy, drawn by the historical rootedness, the sacramental theology, and the contemplative tradition that evangelicalism, in its emphasis on personal experience and biblical propositionalism, often lacks. The irony is not lost on anyone: traditions that evangelicalism spent decades dismissing as dead, ritualistic, or insufficiently biblical are becoming places of refuge for people whom evangelicalism failed.

A significant number have not landed anywhere institutionally. They exist in a kind of ecclesiastical diaspora — reading theology, listening to podcasts, meeting informally with others on similar journeys, practicing faith in forms that do not fit any denominational category. This is not, as critics charge, mere consumerism or spiritual laziness. It is the honest response of people who have been deeply wounded by institutional religion and who need time — sometimes years — before they can trust an institution again.

The Grief of Leaving

What is often overlooked in discussions of the exvangelical movement is the grief. Leaving evangelicalism is not like leaving a club or changing a preference. For people raised in the tradition, evangelicalism was not a part of their life. It was their life. It was their community, their social world, their moral framework, their understanding of reality, their source of meaning and identity. To leave it is to lose, in one motion, friends, family relationships, community, certainty, and a coherent narrative about who you are and what the world means.

The grief is compounded by the fact that evangelical communities often treat departure as betrayal. The person who leaves is not merely someone who made a different choice. They are a backslider, a prodigal, a cautionary tale. Former friends distance themselves. Family relationships become strained or fractured. The leaver finds themselves grieving not only the community they lost but the relationships that community withdrew.

This grief is real and should be honored. It is not a sign of weakness or indecision. It is the natural response of a human being who has lost a world. And it is, for many exvangelicals, one of the most painful experiences of their lives — more painful, often, than the specific grievances that precipitated their departure.

The church that takes this grief seriously — that acknowledges its own role in causing it, that reaches out with compassion rather than condemnation, that says "we understand why you left and we are sorry for the pain we caused" — is a church that has begun to reckon with the reality of what the exvangelical movement represents. It represents not the triumph of secularism or the weakness of faith but the failure of a particular tradition to embody the love it proclaims.

The exvangelical is not the enemy of Christianity. The exvangelical is the church's most honest mirror. And what the mirror shows is not comfortable — but it is, for those with the courage to look, a gift.
excerpt: A growing movement of former evangelicals is redefining what it means to leave a tradition without leaving the faith that tradition claimed to own.

title: Purity Culture and Its Wreckage
body:
In 1993, the Southern Baptist Convention launched a campaign called "True Love Waits." Teenagers were invited to sign pledge cards committing to sexual abstinence until marriage. The cards were collected, stacked, and displayed in public spectacles designed to demonstrate the movement's scale: 210,000 cards staked on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., 350,000 more displayed at subsequent events. The campaign spread to churches across the evangelical world, spawning an entire industry of conferences, curricula, rings, t-shirts, and branded merchandise built around a single message: your sexual purity is the most important thing about you, and if you lose it, you have lost something that can never be recovered.

Four years later, Joshua Harris, a homeschooled Christian who had written it at twenty-one, published I Kissed Dating Goodbye, a book that extended the purity framework beyond sex to encompass all romantic relationships. Harris argued that the modern dating system was fundamentally broken, that emotional attachments before marriage were spiritually dangerous, and that the godly alternative was "courtship" — a parent-supervised process in which romantic relationships were undertaken only with the explicit intention of marriage. The book sold over a million copies and became a foundational text for a generation of young evangelicals.

These two phenomena — True Love Waits and Harris's book — were the most visible expressions of what has come to be called "purity culture," a broad movement within American evangelicalism that placed sexual behavior at the center of Christian identity and made virginity the primary marker of spiritual faithfulness. The movement was enormous in its reach, deeply formative in its effects, and, as a growing body of testimony and research now makes clear, profoundly damaging in its consequences.

The Theology Behind the Movement

Purity culture presented itself as simple biblical fidelity — a straightforward application of scriptural teaching about sexual ethics to the challenges of contemporary adolescence. But the theology that actually undergirded the movement was considerably thinner and more ideologically driven than its proponents acknowledged.

The movement drew selectively from Scripture, emphasizing certain texts (Paul's instructions about sexual immorality, the Proverbs warnings about the "adulterous woman") while ignoring others (the Song of Solomon's celebration of erotic desire, the complex sexual ethics of the patriarchal narratives, the conspicuous absence of sexual purity as a topic in Jesus's recorded teaching). It constructed a theology of sexuality that was, in practice, less about what the Bible says than about what a particular strand of twentieth-century American evangelicalism believed the Bible should say.

At the center of this theology was a set of interconnected assumptions. First, that sexual sin was categorically different from and worse than other sins — that it damaged the soul in a way that lying, greed, or cruelty did not. Second, that sexual purity was primarily a female responsibility, since women were the "gatekeepers" of sexual behavior and bore the greater consequence of its violation. Third, that virginity was a kind of spiritual commodity — something possessed, something that could be "given away" or "lost," something whose absence permanently diminished a person's value as a marriage partner and, implicitly, as a human being.

Fourth, and perhaps most damaging, purity culture taught that sexual desire itself was dangerous and suspect — that the body's natural response to attraction was a temptation to be suppressed rather than a capacity to be understood, stewarded, and eventually celebrated within its proper context. The message was not "sexuality is a gift that requires wisdom and care." The message was "sexuality is a threat that requires constant vigilance and control."

The Gendered Architecture of Purity

Purity culture was ostensibly directed at both young men and young women, but its actual architecture was profoundly gendered. Young women bore the disproportionate weight of the movement's expectations and the disproportionate punishment for its violations.

Girls were taught that their bodies were sources of temptation to boys and men — that the way they dressed, moved, and presented themselves was responsible for the sexual thoughts and behaviors of the males around them. The modesty teachings that accompanied purity culture placed the burden of male self-control on female bodies. A girl who wore a tank top was not simply making a clothing choice; she was "causing her brother to stumble." The theological framework that was supposed to protect young women instead taught them that they were inherently dangerous — that their bodies were problems to be managed rather than selves to be inhabited.

Boys received a different but equally distorted message. They were taught that they were fundamentally unable to control their sexual impulses — that male sexuality was a raging fire that, if not rigorously contained, would inevitably consume everything in its path. This teaching was simultaneously demeaning and exculpatory: it reduced young men to their libidos while providing a ready-made excuse for predatory behavior. "Boys will be boys" is not a Christian theology of masculinity. It is the abdication of one.

The combined effect of these gendered messages was a system in which girls were responsible for everyone's purity and boys were responsible for no one's. When sexual boundaries were violated — and in the real world, they frequently were — the girl bore the shame. She was the one who had "lost" something. She was the one who was damaged goods. She was the one who would need to confess her failure to a future spouse and hope for his gracious acceptance of her diminished state.

Purity culture did not elevate women. It commodified them. It reduced their worth to a biological status and their identity to a single metric of compliance.

What the Research Shows

The empirical evidence on purity culture's effects has been accumulating for two decades, and it paints a damning picture. First, on its own terms, purity culture failed. Studies consistently show that abstinence pledges have little long-term effect on sexual behavior. A landmark study by Peter Bearman and Hannah Bruckner, published in the American Journal of Sociology in 2001, found that while virginity pledges delayed the onset of sexual activity by an average of eighteen months, their 2005 follow-up in the Journal of Adolescent Health found that pledge-takers who did become sexually active were significantly less likely to use contraception than their non-pledging peers. They were not having less sex. They were having less safe sex.

A subsequent study by Janet Rosenbaum, published in Pediatrics, found that five years after taking a virginity pledge, pledgers and non-pledgers had the same rates of premarital sexual activity and sexually transmitted infections — but pledgers were less likely to have used contraception. The pledge produced guilt, not abstinence; shame, not safety.

Beyond the public health data, a growing body of research documents the psychological damage purity culture inflicts. Linda Kay Klein, in her book Pure: Inside the Evangelical Movement That Shamed a Generation of Young Women and How I Broke Free, draws on over a decade of interviews with women raised in purity culture. Her findings are consistent and disturbing: anxiety, depression, sexual dysfunction, chronic shame, difficulty experiencing pleasure, inability to trust their own bodies, and a persistent sense of being fundamentally damaged — even among women who "did everything right" and remained virgins until marriage.

The sexual dysfunction finding is particularly significant. Purity culture teaches young people to suppress and pathologize their sexual responses for years or decades, then expects them to flip a switch on their wedding night and experience sexuality as a joyful gift. The psychological research on conditioned responses makes clear that this expectation is not merely unrealistic but neurologically incoherent. You cannot train a person to associate sex with shame, danger, and contamination for fifteen years and then expect that association to disappear because a ceremony was performed.

The Theological Correction

The theological problems with purity culture are not minor. They are foundational. And correcting them does not require abandoning a Christian sexual ethic. It requires recovering one.

First, purity culture's elevation of sexual sin above all other sins has no basis in the teaching of Jesus. In the Gospels, Jesus reserves his harshest condemnation not for sexual sinners but for religious hypocrites — for those who use their piety as a weapon against the vulnerable, who bind heavy burdens on others' shoulders while refusing to lift a finger to help. The woman caught in adultery is not condemned; the Pharisees who brought her are challenged. The tax collectors and prostitutes, Jesus says, are entering the kingdom of God ahead of the religious establishment (Matthew 21:31). Purity culture inverted Jesus's moral priorities.

Second, the Bible's understanding of purity is not primarily about sex. The Hebrew concept of taharah (ritual purity) encompasses a vast range of conditions and practices — dietary laws, skin diseases, bodily emissions, contact with death — and it is fundamentally about readiness to enter God's presence, not about moral status. When Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and touched lepers without contracting impurity, he was dismantling the purity system's power to exclude. Purity culture, ironically, rebuilt a system of exclusion that Jesus came to abolish.

Third, the commodification of virginity — the idea that a person's worth is diminished by sexual experience — is incompatible with a gospel of grace. If the central claim of Christianity is that human worth is not earned by performance but given by God, then a theology that locates a person's value in a biological status is not Christian theology. It is works-righteousness applied to the body. The doctrine of grace means, among other things, that no experience — sexual or otherwise — can diminish a person's worth in the eyes of God.

Fourth, the biblical tradition contains a rich, positive theology of sexuality that purity culture systematically ignored. The Song of Solomon celebrates erotic desire with language so explicit that rabbinical tradition forbade its reading by anyone under thirty. The creation narrative in Genesis describes the union of man and woman not as a concession to human weakness but as a fundamental expression of what it means to be made in God's image. Paul's metaphor of the body as a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19) is not, in context, a warning against contamination. It is a statement of dignity — the body is sacred, not because it is fragile and easily ruined, but because it is inhabited by God and therefore worthy of honor.

Toward a Healthy Sexual Theology

A Christian sexual theology worthy of the name would look radically different from what purity culture offered. It would begin not with prohibition but with affirmation — the affirmation that sexuality is a good gift, created by God, embedded in the very structure of human existence, and intended for joy, intimacy, and connection. It would treat sexual desire not as a problem to be solved but as a capacity to be understood and wisely directed.

It would place sexual ethics within the broader framework of Christian ethics — the ethics of love, justice, mutuality, and care for the other. The question would not be "How far can I go without sinning?" but rather "How can I honor the full humanity of the other person and my own?" This is a more demanding ethic than purity culture's rule-based approach, because it requires moral discernment rather than mere compliance. But it is also a more humane one, because it treats people as moral agents rather than potential contaminants.

It would refuse the gendered double standard that purity culture both created and reinforced. It would insist that men are capable of self-control and that women are not responsible for men's thoughts. It would teach young people of all genders that their bodies are their own — sacred, worthy of care, and not available for the regulation of others.

It would hold whatever boundaries it holds with compassion rather than shame. A tradition that believes certain sexual behaviors are reserved for certain contexts can hold that belief without treating those who fall short as damaged goods. The difference between a boundary held with love and a boundary enforced with shame is the difference between a community that forms people and a system that breaks them.

The church does not need to abandon sexual ethics. It needs to abandon the toxic distortion of sexual ethics that reduced human bodies to commodities, human worth to a biological status, and God's grace to a reward for compliance.

Joshua Harris himself eventually came to this reckoning. In 2019, he publicly apologized for the harm caused by I Kissed Dating Goodbye, asked his publisher to discontinue the book, announced the end of his marriage, and declared that he no longer considered himself a Christian. The trajectory of his personal journey — from purity culture's most visible spokesman to its most visible casualty — encapsulates the movement's fundamental problem: it built a theology on a foundation too narrow to sustain a human life.

The wreckage of purity culture is real, and it is extensive. It lives in the bodies and psyches of a generation of adults who were taught to fear their own desires, to measure their worth by their virginity, and to believe that God's love was conditional on their sexual performance. Healing that damage requires more than better sex education or more progressive theology. It requires a fundamentally different understanding of what the body is, what sexuality means, and what kind of God we are dealing with. It requires, in other words, the gospel — the actual gospel, not the counterfeit one that purity culture sold in its name.
excerpt: A generation was taught that their sexual worth was a commodity to be preserved. The theology was thin, the damage was deep, and the reckoning is long overdue.

title: The Prosperity Gospel Is Not the Gospel
body:
In 2011, Senator Chuck Grassley concluded a three-year Senate Finance Committee inquiry, opened in 2007, into the finances of six prominent televangelists. The investigation, which examined the ministries of Benny Hinn, Creflo Dollar, Eddie Long, Joyce Meyer, Kenneth Copeland, and Paula White, revealed a pattern of extraordinary personal wealth accumulated through tax-exempt religious organizations: private jets, luxury homes, Rolls-Royces, designer clothing, and multi-million-dollar compensation packages — all funded, directly or indirectly, by the donations of believers, many of them poor, who had been told that their financial gifts would be returned to them by God multiplied many times over.

The investigation produced no legislative action. But it provided a documentary portrait of something that millions of Americans already knew from personal experience: the prosperity gospel — the theological movement that promises health, wealth, and divine favor as the guaranteed results of sufficient faith and generous giving — is one of the most powerful and most destructive forces in contemporary Christianity. It is also, by any rigorous theological standard, a heresy. Not a minor doctrinal variation, not a difference of emphasis, not a matter of legitimate theological disagreement — but a fundamental distortion of the Christian message that inverts the gospel's priorities, exploits the vulnerable, and blasphemes the character of God.

Origins: From New Thought to Word of Faith

The prosperity gospel did not emerge from the mainstream of Christian theological reflection. Its intellectual roots lie in the New Thought movement of the nineteenth century — a loose collection of metaphysical teachings that emphasized the power of the mind to shape material reality. Phineas Quimby, a New England clockmaker and mesmerist, developed a system of "mental healing" that attributed disease and poverty to incorrect thinking. His ideas influenced Mary Baker Eddy (who founded Christian Science) and, through a chain of transmission, the Pentecostal healing evangelists of the twentieth century.

The key figure in bridging New Thought metaphysics and evangelical Christianity was E.W. Kenyon, a Baptist minister and educator who spent time at Emerson College, an institution heavily influenced by New Thought philosophy. Kenyon developed a theology that merged Pentecostal spirituality with New Thought principles: the spoken word, empowered by faith, had the power to create reality. "What I confess, I possess," Kenyon taught. Faith was not trust in God's character or submission to God's will. Faith was a force — a mechanism for activating spiritual laws that governed the material world.

Kenneth Hagin, a Pentecostal evangelist from Texas widely regarded as the father of the Word of Faith movement, adopted and popularized Kenyon's ideas — in some cases reproducing Kenyon's writings nearly verbatim without attribution. Hagin taught that God had established spiritual "laws" that operated with the regularity of natural laws. Faith, properly exercised through "positive confession" (declaring desired outcomes as already accomplished), would invariably produce material results. Poverty and sickness were not features of life in a fallen world. They were the results of insufficient faith or incorrect speech — spiritual malfunctions that the properly instructed believer could correct.

From Hagin, the theology spread to a second generation of teachers who would become household names: Kenneth Copeland, Fred Price, Jerry Savelle, Charles Capps, and others. Each added their own emphasis, but the core theology remained consistent: God wants you to be wealthy and healthy; if you are not, the problem is your faith; and the primary mechanism for activating God's blessing is financial giving to the ministry.

The Theology: What the Prosperity Gospel Actually Teaches

The prosperity gospel rests on several interlocking theological claims, each of which represents a significant departure from historic Christian orthodoxy.

Positive confession. The prosperity gospel teaches that words have creative power — that the believer can literally speak things into existence by declaring them in faith. This teaching draws on a distorted reading of Genesis 1 (God spoke the world into existence, and believers, made in God's image, share this creative capacity) and Proverbs 18:21 ("death and life are in the power of the tongue"). The practical application is that believers must never "confess" negative realities — never acknowledge sickness, poverty, or failure — because to do so is to empower those conditions. The faithful believer declares health, wealth, and victory regardless of present circumstances, and the declaration itself produces the reality.

Seed-faith. The doctrine of seed-faith, popularized by Oral Roberts, teaches that financial gifts to the ministry function as "seeds" that God is obligated to multiply and return to the giver. The metaphor is drawn from agricultural imagery in Scripture (Galatians 6:7, 2 Corinthians 9:6), but it is extended far beyond anything the biblical texts support. In prosperity theology, giving is not an act of generosity or worship. It is an investment — a transaction in which the giver deposits money with God and expects a material return. The larger the seed, the larger the harvest. The implication, rarely stated explicitly but always present, is that giving to the ministry is the most reliable path to personal wealth.

The Abrahamic covenant. Prosperity teachers frequently appeal to God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12:1-3) as the basis for material blessing. Since believers are Abraham's spiritual descendants (Galatians 3:29), they are heirs to the promises God made to Abraham — including, prosperity teachers argue, the promise of material wealth. This reading ignores the context of the Abrahamic covenant, which is primarily about God's promise to create a people and bless the world through them, not about individual financial prosperity.

Atonement and material blessing. Some prosperity teachers extend the doctrine of the atonement to include material provision. Just as Christ's death secured forgiveness of sins and (in some Pentecostal traditions) physical healing, it also secured material prosperity. Poverty, in this framework, is a form of bondage from which Christ has redeemed the believer. To remain poor is to deny the fullness of what Christ accomplished on the cross.

The prosperity gospel does not merely misinterpret the Bible. It constructs an alternative religion — one in which God is a cosmic vending machine, faith is the currency, and the preacher is the broker who takes a commission on every transaction.

The Major Figures

The prosperity gospel's influence is concentrated in a network of megachurch pastors, televangelists, and media personalities whose reach extends across denominations and national borders. Joel Osteen, pastor of Lakewood Church in Houston — the largest church in the United States — preaches a softer version of prosperity theology, emphasizing positive thinking, personal empowerment, and the expectation that God wants to bless believers with "favor." His bestselling books, including Your Best Life Now, distill prosperity theology into a self-help framework accessible to audiences well beyond the Pentecostal tradition.

Kenneth Copeland, whose net worth is estimated at over $300 million, is among the most uncompromising proponents of prosperity theology. Copeland's ministry owns multiple private jets — a subject that produced one of the most revealing moments in prosperity gospel history when Copeland, in a televised conversation with fellow preacher Jesse Duplantis about his aviation fleet, explained that he could not fly commercial because he would be trapped in "a long tube with a bunch of demons."

Creflo Dollar, T.D. Jakes, Paula White, and a host of others have built enormous ministries on prosperity theology, each with their own stylistic variations but all sharing the fundamental conviction that material wealth is a sign of God's favor, that poverty is a sign of spiritual deficiency, and that the pathway from the latter to the former runs through generous giving to the ministry.

The global reach of the prosperity gospel is staggering. It is the dominant form of Christianity in much of sub-Saharan Africa, where it has been exported by American televangelists and adopted by local preachers. It is growing rapidly in Latin America and parts of Asia. In some of the poorest communities on earth, people who can barely feed their families are being told that the solution to their poverty is to give what little they have to a preacher who promises that God will multiply it.

The Biblical Problems

The prosperity gospel's biblical foundation is, upon serious examination, almost entirely illusory. The texts it cites are either taken out of context, stretched beyond recognition, or flatly contradicted by the broader witness of Scripture.

The book of Job is a sustained refutation of prosperity theology. Job's friends make precisely the prosperity gospel's argument: suffering is the result of sin, and faithfulness produces material blessing. God explicitly rejects this theology. Job's suffering is not the result of insufficient faith. It is not a problem to be solved by positive confession. It is a mystery that resists human comprehension, and God's response to Job is not an explanation but a revelation of divine sovereignty that transcends human categories of reward and punishment.

Paul's testimony in 2 Corinthians 11-12 is equally devastating to prosperity theology. Paul catalogs his sufferings — beatings, shipwrecks, imprisonment, hunger, exposure — not as evidence of spiritual failure but as credentials of authentic apostleship. His "thorn in the flesh" (2 Corinthians 12:7-10), whatever its precise nature, was a persistent affliction that God chose not to remove despite Paul's repeated requests. "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness," God tells Paul. This is the opposite of prosperity theology. God's power is manifest not in the removal of suffering but in the ability to endure it.

Jesus himself lived in poverty, owned no property, relied on the hospitality of others, and died with nothing. He warned repeatedly about the spiritual dangers of wealth. "Blessed are the poor," he said — not "blessed are the rich who gave enough to become poor before becoming rich again." "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God." "You cannot serve God and money." The prosperity gospel must systematically ignore or reinterpret virtually everything Jesus said about money in order to sustain its theology.

The Sociological Appeal

If the prosperity gospel is so theologically bankrupt, why is it so popular? The answer lies not in its theological merits but in its sociological functions.

The prosperity gospel offers certainty in a world of radical uncertainty. For people living with economic precarity — which is, globally, most of the prosperity gospel's audience — the promise that there is a reliable mechanism for escaping poverty is enormously appealing. The prosperity gospel tells people that their poverty is not the result of structural injustice, historical oppression, or the ordinary vicissitudes of life. It is the result of a spiritual deficiency they can correct. This is, in a terrible way, empowering: if the problem is your faith, then the solution is in your hands.

The prosperity gospel also offers a theodicy — an explanation for suffering — that is simple and actionable. Suffering is not a mystery. It is a malfunction. And the fix is available to anyone willing to believe hard enough and give generously enough. This theodicy is psychologically comforting even when it is theologically ruinous, because it eliminates the most terrifying possibility of all: that suffering is sometimes random, sometimes unjust, and sometimes beyond anyone's control.

Finally, the prosperity gospel succeeds because it confirms the values of consumer capitalism. In a culture that measures human worth by material success, a theology that equates material success with divine favor is culturally seamless. The prosperity gospel does not challenge the culture's values. It baptizes them.

The Damage

The damage inflicted by the prosperity gospel is both material and spiritual. Materially, it extracts money from people who cannot afford to give it, directing their resources to ministries that use them to fund the leaders' extravagant lifestyles. The people who suffer most are the poorest and most desperate — the single mother who gives her rent money because she was told God would multiply it, the cancer patient who refuses treatment because she was told her faith should be sufficient, the elderly person on a fixed income who writes checks to a televangelist because she was promised a hundred-fold return.

Spiritually, the prosperity gospel destroys faith more efficiently than any atheist argument ever could. When a person gives sacrificially, believes with everything they have, confesses positively, and still remains poor or sick, the prosperity gospel has only one explanation: your faith was insufficient. The problem is not the theology. The problem is you. This message — that God's failure to deliver on the prosperity gospel's promises is actually your failure — produces not faith but despair. It tells people that they are not good enough for God's love, and it says this in God's name.

The prosperity gospel is not a different emphasis within Christianity. It is a different religion wearing Christianity's clothes — a religion of transaction rather than grace, of manipulation rather than trust, of wealth rather than love.

The church's task is not to find a moderate version of the prosperity gospel that retains its appeal while mitigating its excesses. The church's task is to name it for what it is — a heresy that exploits the vulnerable, distorts the character of God, and replaces the gospel of grace with a gospel of commerce — and to offer in its place a theology that is honest about suffering, generous in its understanding of God's purposes, and rooted in the actual witness of Scripture rather than the financial interests of those who preach it.
excerpt: The theology that promises health, wealth, and divine favor in exchange for faith and financial gifts is among the most successful and most destructive heresies in modern Christianity.

title: When Politics Replaced Theology
body:
The standard narrative goes something like this: In 1973, the Supreme Court handed down Roe v. Wade, and evangelical Christians, roused by the slaughter of the unborn, organized politically to defend the sanctity of life. Out of this moral conviction, the Religious Right was born — a grassroots movement of people of faith who reluctantly entered the political arena because the stakes were too high for silence.

This narrative is tidy, morally flattering, and almost entirely false.

The actual history of the Religious Right's formation is more complicated, less noble, and far more revealing about the relationship between American evangelicalism and political power. It is a history in which the initial mobilizing issue was not abortion but segregation, in which the key players were not pastors but political operatives, and in which theological conviction was not the driver of political engagement but its casualty. Understanding this history is essential for anyone who wants to understand how a tradition that once prized its distance from worldly power became one of the most potent political forces in American life — and what it lost in the transaction.

The Myth of Apolitical Fundamentalism

It is often said that fundamentalist and evangelical Christians were apolitical before the late 1970s — that they retreated from public life after the Scopes Trial of 1925 and did not re-emerge until Jerry Falwell summoned them back. This is an oversimplification, but it contains an important truth. For much of the twentieth century, the dominant posture of conservative Protestantism toward politics was one of suspicion or indifference. The world was fallen, politics was worldly, and the Christian's primary obligation was evangelism — saving souls, not reforming systems.

This posture had theological roots. Dispensational premillennialism — the eschatological framework that dominated fundamentalist thought — taught that the world was in irreversible decline, heading toward a tribulation from which the faithful would be raptured before Christ's return to establish his kingdom. In this framework, political engagement was not merely unnecessary; it was theologically pointless. You do not rearrange the deck chairs on the Titanic. You get people into the lifeboats.

The political abstention was also selective. While fundamentalists and many evangelicals avoided electoral politics as a form of organized engagement, they were deeply embedded in the structures of American society — particularly in the Jim Crow South, where white evangelical churches were foundational institutions of a racially segregated social order. The idea that these communities were "apolitical" ignores the most basic insight of political analysis: the defense of an existing social order is itself a political act, even when it does not take the form of organized political advocacy.

The Real Catalyst: Race, Not Abortion

The conventional account credits Roe v. Wade as the event that galvanized evangelical political engagement. But the historical record, meticulously documented by scholars including Randall Balmer, tells a different story.

In 1971 — two years before Roe — the Southern Baptist Convention passed a resolution affirming that legislation should allow for abortion in cases of rape, incest, fetal deformity, and evidence of damage to the mother's emotional, mental, or physical health. W.A. Criswell, the conservative pastor of First Baptist Church in Dallas and a towering figure in SBC life, told the Baptist Press after the Roe decision: "I have always felt that it was only after a child was born and had a life separate from its mother that it became an individual person, and it has always, therefore, seemed to me that what is best for the mother and for the future should be allowed." The Southern Baptist Convention reaffirmed its moderate position on abortion in 1974 and again in 1976.

This is not to say that no evangelicals opposed abortion before the late 1970s. Some did, particularly those influenced by Francis Schaeffer's work. But abortion was not the issue that created the Religious Right as an organized political movement. That issue, as Balmer and others have demonstrated, was the defense of racial segregation in Christian institutions — specifically, the IRS's revocation of tax-exempt status from racially discriminatory private schools.

The story centers on Bob Jones University, a fundamentalist institution in Greenville, South Carolina, that prohibited interracial dating and marriage among its students. In 1970, the IRS began denying tax-exempt status to private schools that practiced racial discrimination. When the policy was applied to Bob Jones University, the school fought back, eventually taking the case to the Supreme Court (Bob Jones University v. United States, 1983, which the university lost 8-1). The IRS action against racially discriminatory schools — which also affected a network of "segregation academies" that white families had established across the South in response to public school desegregation — was the event that galvanized the conservative Christian leaders who would form the Religious Right.

Paul Weyrich, the conservative political operative who co-founded the Heritage Foundation and who would later co-found the Moral Majority with Jerry Falwell, was explicit about this. In remarks at a 1990 conference, recounted by the historian Randall Balmer, Weyrich stated: "What galvanized the Christian community was not abortion, school prayer, or the ERA. I am living witness to that because I was trying to get those people interested in those issues and I utterly failed. What changed their mind was Jimmy Carter's intervention against the Christian schools, trying to deny them tax-exempt status on the basis of so-called de facto segregation."

The Religious Right was not born from a moral conviction about the sanctity of unborn life. It was born from a political grievance about the federal government's interference with racially segregated institutions. Abortion was adopted later as a more palatable public justification for a movement whose actual origins could not be acknowledged.

The Architects: Weyrich, Falwell, and the Construction of a Movement

The Religious Right was not a spontaneous grassroots uprising. It was a strategically constructed political movement, assembled by political operatives who recognized the electoral potential of mobilizing conservative Christians as a voting bloc.

Paul Weyrich, a Catholic political strategist with deep ties to the conservative movement, saw in evangelical Christians an untapped political resource — a large, geographically concentrated, socially connected population that shared conservative cultural values but had not been organized politically. Weyrich and his allies — including Richard Viguerie, a direct-mail pioneer, and Howard Phillips, a conservative activist — set about building the organizational infrastructure that would turn this population into a political force.

Jerry Falwell, the pastor of Thomas Road Baptist Church in Lynchburg, Virginia, became the movement's public face. In 1979, Weyrich and Falwell co-founded the Moral Majority, an organization dedicated to mobilizing conservative Christians to vote on a platform that included opposition to abortion, opposition to the Equal Rights Amendment, opposition to homosexual rights, and support for school prayer and a strong national defense. The name itself was Weyrich's suggestion — a masterstroke of branding that implied that conservative Christians represented the majority of Americans and that their political agenda was, by definition, the moral one.

Pat Robertson built a parallel infrastructure through the Christian Broadcasting Network, the 700 Club, and eventually his own presidential campaign in 1988. Robertson's candidacy failed, but it produced something arguably more significant: the Christian Coalition, led by Ralph Reed, which became the most sophisticated grassroots political organization in the Republican Party. Reed's strategy was to embed Christian Coalition activists in local Republican Party structures — county committees, state conventions, school boards — building power from the ground up in a way that gave the movement influence far beyond its numerical size.

The result was a political machine of extraordinary effectiveness. By the early 1990s, the Religious Right was the most reliable constituency in the Republican coalition. Republican candidates could not win national elections without evangelical support, and evangelical leaders learned to convert that dependence into political influence. The relationship was symbiotic: politicians got votes; religious leaders got access, prestige, and the appearance of power.

Single-Issue Politics and the Narrowing of the Moral Imagination

One of the most consequential effects of the church's political captivity has been the narrowing of its moral agenda to a handful of issues — primarily abortion and opposition to LGBTQ+ rights — at the expense of the full breadth of biblical concern.

The Bible speaks extensively about poverty, justice, care for the stranger, the dangers of wealth, the responsibility of the powerful toward the vulnerable, stewardship of creation, peacemaking, and the priority of mercy over sacrifice. The prophetic tradition — Amos, Isaiah, Micah, Jeremiah — thunders against economic exploitation, judicial corruption, and the abuse of power. Jesus's own ministry was oriented overwhelmingly toward the poor, the sick, the marginalized, and the excluded.

The Religious Right reduced this vast moral landscape to two issues, creating what ethicist David Gushee has called a "thin" moral agenda that was conveniently aligned with the Republican Party platform on precisely the issues where it needed religious cover, and conveniently silent on the issues — poverty, healthcare, racial justice, environmental protection — where the Republican platform conflicted with the church's broader moral tradition.

This narrowing was not accidental. It was strategic. A church that took the full scope of biblical justice seriously would be an uncomfortable ally for either political party. A church that reduced its moral agenda to abortion and same-sex marriage was a perfect fit for the Republican coalition. The narrowing served the party's interests admirably. Whether it served the gospel's interests is a different question entirely.

The Cost to Prophetic Voice

The most devastating consequence of the church's political alignment has been the loss of its prophetic voice. The prophetic tradition in Scripture is characterized by a willingness to speak truth to power regardless of political consequence — to challenge kings, to confront empires, to name injustice wherever it is found, including and especially within the community of faith itself. The prophet stands outside the structures of power and speaks into them. The prophet is beholden to God, not to any political faction.

A church that has become a subsidiary of a political party cannot function prophetically. It cannot challenge the party's moral failures without jeopardizing its political access. It cannot speak against the party's candidate without fracturing its constituency. It cannot address the full scope of biblical justice without alienating the political allies on whom its influence depends. The result is a church that is prophetic about the sins of the opposing party and studiously silent about the sins of its own.

This dynamic was on full display during the Trump presidency, when evangelical leaders who had spent decades insisting on the importance of personal character in political leaders — who had excoriated Bill Clinton for his sexual immorality and declared that character was the indispensable quality of leadership — suddenly discovered that character was negotiable when the leader in question delivered on their political priorities. The spectacle of evangelical pastors laying hands on a president whose life was a catalog of the very behaviors they had spent careers condemning did more damage to the church's moral credibility than any secular critic could have accomplished.

The problem is not that Christians participated in politics. Political participation is a legitimate and important expression of civic responsibility. The problem is that a particular political movement captured the church — co-opted its language, exploited its networks, and redirected its moral energy toward partisan ends — and the church, seduced by access to power, allowed it to happen.
