The church did not enter politics. Politics entered the church. And once inside, it consumed the theology, replacing the prophetic with the partisan, the kingdom of God with the Republican platform, and the gospel of grace with a gospel of power.

The Theological Wreckage

The political captivity of the church has produced theological consequences that extend far beyond the political arena. When a church organizes its identity around political positions, those positions gradually take on the character of doctrines — non-negotiable convictions that define who is in and who is out. Opposition to abortion becomes not merely a moral position but a test of Christian faithfulness. Support for a particular candidate becomes not merely a political choice but a spiritual obligation. Dissent from the political consensus becomes not merely a difference of opinion but evidence of spiritual compromise.

This process — the theologization of politics — is the mirror image of the politicization of theology, and it is equally destructive. It produces a faith in which the boundary markers are political rather than theological, in which loyalty to the party is indistinguishable from loyalty to God, and in which the church's energy is directed not toward the formation of disciples but toward the mobilization of voters.

The result is a generation of Christians who cannot distinguish between their faith and their politics — who genuinely believe that their political positions are the direct and necessary consequence of their theological convictions, and who therefore cannot understand why anyone who shares their faith might hold different political views. This is not theological seriousness. It is theological captivity. And it is the inevitable consequence of a church that traded its prophetic independence for a seat at the table of political power.

Is There a Way Back

The path back from political captivity is narrow and costly. It requires the church to do something it has shown little willingness to do: relinquish power. It requires evangelical leaders to say, publicly and without qualification, that the church's alliance with the Republican Party was a mistake — that it produced short-term political gains at the cost of long-term spiritual integrity, and that the church's credibility cannot be restored without a decisive break from partisan politics.

This does not mean the church should be politically silent. It means the church should be politically independent — willing to challenge any party, any candidate, any movement that violates the principles of justice, mercy, and human dignity that the gospel demands. A politically independent church will sometimes align with the left and sometimes with the right and sometimes with neither, because its allegiance is not to any party but to the kingdom of God, which transcends and judges all human political arrangements.

The prophetic tradition has always been costly. Prophets are not popular. They are not invited to the White House. They do not receive standing ovations at political conventions. They speak truth that power does not want to hear, and they pay the price for it. The question before the American church is whether it wants to be prophetic or powerful — because the history of the past fifty years demonstrates, with painful clarity, that it cannot be both.
excerpt: The story of how American evangelicalism traded its prophetic voice for political power is not the story most evangelicals have been told. The real history is more revealing — and more damning.

title: Religious Trauma Is Real
body:
In 2011, a psychologist named Marlene Winell published an article in the magazine of the British Association for Behavioural and Cognitive Psychotherapies introducing a concept she called Religious Trauma Syndrome (RTS). The term described a set of symptoms she had observed repeatedly in her clinical practice among clients who had been raised in authoritarian religious environments: anxiety, depression, difficulty trusting, cognitive difficulties related to critical thinking and decision-making, a damaged sense of self, problems with social functioning, and struggles with sexuality and emotional expression.

The response from the religious establishment was predictable: dismissal, defensiveness, and hostility. Religious trauma, critics argued, was not a real clinical category. It was an invention of secular psychologists who were hostile to religion. The people who claimed to have been traumatized by their religious upbringing were simply weak, or rebellious, or insufficiently committed. The problem was not the religion. The problem was the person.

This response is itself a textbook example of the dynamic that produces religious trauma: the subordination of individual experience to institutional authority, the silencing of suffering in the name of protecting the institution, and the insistence that any critique of the system is evidence of the critic's spiritual failure. The people who most need to hear that religious trauma is real are often the people most invested in denying it.

What Religious Trauma Is

Religious trauma is the damage caused by involvement in a religious community or ideology that uses fear, shame, isolation, and control as mechanisms of authority. It is not the normal difficulty of navigating a demanding faith tradition. It is not the ordinary struggle of trying to live up to high moral standards. It is the systematic use of God, Scripture, and religious authority to manipulate, coerce, and harm — the weaponization of the sacred against the people it is supposed to serve.

Winell's framework identifies several core features of toxic religious environments that produce trauma. These include: an authoritarian power structure in which questioning is prohibited and obedience is absolute; a theology centered on fear (of hell, of divine punishment, of demonic influence); a totalistic worldview that divides reality into rigid categories of good and evil with no room for ambiguity; an emphasis on sin, guilt, and shame as primary motivators of behavior; isolation from the broader culture, which is characterized as dangerous and corrupt; and conditional love — the implicit or explicit message that belonging, acceptance, and even divine favor are contingent on compliance.

The symptoms of religious trauma mirror those of other forms of complex trauma. They include chronic anxiety (often manifesting as a persistent fear of hell or divine punishment that persists long after the person has left the community), depression, difficulty with trust and attachment, perfectionism and people-pleasing, suppressed anger, sexual dysfunction, identity confusion, and what Winell calls "black-and-white thinking" — the cognitive rigidity that results from years of being trained to sort the world into absolute categories with no room for nuance.

The comparison to other forms of trauma is not casual. Research in the psychology of trauma has established that the conditions most likely to produce lasting psychological damage are precisely the conditions that characterize authoritarian religious environments: an inescapable authority figure who is both the source of comfort and the source of threat; a system of rules that is inconsistently enforced, creating chronic uncertainty about what will trigger punishment; the requirement to suppress one's own perceptions and emotions in favor of the authority's version of reality; and the absence of any external reference point by which to evaluate one's experience, because the system claims to mediate all truth.

The power of religious trauma lies in its use of the ultimate authority — God — as the enforcer. When the source of your suffering is presented as the source of all goodness, the psychological trap is nearly inescapable.

Sources of Religious Trauma

Religious trauma can be produced by a wide range of experiences, but several patterns recur with particular frequency in clinical literature and survivor testimony.

Authoritarian leadership. In many religious communities, the pastor or spiritual leader functions with unchecked authority. Dissent is characterized as rebellion against God. Questions are treated as lack of faith. The leader's interpretation of Scripture is treated as synonymous with Scripture itself. Members who challenge the leader's authority are subjected to public shaming, removal from positions of responsibility, or expulsion from the community. In the most extreme cases, the leader exercises control over members' finances, relationships, career decisions, and daily activities — a pattern that mirrors the dynamics of domestic abuse and cultic control.

Fear-based theology. A theology centered on the threat of hell, the imminence of divine judgment, and the pervasiveness of demonic influence creates a psychological environment of chronic terror. Children raised in these environments often develop anxiety disorders that persist into adulthood. The fear is not abstract — it is visceral, embodied, and totalizing. A child who has been taught that a single unconfessed sin could result in eternal conscious torment experiences a level of existential anxiety that no child should bear. The theological question of whether hell is a legitimate doctrine is separate from the psychological question of how that doctrine functions when used as a tool of control over developing minds.

Purity culture and sexual shaming. As discussed elsewhere in this series, the purity culture movement produced widespread psychological damage through its commodification of virginity, its gendered assignment of sexual responsibility, and its treatment of sexual desire as inherently dangerous. For many survivors, the shame instilled by purity culture teachings has produced lasting sexual dysfunction, difficulty with intimacy, and a deep-seated sense of being fundamentally contaminated or broken.

The suppression of doubt. In authoritarian religious environments, doubt is not a normal part of spiritual development. It is a sin — a sign of weak faith, a foothold for demonic influence, a danger to the community. The person who doubts must either suppress their doubts (producing a chronic internal conflict between what they are told to believe and what they actually experience) or express them and face the consequences (social punishment, spiritual labeling, loss of community). Either option is psychologically damaging. The first produces what psychologists call "cognitive dissonance" at a level that can become debilitating. The second produces shame, isolation, and the loss of one's entire social world.

Exclusion and conditional belonging. In many religious communities, belonging is contingent on conformity. Members who deviate from the community's norms — in belief, behavior, identity, or lifestyle — are subjected to formal or informal exclusion. For LGBTQ+ individuals raised in communities that teach that their identity is sinful, the damage is particularly severe: they are told that the most fundamental aspect of who they are is an abomination to God, and that the only path to acceptance is the suppression or denial of their own identity. The psychological cost of this message — measured in depression, anxiety, suicidality, and self-harm — is well documented.

The Difference Between Hard Teaching and Abusive Teaching

It is important to distinguish between religious teaching that is difficult and religious teaching that is abusive. Not all demanding theology produces trauma. Not all moral rigor is harmful. The Christian tradition has always included elements that challenge, discomfort, and confront — and these elements are not inherently traumatizing. The call to take up one's cross, to love one's enemies, to forgive seventy times seven, to sell all one has and give to the poor — these are demanding teachings, but they are not abusive ones.

The difference lies not in the content of the teaching but in the conditions under which it is delivered and enforced. A hard teaching delivered in a context of genuine love, freedom, and respect for the individual's autonomy is a challenge. A hard teaching delivered in a context of fear, control, and conditional belonging is a weapon.

A church that says "we believe X, and here is why, and we recognize that this is difficult, and we will walk with you as you wrestle with it" is engaging in legitimate moral formation. A church that says "believe X or you are damned, and if you question X you will be punished, and the fact that X causes you pain is evidence of your spiritual failure" is engaging in abuse. The content may be identical. The conditions are everything.

Similarly, a community that holds high standards while also extending grace, acknowledging complexity, and making room for dissent is a demanding community but not an abusive one. A community that holds high standards while punishing those who fall short, silencing those who question, and expelling those who disagree is not demanding. It is controlling. The difference is not always easy to discern from the inside — which is precisely what makes religious trauma so insidious.

Trauma-Informed Theology

The response to religious trauma should not be the abandonment of theology but the development of a theology that is informed by what we know about trauma — a theology that takes seriously both the claims of faith and the realities of psychological harm.

A trauma-informed theology begins with the recognition that God is not the abuser. When people have been harmed in God's name, the first theological task is to separate God from the harm done by God's self-appointed representatives. This is not easy. For many survivors, the association between God and their trauma is so deep that any mention of God triggers a trauma response. Healing requires patience, gentleness, and a willingness to sit with the survivor's pain without rushing to theological reassurance.

A trauma-informed theology insists on the freedom of the individual conscience. The Reformation principle of the priesthood of all believers — the idea that every person has direct access to God and does not require a human mediator — is, at its core, a safeguard against the kind of authoritarian leadership that produces religious trauma. When this principle is taken seriously, no pastor, no teacher, no institution can claim absolute authority over another person's spiritual life. The individual's conscience, informed by Scripture, reason, and the witness of the community, is the final arbiter of their own faith.

A trauma-informed theology holds its convictions with humility. It acknowledges that all theology is human interpretation of divine mystery, and that human interpretation is always partial, always situated, always subject to correction. This is not relativism. It is honesty. And it is the only posture that prevents theology from becoming a weapon.

A trauma-informed theology prioritizes safety. It creates communities in which power is distributed rather than concentrated, in which accountability flows in all directions, in which dissent is welcomed as a sign of health rather than punished as a sign of rebellion, and in which the most vulnerable members are protected rather than exploited.

The measure of a theology is not its rigor or its orthodoxy. It is its fruit. A theology that produces fear, shame, and broken people is a theology that has failed, regardless of how correct its propositions may be.

The Path Forward

For survivors of religious trauma, healing is possible but rarely linear. It often involves therapy with a practitioner who understands the specific dynamics of religious harm — not all therapists do, and well-meaning but uninformed therapists can inadvertently minimize or dismiss the significance of the trauma. It may involve a period of complete separation from organized religion, during which the survivor learns to distinguish between their experience of toxic religion and the broader landscape of spiritual possibility. It may eventually involve a return to faith in some form — but a return on the survivor's terms, at the survivor's pace, in a community that has earned the survivor's trust.

For the church, the path forward begins with acknowledgment. Religious trauma is real. It is not a fabrication of hostile secularists. It is not the invention of people who are too sensitive or too weak for serious faith. It is the predictable, documented, empirically verified consequence of religious environments that use fear, shame, and control as mechanisms of authority. Until the church can say this clearly and without qualification, it will continue to produce the very trauma it denies.

The church that takes religious trauma seriously is not a church that has abandoned its convictions. It is a church that has examined the conditions under which it holds and teaches those convictions, and has committed itself to holding them in a way that heals rather than harms. This is not a lowering of standards. It is, by any measure that matters, the raising of them.
excerpt: For millions of people, the most damaging experiences of their lives happened in the name of God. Acknowledging religious trauma is not an attack on faith — it is a prerequisite for healing.

title: Spiritual Abuse: How Good Theology Gets Weaponized
body:
The phrase "spiritual abuse" entered public discourse through the work of David Johnson and Jeff VanVonderen, whose 1991 book The Subtle Power of Spiritual Abuse named and described a phenomenon that millions of Christians had experienced but could not articulate. Johnson and VanVonderen defined spiritual abuse as "the mistreatment of a person who is in need of help, support, or greater spiritual empowerment, with the result of weakening, undermining, or decreasing that person's spiritual empowerment."

The definition is deliberately broad, and its breadth is important. Spiritual abuse is not limited to the obvious extremes — the cult leader who demands total obedience, the pastor who sexually exploits a congregant, the televangelist who defrauds the elderly. These are genuine instances of spiritual abuse, but they are also the cases that the church finds easiest to condemn, precisely because they are so extreme. The more common forms of spiritual abuse are subtler, more pervasive, and more difficult to identify — both for the victims and for the communities in which the abuse occurs.

A pastor who uses the pulpit to shame a member who questioned his authority is engaging in spiritual abuse. An elder board that threatens a family with church discipline for raising concerns about financial transparency is engaging in spiritual abuse. A youth leader who tells a teenager that their doubts are evidence of demonic influence is engaging in spiritual abuse. A worship leader who creates an emotional environment designed to overwhelm critical thinking and produce compliance is engaging in something that, while not typically categorized as abuse, shares its essential features.

The critical insight is this: spiritual abuse does not require bad theology. It requires only an environment in which theology — any theology, including perfectly orthodox theology — is used as a mechanism of control rather than a source of liberation. Good doctrine, wielded by controlling leaders in a system without accountability, becomes a weapon. And the better the doctrine, the more effective the weapon, because the victim's own reverence for the teaching is used against them.

The Patterns: How Spiritual Abuse Operates

Spiritual abuse follows recognizable patterns that recur across denominations, theological traditions, and cultural contexts. These patterns are not accidental. They are structural features of systems that concentrate spiritual authority without adequate safeguards.

Isolation. Abusive religious systems tend to separate their members from outside relationships, information, and perspectives. This isolation may be physical (a closed community that discourages contact with non-members) or psychological (a worldview that characterizes the outside world as dangerous, corrupt, or demonically controlled). The effect is the same: the member's only reference point for evaluating their experience is the system itself. When the only people you trust are the people who are harming you, the harm becomes invisible.

Control. In spiritually abusive systems, the leader or leadership structure exercises control over areas of life that extend far beyond legitimate pastoral concern. Members may be told how to dress, whom to date or marry, what careers to pursue, how to spend their money, what media to consume, and how to raise their children. This control is presented as spiritual guidance — the leader is simply helping the member discern God's will — but it functions as the systematic removal of the member's autonomy. The member learns to distrust their own judgment, to defer to the leader's authority in all things, and to interpret their own desires and instincts as spiritually suspect.

Shaming. Shame is the primary currency of spiritually abusive systems. Members who fail to meet the system's expectations are not merely corrected; they are shamed — publicly or privately, explicitly or through implication. The shame is theological in nature: the member has not merely made a mistake; they have sinned against God, grieved the Holy Spirit, or demonstrated a deficiency of faith. Because the shame is attached to one's relationship with God rather than merely to one's behavior, it is existentially totalizing. It does not say "you did something wrong." It says "you are wrong, at the deepest level of your being."

The spiritualization of dissent. In healthy organizations, dissent is recognized as a normal and often valuable part of institutional life. In spiritually abusive systems, dissent is spiritualized — reinterpreted as a symptom of spiritual pathology. The person who questions the pastor's decision is not exercising appropriate critical judgment; they have a "rebellious spirit." The person who raises concerns about the church's finances is not being a responsible steward; they are "sowing discord." The person who expresses doubt about a doctrinal position is not engaging in honest intellectual inquiry; they are "under spiritual attack." By reframing every challenge as a spiritual problem, the system insulates itself from accountability.

The misuse of forgiveness and reconciliation. One of the most insidious features of spiritual abuse is the weaponization of forgiveness. When a leader harms a member and the harm is exposed, the member is often pressured to "forgive" — immediately, unconditionally, and without any requirement that the leader acknowledge wrongdoing, make amends, or change behavior. The theological language of forgiveness and reconciliation, which in its proper context is a profound and liberating reality, is deployed to silence the victim and protect the perpetrator. "If you don't forgive, you are the one in sin" is a statement that, in the context of ongoing abuse, functions not as pastoral counsel but as spiritual coercion.

Spiritual abuse thrives in the gap between the church's theology of power and its practice of power. The theology says that leaders are servants. The practice often says otherwise.

Case Studies: When Systems Fail

The past two decades have produced a series of high-profile cases that illustrate the dynamics of spiritual abuse with painful clarity.

Mars Hill Church in Seattle, led by Mark Driscoll, became one of the fastest-growing churches in America in the 2000s. Driscoll was a charismatic preacher whose aggressive, combative style attracted large crowds and significant media attention. Behind the public persona, former members and staff have described a culture of bullying, intimidation, and authoritarian control. Driscoll allegedly subjected staff to public humiliation, demanded absolute loyalty, and retaliated against those who challenged his authority. When a group of former elders brought formal charges of "domineering and abusive" behavior, the church's governance structure — which Driscoll had designed to concentrate power in his hands — proved inadequate to hold him accountable. The church announced its dissolution in late 2014 and formally dissolved on January 1, 2015, leaving thousands of former members to reckon with the damage.

The Institute in Basic Life Principles (IBLP), founded by Bill Gothard, operated for decades as one of the most influential parachurch organizations in American evangelicalism. Gothard's seminars, attended by millions, taught a system of hierarchical authority in which wives submitted to husbands, children submitted to parents, and everyone submitted to Gothard's interpretation of Scripture. The system's emphasis on obedience, authority, and the suppression of individual autonomy created conditions in which abuse could flourish unchecked. In 2014, more than thirty women accused Gothard of sexual harassment and molestation. The organization's board, which Gothard had personally selected and which functioned as an extension of his authority, initially defended him before eventually accepting his resignation.

The Southern Baptist Convention's abuse crisis, documented in a devastating 2022 report by the firm Guidepost Solutions, revealed patterns of institutional behavior that constitute spiritual abuse on a massive scale. Survivors who reported sexual abuse by SBC pastors and leaders were routinely dismissed, blamed, or threatened with legal action. The SBC's Executive Committee maintained a secret internal list of accused abusers while publicly opposing the creation of a database that would make that information accessible to churches. Leaders who advocated for survivors were marginalized and removed from positions of influence. The theological framework of pastoral authority and congregational autonomy — both legitimate doctrines — was deployed to shield predators and silence victims.

Why Churches Are Vulnerable

The church is not more inherently abusive than other institutions. But it possesses several structural features that make it uniquely vulnerable to abuse — and that make the abuse, when it occurs, uniquely difficult to identify, address, and heal.

First, the church claims divine authority. A corporation that mistreats its employees is behaving badly. A church that mistreats its members is behaving badly in the name of God. The invocation of divine authority raises the stakes of every interaction and makes resistance exponentially more difficult. To challenge the pastor is to challenge God's anointed. To leave the church is to leave God's community. To report abuse is to bring reproach on the body of Christ. These theological frames, whether explicitly stated or implicitly communicated, function as barriers to accountability.

Second, the church operates on trust. Members enter a church community with an expectation of safety, honesty, and care that they would not bring to a business transaction or a political affiliation. This trust is appropriate — it is, in fact, what community is built on — but it also creates vulnerability. Predators and controllers know that religious communities offer a ready-made supply of trusting people who have been conditioned to defer to authority, to give the benefit of the doubt, and to interpret their own discomfort as a spiritual problem rather than a warning sign.

Third, many churches lack adequate governance structures. In congregational polity traditions, the pastor may have no formal accountability structure beyond a board that he selected, that shares his vision, and that regards challenging him as an act of disloyalty. In hierarchical traditions, the accountability structures exist but may be designed to protect the institution rather than its members. In independent and nondenominational churches, there may be no external authority of any kind. The result, across traditions, is that leaders who are inclined to abuse have fewer structural obstacles to doing so than leaders in most other institutional settings.

Fourth, the church's theology of forgiveness and reconciliation can be weaponized to short-circuit accountability. In a healthy theological framework, forgiveness and accountability are complementary: one can forgive a person while also insisting that they face consequences for their actions and make meaningful changes to their behavior. In practice, however, the pressure to forgive often functions as pressure to forget — to move past the harm without addressing it, to restore the relationship without establishing safety, to reconcile without requiring repentance. This dynamic is profoundly destructive, and it is one of the most consistent patterns in cases of institutional spiritual abuse.

Theology That Prevents Abuse

The church does not need a new theology to prevent spiritual abuse. It needs to take its existing theology seriously.

The doctrine of human depravity — the teaching that all people, including and perhaps especially leaders, are capable of sin and self-deception — should function as a standing argument for accountability structures. If no one is above sin, then no one should be above scrutiny. The Calvinist tradition, in particular, has a robust theology of total depravity that should, if taken seriously, produce the most stringent accountability structures in Christendom. The fact that it often does not is a failure not of theology but of institutional will.

The doctrine of the priesthood of all believers should function as a safeguard against the concentration of spiritual authority. If every believer has direct access to God, then no leader can claim to be the exclusive mediator of God's will for another person's life. The pastoral role is to guide, teach, and support — not to control, dictate, or coerce. Any exercise of pastoral authority that undermines a person's direct relationship with God is, by the church's own theological standards, a violation of that person's spiritual dignity.

The example of Jesus should function as the definitive model of spiritual leadership. Jesus washed his disciples' feet. He said that the greatest among them would be the servant of all. He rebuked the disciples who sought positions of authority and power. He was accessible to the marginalized, gentle with the broken, and fierce only with the religious leaders who used their authority to burden and exclude the vulnerable. A church that takes Jesus's model of leadership seriously will produce communities in which spiritual abuse is structurally difficult — not because the leaders are perfect but because the systems are designed to prevent the concentration of unchecked power.

The antidote to spiritual abuse is not less theology. It is theology taken seriously enough to be applied to the theologians — a church that holds its leaders to the same standards it preaches to its members, and that refuses to let the language of faith become the instrument of harm.

The church that cannot name spiritual abuse cannot prevent it. The church that cannot hear its survivors cannot heal them. And the church that treats every critique as an attack will never learn the difference between a wound inflicted by an enemy and a wound revealed by a friend. The prophets were not popular. But they were necessary. And the church's willingness to listen to the prophetic voices within its own community — including the voices of those who have been harmed — is the measure of its spiritual health.
excerpt: Spiritual abuse does not require bad theology. It requires only an environment in which theology — any theology — is used to control, manipulate, and silence. The church's vulnerability to this dynamic is a structural problem, not merely a personnel one.

title: Why Young Adults Aren't Coming Back
body:
The statistics have been recited so often that they have acquired the quality of liturgy. Roughly 60 to 65 percent of young adults who were regular churchgoers in their teens disengage from church life by their mid-twenties. The decline in religious affiliation among 18-to-35-year-olds has been steeper and faster than in any other age cohort. Only about 30 percent of millennials and an even smaller percentage of Gen Z say they attend religious services regularly. The church is aging, graying, and shrinking, and the generation that should be replenishing its ranks is, with remarkable consistency, choosing not to.

The church's response to these statistics has been, for the most part, a case study in misdiagnosis. Assuming that the problem is one of presentation rather than substance, churches across America have invested heavily in aesthetic and experiential upgrades designed to make the church more attractive to young adults. Better coffee. Fog machines. LED light shows. Worship bands that sound like Coldplay. Sermon series with cinematic title sequences. Apps for everything. Pastors in skinny jeans. The operating assumption is that young adults are consumers who will attend church if the product is sufficiently polished, and that the church's competitive disadvantage is one of production values rather than credibility.

This assumption is not merely wrong. It is insulting. And it has produced two decades of strategic investment in precisely the things that young adults are not looking for, while neglecting the things they are.

The Data Behind the Departure

The research on why young adults leave the church is extensive, and its findings are consistent across methodologies and research organizations. The Barna Group's landmark study, published as You Lost Me by David Kinnaman, identified six broad themes in the reasons young adults give for their disengagement.

First, they experience the church as overprotective — creating an insular environment that shields its members from the broader culture rather than equipping them to engage it. Second, they find the church shallow — offering simplistic answers to complex questions and substituting emotional experience for intellectual substance. Third, they perceive the church as anti-science — demanding that they choose between their faith and the evidence of the natural world. Fourth, they experience the church as repressive regarding sexuality — imposing rigid rules without engaging the complexity of human sexual experience. Fifth, they find the church exclusive — unwilling to coexist with difference, unable to make space for those who do not conform to a narrow set of cultural expectations. Sixth, they perceive the church as hostile to doubt — treating questions as threats rather than signs of genuine engagement.

The Public Religion Research Institute's data tells a complementary story. Among young adults who have left religion, the most commonly cited reasons involve the church's treatment of LGBTQ+ people, its association with partisan politics, and its perceived hypocrisy — the gap between what the church preaches and what it practices. These are not complaints about worship style or programming quality. They are indictments of institutional character.

Sociologist Tim Clydesdale's longitudinal research, published in The First Year Out, found that most young adults do not experience a dramatic crisis of faith in college. Instead, they place their religious identity in a "lockbox" — setting it aside as they navigate the demands of early adulthood — and many simply never retrieve it. The church, which has long blamed secular universities for "stealing" its young people, has largely failed to reckon with the more prosaic reality: many young adults simply find that the church has become irrelevant to the life they are actually living.

What Doesn't Work

The strategies the church has deployed to attract young adults have, with some exceptions, failed — and the reasons for their failure are instructive.

The cool church strategy. The attempt to make church "cool" — through contemporary music, casual dress codes, trendy aesthetics, and culturally relevant branding — rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of what young adults are looking for. Young adults are not looking for a church that imitates the culture. They are looking for a church that offers something the culture does not. When a church invests its energy in replicating the sensory experience of a concert venue or a coffee shop, it communicates that it has nothing distinctive to offer — that its value proposition is the same as every other entertainment option, just slightly less competent. The young adult who wants a good concert will go to a concert. The young adult who wants a good latte will go to a coffee shop. The church that competes on these terms has already lost.

The personality-driven church. The megachurch model, built around the charisma and communicative gifts of a single pastor, has proven particularly fragile in its appeal to young adults. The celebrity pastor model — which concentrates spiritual authority in one individual, creates parasocial relationships between the pastor and the congregation, and measures success by attendance and platform — is precisely the model that young adults have identified as inauthentic, unsustainable, and prone to abuse. The collapse of high-profile personality-driven churches — Mars Hill, Hillsong, Willow Creek — has confirmed what many young adults already suspected: institutions built around individuals are institutions built on sand.

The apologetics approach. The assumption that young adults leave because they have unanswered intellectual objections — and that the solution is better arguments for God's existence, the reliability of Scripture, or the truth of Christian doctrine — misidentifies the nature of the departure. Most young adults who leave the church do not leave because they have been persuaded by the arguments of atheist philosophers. They leave because of what they have experienced within the church itself. A person who was shamed by purity culture, silenced when they expressed doubt, and watched their church fight against LGBTQ+ rights does not need a more sophisticated cosmological argument. They need an institution that behaves differently.

The programmatic approach. The creation of young adult-specific programs — young adult services, young adult small groups, young adult ministries with their own budgets and staffing — can inadvertently communicate that young adults are a problem to be solved rather than members of a community to be included. When the church creates a separate space for young adults rather than integrating them into the full life of the congregation, it often produces a ghetto rather than a home — a space where young adults are contained and managed rather than welcomed and empowered.

What They Actually Want: Authenticity

The word "authenticity" has been so overused in church leadership literature that it has nearly lost its meaning. But when young adults use the word — and they use it constantly — they are describing something specific and important. They are describing a community that does not perform its faith but practices it. A community where the pastor does not project a curated image of spiritual authority but speaks honestly about doubt, failure, and uncertainty. A community where the gap between what is preached on Sunday and what is practiced on Monday is acknowledged and addressed rather than papered over with better production values.

Authenticity, for young adults, is not a style. It is a substance. It means telling the truth about the church's history — including its complicity in racism, colonialism, and abuse. It means acknowledging that the church has been wrong about things and is capable of being wrong about things now. It means creating space for people to bring their whole selves — including their doubts, their struggles, and their identities — without being required to leave parts of themselves at the door.

Young adults have finely calibrated detectors for inauthenticity. They have grown up in a media environment saturated with branding, marketing, and performance. They can spot a curated image from a distance. And when they encounter one in a church — a pastor whose vulnerability is scripted, a community whose welcome is conditional, an institution whose values are selectively applied — they recognize it immediately and respond accordingly.

What They Actually Want: Justice

The generation that is leaving the church in the largest numbers has been profoundly shaped by movements for social justice. They have marched for Black lives. They have advocated for LGBTQ+ rights. They have organized around climate justice, economic inequality, immigration reform, and gun violence prevention. These are not peripheral concerns for this generation. They are central moral commitments that shape their identity and their understanding of what it means to live a good life.

When they look at the institutional church, they see an institution that has historically been on the wrong side of virtually every major justice movement — that defended slavery, resisted civil rights, opposed women's suffrage, fought LGBTQ+ equality, and denied climate science. They see an institution that, in the present, is more likely to be found opposing justice movements than supporting them. And they draw a reasonable conclusion: if the church is consistently on the wrong side of justice, then the church's claim to moral authority is not credible.

This is not to say that young adults expect the church to adopt a progressive political platform. Many young adults hold complex, non-partisan moral positions that do not map neatly onto either party's agenda. What they expect is moral seriousness — a church that cares about justice because Jesus cared about justice, that reads the prophets and takes them seriously, that sees the poor, the marginalized, and the oppressed not as objects of charity but as the people to whom the gospel is primarily addressed.

Young adults are not asking the church to be politically correct. They are asking the church to be prophetically faithful — to care about the things Jesus cared about with the same urgency and consistency.

What They Actually Want: Honesty

The demand for honesty cuts across every other concern. Young adults want a church that is honest about the Bible — that can engage the complexities of biblical interpretation without resorting to fundamentalist rigidity or pretending that every difficult text has a simple explanation. They want a church that is honest about science — that does not demand they choose between their faith and the empirical evidence of the natural world. They want a church that is honest about its own failures — that does not rewrite its history, minimize its complicity, or dismiss its critics.

They want a church that is honest about what it does not know. The posture of absolute certainty — the insistence that the church has definitive answers to every question, from the age of the earth to the mechanics of the afterlife — is not experienced as confidence by young adults. It is experienced as dishonesty. A church that says "we don't know, and we are comfortable not knowing, and we trust that God is bigger than our certainty" is far more credible to this generation than a church that claims to have every answer neatly systematized.

They want a church that is honest about doubt. Not a church that reluctantly tolerates doubt as a temporary condition to be overcome, but a church that embraces doubt as a permanent and valuable feature of a living faith. The theologian Paul Tillich insisted that doubt is not the opposite of faith but an element within it, and young adults instinctively understand this even when they lack the theological vocabulary to articulate it. A faith that cannot accommodate doubt is a faith that cannot accommodate reality. And a church that cannot accommodate reality will not accommodate this generation.

The Hypocrisy Factor, Revisited

It is worth dwelling on the hypocrisy issue, because it appears in virtually every study of young adult disengagement and because it is the factor that church leaders are most likely to dismiss. "Everyone is a hypocrite," the standard response goes. "The church is a hospital for sinners, not a museum for saints. If you leave the church because of hypocrisy, you are holding an impossible standard."

This response misses the point. Young adults are not leaving because individual Christians fail to live up to their ideals. Every human being fails to live up to their ideals. What young adults are identifying as hypocrisy is not personal imperfection but institutional dishonesty — the systematic gap between the church's public proclamations and its actual behavior, combined with the church's refusal to acknowledge that gap.

A church that preaches grace but practices judgment. A church that proclaims the dignity of every person but actively works to deny rights to LGBTQ+ people. A church that demands sexual purity from its young people while covering up sexual abuse by its leaders. A church that preaches humility while building empires of personal brand and celebrity. These are not instances of individuals falling short. They are instances of institutions behaving in ways that systematically contradict their stated values. And the church's refusal to acknowledge this contradiction — its insistence that the critics are the problem, not the behavior — is itself the most damning form of the hypocrisy they are describing.

The Question the Church Must Answer

The church has spent two decades asking "How do we get young adults to come to church?" This is the wrong question. It assumes that the church is fine as it is and that the problem lies with the young adults who are not attending. It treats young adults as a demographic to be captured rather than a generation to be heard.

The right question is: "What kind of church would young adults want to be part of?" And the answer, distilled from two decades of research, testimony, and conversation, is not complicated. They want a church that tells the truth. They want a church that practices what it preaches. They want a church that cares about justice. They want a church that welcomes doubt. They want a church that does not demand the surrender of their intellect as the price of belonging. They want a church that treats every human being with dignity. They want a church that is more interested in following Jesus than in defending its own institutional prerogatives.

None of these desires are unreasonable. None of them require the church to abandon its core convictions. All of them require the church to become more fully what it already claims to be.

Young adults are not leaving the church because they want less. They are leaving because they want more — more honesty, more justice, more authenticity, more of the Jesus they read about in the Gospels and less of the institution that claims his name while contradicting his example.

The church that cannot hear this is a church that has chosen institutional preservation over prophetic faithfulness. And a church that has chosen institutional preservation over prophetic faithfulness has already lost the generation it is trying to reach — not because that generation is faithless, but because it is looking for a faith the institution is unwilling to embody.

The young adults are not the problem. They may, in fact, be the answer — if the church has the courage to listen to what they are saying rather than devising new strategies to say it louder in return.
excerpt: The church has spent two decades trying to make itself more appealing to young adults. The effort has largely failed — not because the tactics were wrong, but because the diagnosis was.

title: Is God Real? An Honest Assessment
body:
The question is not going away. It has not gone away in twenty-five centuries of sustained philosophical inquiry, and it will not go away because a New Atheist bestseller declares it settled or because a revival preacher insists it was never really a question at all. "Is God real?" is the question that sits beneath every other question a human being can ask — about meaning, about morality, about whether the universe is the kind of place that notices us or the kind of place that does not. It deserves better than the treatment it typically receives, which is to say it deserves more than slogans, more than bumper stickers, more than the false confidence of people who have never honestly reckoned with the strongest version of the opposing case.

I am a pastor. I have staked my life on the conviction that God is real. But I have also sat across the table from enough honest atheists and enough anguished doubters to know that the question cannot be waved away with a Bible verse or a sunset. The arguments matter. The objections matter. And what we do with the space between the arguments and the objections — that matters most of all.

The Classical Arguments for God's Existence

The case for God's existence is not a single argument but a family of arguments, each approaching the question from a different angle. They do not prove God in the way a mathematical theorem proves a conclusion. But they were never designed to. They are arguments to the best explanation — attempts to account for features of reality that seem to require something beyond the natural order to explain.

The cosmological argument, in its simplest form, asks why there is something rather than nothing. Leibniz formulated it as the principle of sufficient reason: every contingent thing requires an explanation outside itself. The universe is contingent — it did not have to exist, and it has not always existed in its present form. The Big Bang, confirmed by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson's detection of cosmic microwave background radiation in 1965, established that the universe had a beginning approximately 13.8 billion years ago. If the universe began to exist, what caused it? The argument does not claim to identify this cause as the God of Christianity specifically. It claims that the existence of the universe points beyond itself to something uncaused, necessary, and sufficient to account for why anything exists at all.

The Kalam cosmological argument, revived by William Lane Craig from medieval Islamic philosophy, sharpens the point: whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore, the universe has a cause. The second premise has been challenged — some physicists, notably Lawrence Krauss, have argued that the universe could have emerged from a quantum vacuum. But as the philosopher David Albert pointed out in his review of Krauss's work, a quantum vacuum is not nothing. It is a highly structured state of affairs governed by physical laws. The question of why those laws exist, why that vacuum exists, remains unanswered.

The teleological argument observes that the universe appears to be fine-tuned for the existence of life. The cosmological constants — the gravitational constant, the strong nuclear force, the cosmological constant governing the expansion of the universe — are calibrated within extraordinarily narrow ranges. The physicist Roger Penrose calculated that the odds of the initial low-entropy state of the universe occurring by chance are on the order of one in ten to the power of ten to the power of 123 — a number so large that it exceeds the number of particles in the observable universe. Martin Rees, the Astronomer Royal, identified six numbers that, if altered even slightly, would render the universe incapable of producing stars, planets, or life. The argument does not claim that this fine-tuning proves a designer. It claims that design is a more plausible explanation than chance, particularly when the alternative — the multiverse hypothesis — is itself an extraordinary metaphysical claim that lacks direct empirical evidence.

The moral argument, advanced by C.S. Lewis in Mere Christianity and given more rigorous philosophical treatment by Robert Adams and William Lane Craig, begins with the observation that human beings experience moral obligations as objective — as binding, as real, as independent of personal preference. If moral values are objective, the argument runs, they require a ground that transcends human opinion. A universe that is nothing but matter in motion cannot generate the category of "ought." Something beyond nature must account for the fact that we experience cruelty as genuinely wrong, not merely as something we happen to dislike. The argument is not that atheists cannot be moral. They manifestly can. The argument is that the moral realism most people instinctively hold — the conviction that torturing children is objectively wrong, not merely culturally disfavored — sits more comfortably within a theistic framework than a purely naturalistic one.

The ontological argument, first formulated by Anselm of Canterbury in the eleventh century and reformulated by Alvin Plantinga using modal logic in the twentieth, argues that the very concept of a maximally great being — a being possessing all perfections in every possible world — entails that such a being exists. This argument has always been the most controversial, and the most brilliant minds have disagreed about it. Kant objected that existence is not a predicate. Plantinga's modal version avoids that objection but introduces a new question: is the premise that a maximally great being is possible itself warranted? The ontological argument is less a proof than an invitation to consider whether the concept of God is coherent — and if it is, what follows.

The Strongest Objections

The case against God's existence is not a matter of intellectual laziness or moral rebellion, whatever some apologists may claim. It is a serious philosophical position with serious arguments behind it, and anyone who dismisses it without engagement has not earned the right to their own belief.

The problem of evil remains the most powerful argument against theism. Epicurus stated it with devastating clarity in the third century before Christ: Is God willing to prevent evil but not able? Then he is not omnipotent. Is he able but not willing? Then he is malevolent. Is he both able and willing? Then why does evil exist? David Hume restated it in his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion. J.L. Mackie formalized it as the logical problem of evil: an omnipotent, omniscient, wholly good God is logically incompatible with the existence of evil. The argument hits with particular force not in the philosopher's study but in the children's hospital, at the mass grave, in the aftermath of the earthquake that buried a village. It is one thing to discuss evil as a logical category. It is another to stand in its presence.

The argument from divine hiddenness, developed by J.L. Schellenberg, asks why, if God exists and desires a relationship with human beings, so many people find no evidence of God despite sincere searching. A loving God, Schellenberg argues, would not permit "nonresistant nonbelief" — the situation in which a person is genuinely open to God's existence but cannot find sufficient reason to believe. The hiddenness of God is not merely an intellectual puzzle. It is, for many, a source of genuine anguish. They have prayed. They have searched. They have found silence. And they deserve more than the accusation that they did not search hard enough.

Naturalistic explanations for religion — the cognitive science of religion developed by scholars like Pascal Boyer, Justin Barrett, and Ara Norenzayan — offer an account of why human beings tend to believe in gods without requiring that any gods actually exist. Our cognitive architecture, shaped by evolution, disposes us toward agency detection (we see intentions behind events), toward teleological thinking (we see purposes in nature), and toward belief in minds without bodies. These cognitive tendencies, the argument goes, are sufficient to explain why every human culture has developed religious beliefs. You do not need God to explain belief in God. The explanation is in the wiring.

What We Can Know and What We Cannot

Here is what honesty requires: neither side has a knockdown argument. The classical arguments for God's existence are strong but not conclusive. The objections are serious but not decisive. The cosmological argument points to something beyond the universe, but it does not specify what. The problem of evil is devastating, but Alvin Plantinga's free will defense has shown that the logical problem of evil — the claim that God and evil are logically incompatible — does not hold. The evidential problem of evil — the claim that the amount and distribution of suffering makes God's existence unlikely — is harder to answer, but it depends on the assumption that we should expect to understand why God permits what God permits, and that assumption is itself debatable.

The cognitive science of religion explains why we are disposed to believe in gods. It does not explain whether any god is actually there. Evolutionary debunking arguments cut both ways: if our cognitive faculties are unreliable when they produce belief in God, why should we trust them when they produce belief in atheism? Alvin Plantinga's evolutionary argument against naturalism presses exactly this point. If our cognitive faculties were shaped entirely by natural selection for survival rather than truth, we have no reason to trust them in any domain — including the domain of philosophical reasoning about God's existence.

The multiverse hypothesis can explain fine-tuning without God, but at a cost: it posits the existence of an incomprehensibly vast number of unobservable universes, which is itself a metaphysical commitment of staggering proportions. Trading one unobservable reality for another is not obviously a gain in parsimony.

The Difference Between Proof and Evidence

Much of the frustration in the God debate arises from a confusion between proof and evidence. Proof belongs to mathematics and formal logic. It is deductive, airtight, and conclusive. Evidence belongs to virtually every other domain of human inquiry. It is cumulative, probabilistic, and subject to interpretation. We do not prove the guilt of a defendant; we weigh the evidence. We do not prove a scientific hypothesis; we test it against the data and judge whether it is the best available explanation. We do not prove that our spouse loves us; we live inside a web of evidence — words, actions, presence, sacrifice — that makes the conclusion reasonable.

The question of God's existence belongs to the domain of evidence, not proof. And the evidence is not all on one side. There is evidence that the universe is the product of intelligence: its fine-tuning, its mathematical elegance, its capacity to produce minds capable of comprehending it. There is evidence that points in the other direction: the gratuitous suffering of innocents, the silence of God in the face of desperate prayer, the capacity of naturalistic explanations to account for much of what was once attributed to divine action. The honest inquirer must weigh both sets of evidence and make a judgment — a judgment that will inevitably be shaped not only by logic but by experience, by temperament, by the communities in which one is embedded, and by what one is willing to risk.

This is not relativism. It is realism about the kind of question we are asking. The question of God is not a question that can be resolved by a single argument, however elegant. It is a question that must be lived into.

Why Certainty Is Not the Goal

The demand for certainty — a demand made by both aggressive atheists and anxious believers — is itself a distortion. It treats faith as an intellectual achievement rather than a posture of trust. It assumes that the goal of the inquiry is to arrive at a conclusion so ironclad that doubt becomes impossible. But this has never been the biblical model of faith. Abraham left Ur without a map. Moses argued with the burning bush. The psalms are saturated with the language of doubt, complaint, and bewildered protest. Thomas demanded to put his fingers in the wounds — and Jesus did not rebuke him for the demand. He showed up.

The philosopher Paul Ricoeur described the movement of mature faith as a passage from "first naivete" through "critical distance" to "second naivete." The first naivete is the uncritical faith of childhood — accepting what one is told without examination. Critical distance is the period of questioning, deconstruction, and doubt that dismantles the childhood faith. Second naivete is the return to faith on the other side of criticism — a faith that has passed through the fire of honest inquiry and emerged not as certainty but as trust. Trust that is deeper than certainty because it knows what it has survived.

I believe God is real. I believe it because the cosmological and teleological arguments point toward a reality beyond the material. I believe it because the moral argument accounts for the sense of obligation I cannot shake. I believe it because the historical evidence for the resurrection of Jesus — the empty tomb, the post-mortem appearances, the transformation of the disciples, the emergence of the church — is, in my judgment, best explained by the hypothesis that God raised Jesus from the dead. I believe it because I have experienced, in prayer and in the community of faith, a presence that I cannot reduce to psychology or wish fulfillment.

But I hold this belief as trust, not as proof. I hold it with the full awareness that I could be wrong — and that the willingness to be wrong is not the enemy of faith but its condition. A faith that cannot survive doubt was never faith to begin with. It was denial wearing the mask of conviction.

The question "Is God real?" will not be settled by this essay or any other. It will be settled — if it is settled at all — in the life of the person who asks it honestly, follows the evidence where it leads, and is willing to live with the weight of a conclusion that can never be fully certain. That is not a weakness. That is what it means to be human, asking the largest question a human being can ask, in a universe that does not hand us the answer key.

The gap between the evidence and the conclusion is not empty space. It is the space where faith lives — or does not. And what you do with that space will shape everything else.
excerpt: The question of God's existence deserves more than slogans from either side. It deserves the best arguments, the hardest objections, and the honesty to sit with what remains when both have had their say.

title: Why Does God Allow Suffering?
body:
The question arrives not in a seminar room but in a hospital corridor. It arrives at 2:00 a.m. when the phone rings with the news that reshapes everything. It arrives in the oncologist's office, in the aftermath of the hurricane, in the silence that follows the funeral of a child who should have outlived every adult in the room. "Why does God allow suffering?" is the most human question ever asked, and anyone who answers it too quickly has not understood the question.

I have been a pastor for fifteen years. I have sat in rooms where the question was not academic. I have held the hands of parents burying their children, of spouses burying their partners, of people whose suffering was so acute and so undeserved that any theological explanation would have been an obscenity. I will not pretend that I have an answer that makes suffering acceptable. What I have is a set of responses — philosophical, theological, biblical, pastoral — that I believe are honest, even where they are incomplete. Especially where they are incomplete.

The Problem Stated Honestly

The problem of evil is the oldest and most powerful objection to belief in God. Epicurus framed it with a precision that has never been improved upon: if God is willing to prevent evil but unable, God is not omnipotent; if God is able but unwilling, God is not good; if God is both able and willing, evil should not exist; but evil exists. Therefore, either God is not omnipotent, or God is not good, or God does not exist.

David Hume, in his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), put the argument in the mouth of Philo, the skeptic: "Is the world, considered in general, and as it appears to us in this life, different from what a man or such a limited being would, beforehand, expect from a very powerful, wise, and benevolent deity?" The answer, Hume suggested, was obvious. No one looking at the world with fresh eyes — at its earthquakes and cancers, its famines and genocides, its random cruelties inflicted on the innocent — would conclude that it was the product of a being that was both all-powerful and all-good.

J.L. Mackie, in his 1955 essay "Evil and Omnipotence," formalized the argument as a logical inconsistency. The following three propositions, Mackie argued, cannot all be true simultaneously: God is omnipotent, God is wholly good, and evil exists. At least one must be false. If God exists, God is either not omnipotent or not good. The only way to hold all three is to introduce some additional premise that resolves the contradiction — which is precisely what theodicy attempts to do.

The argument is not merely philosophical. It is existential. Fyodor Dostoevsky, in the "Rebellion" chapter of The Brothers Karamazov (1880), put it in the mouth of Ivan Karamazov, who catalogs cases of cruelty to children — a girl locked in an outhouse in the cold by her parents, a boy torn apart by a general's hunting dogs — and then delivers his verdict: even if all of this suffering is somehow necessary for the final harmony of the universe, even if it produces some ultimate good that justifies every tear, he refuses to accept it. "It's not God I don't accept," Ivan says. "It's the world he created." He returns his ticket to divine harmony. The suffering of children is too high a price.

Elie Wiesel, in Night (1960), described the hanging of a boy in Auschwitz and the whispered question from the crowd: "Where is God now?" The answer, Wiesel wrote, came from within him: "Here he is — hanging on this gallows." Whatever else one does with that sentence, one must not domesticate it into a tidy theological resolution. It is a scream.

The Free Will Defense

The most influential philosophical response to the logical problem of evil was developed by Alvin Plantinga in God, Freedom, and Evil (1974). Plantinga argued that God's omnipotence does not include the ability to do the logically impossible. Creating beings with genuine free will and simultaneously guaranteeing that those beings will never choose evil is a logical contradiction — like creating a round square. If God values free creatures — creatures capable of love, moral choice, and genuine relationship — then God must permit the possibility that those creatures will use their freedom for evil.

Plantinga's argument is widely regarded, even by atheist philosophers, as having resolved the logical problem of evil. Mackie himself acknowledged that the free will defense showed the three propositions are not logically inconsistent. But the argument has significant limitations. It addresses moral evil — the suffering caused by human choices — but it does not address natural evil: the earthquake that kills thousands, the childhood leukemia, the tsunami that does not discriminate between the guilty and the innocent. No human free will chose the tectonic plates into motion.

Some theologians have extended the free will defense to natural evil by invoking the regularity of natural law. A world in which fire warms but never burns, in which gravity sustains life but never kills, in which bacteria nourish but never infect, would be a world without consistent natural laws — and therefore a world in which rational action, scientific inquiry, and moral development would be impossible. Richard Swinburne has argued along these lines: a world regular enough to permit meaningful human action must also be a world in which natural processes sometimes cause suffering. The argument has force, but it does not comfort the parents of the child swept away in the flood.

The Soul-Making Theodicy

The soul-making theodicy, rooted in the theology of Irenaeus of Lyon (second century) and developed by the philosopher John Hick in Evil and the God of Love (1966), offers a different framework. The Augustinian tradition understood evil as a consequence of the Fall — a corruption of an originally perfect creation. The Irenaean tradition understands creation not as a finished product that was ruined but as an ongoing project in which human beings are created immature and are being shaped, through the challenges and sufferings of life, into the likeness of God.

On this view, the world is not a paradise that was lost. It is a soul-making environment — a place where courage, compassion, perseverance, forgiveness, and love can be forged precisely because they are costly. Courage without danger is not courage. Compassion without suffering is not compassion. Forgiveness without genuine offense is not forgiveness. The qualities that constitute human maturity and moral depth cannot be produced in a world without resistance, without challenge, without pain.

Hick acknowledged that this framework does not account for the worst cases — the suffering that is so extreme, so prolonged, or so pointless that it seems to crush rather than develop the soul. A child dying slowly of a degenerative disease is not being "built up" by the experience. The soul-making theodicy must not be turned into a sanctification of cruelty. It can account for the general structure of a world that includes suffering; it cannot account for every instance of suffering within that world. Hick himself ultimately appealed to eschatology — to the hope that in a life beyond this one, the process of soul-making will be completed and the suffering will be redeemed. This is a hope, not a proof. And it must be held as such.

The Protest Tradition

One of the most neglected resources in the Christian response to suffering is the tradition of protest — the biblical tradition that does not answer the question of suffering but refuses to let it be silenced.

The book of Job is the foundational text. Job is a righteous man who suffers catastrophically — he loses his children, his health, his wealth, his standing. His friends arrive and offer theodicy: you must have sinned; God is disciplining you; there is a hidden purpose. Job rejects all of it. He demands an audience with God. He insists on his innocence. He accuses God of injustice. And the remarkable thing is that when God finally speaks, God does not answer Job's question. God answers out of the whirlwind with a cascade of questions about the foundations of the earth, the habits of the mountain goat, the behavior of the Leviathan — a speech that is, depending on your reading, either a profound assertion of divine mystery or a cosmic change of subject. But the most telling detail comes at the end: God rebukes not Job but his friends. The ones who offered tidy theodicy are the ones God condemns. The one who protested is the one God vindicates.

The lament psalms — Psalm 13, Psalm 22, Psalm 44, Psalm 88 — institutionalize protest as a form of prayer. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" is not a failure of faith. It is a psalm. It is worship. It is the refusal to let go of God even in the experience of God's absence. Psalm 88 is the darkest text in the Psalter — it ends in darkness, with no resolution, no turn to praise, no note of hope. And the tradition preserved it. It included it in the hymnal. It said, in effect: this, too, is a legitimate way to speak to God.

Walter Brueggemann has described this tradition as "the costly loss of lament" — the church's gradual abandonment of the lament tradition in favor of a relentlessly positive worship culture that has no room for darkness, complaint, or protest. The result, Brueggemann argues, is a theology that cannot bear the weight of reality. A God who can only be praised is a God too fragile for the world as it actually is.

What Theodicy Cannot Do

Here is what must be said plainly, with no hedging: theodicy cannot explain a child's death to a parent. It cannot make a genocide intelligible. It cannot redeem the suffering of the Holocaust or the Middle Passage or the cancer ward by fitting it into a system. Any theodicy that claims to have "solved" the problem of evil has betrayed itself. The problem of evil is not a problem like a math problem — something with a solution that, once found, dissolves the difficulty. It is a problem like a wound. It does not want a solution. It wants a presence.

The danger of theodicy is that it can become a way of protecting God from the accusation of the sufferer — and in doing so, it becomes a way of silencing the sufferer. When a parent buries a child and a well-meaning Christian says, "God has a plan," the function of that statement is not to comfort the parent. The function is to comfort the speaker — to preserve their own theological framework from the threat that the parent's grief represents. It is, as Nicholas Wolterstorff wrote in Lament for a Son after the death of his own child, "a way of not looking at the suffering." The sufferer does not need an explanation. The sufferer needs someone willing to sit in the wreckage without explaining it away.

The Cross as God's Answer

The Christian response to suffering is not, finally, a philosophical argument. It is a person nailed to a piece of wood.

The cross is not an explanation of suffering. It is God's entrance into suffering. The incarnation — the claim that God became a human being in Jesus of Nazareth — means that God is not a distant observer of human pain. God has been inside it. God has experienced abandonment, betrayal, torture, and death. The cry of dereliction from the cross — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — is not a theological statement. It is a scream from the center of the abyss, uttered by the one who, Christians believe, is the Creator of the universe.

Jurgen Moltmann, in The Crucified God (1974), argued that the cross reveals a God who suffers — not a God who stands above suffering and permits it for mysterious purposes, but a God who enters into the deepest suffering and bears it from within. The cross does not answer the question "Why?" It answers the question "Where is God?" God is not in the observer's gallery. God is on the gallows. God is in the rubble. God is in the oncology ward at three in the morning when the morphine is not enough.

This does not make suffering acceptable. It does not make it purposeful. It does not resolve the philosophical problem. What it does — if it does anything — is reframe the question. The question is no longer "Why does God allow this?" The question becomes "What kind of God enters this?" And the Christian answer is: a God who would rather die than leave us alone in the darkness.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison cell in 1944, put it this way: "Only the suffering God can help." Not the omnipotent God who could prevent suffering but chooses not to. Not the distant God who watches from above. The suffering God. The God who is with us in it, not above it. The God who does not explain the darkness but enters it and refuses to let it have the last word.

What Remains

I do not have an answer to the problem of suffering. I have a response. The response is not a system but a set of convictions held in tension: that God is good, that the world is broken, that free will matters, that suffering can produce depth but is not justified by its products, that protest is a form of faith, that the cross means God is not a spectator, and that the resurrection means suffering is not the final word.

I hold all of these convictions while standing in a world where children die of cancer and earthquakes bury villages and the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer. I hold them not because they resolve the tension but because they are the most honest framework I have found for living inside the tension without either abandoning God or pretending the suffering is not real.

The parent who buries a child does not need my theodicy. They need my presence. They need the community of faith to sit with them in the ashes, to weep with them, to refuse to fill the silence with explanations that serve the explainer more than the bereaved. They need a faith tradition that has room for protest, for rage, for the unanswerable question hurled at heaven. They need a God who can absorb that question without flinching — who has, in fact, already absorbed it, on a cross, in the darkness, with a cry that shook the earth.

That is not an answer. It is the beginning of one. And it is all I have.
excerpt: The problem of suffering is not an intellectual puzzle to be solved. It is a wound that demands not explanation but presence — and the Christian answer begins at the cross, where God enters the wound.

title: Can You Trust the Bible?
body:
The question "Can you trust the Bible?" is asked by two very different groups of people, and they mean two very different things by it. The skeptic means: Is this ancient collection of texts reliable in any meaningful sense, or is it a repository of myths, contradictions, and outdated moral frameworks that no educated person should take seriously? The anxious believer means: Can I still hold on to this book that shaped my faith, given everything I have learned about its composition, its history, its internal tensions, and the uses to which it has been put?

Both questions deserve honest answers. But honest answers require that we first establish what the Bible actually is — not the Bible of popular imagination, whether that imagination is fundamentalist or secularist, but the Bible as it actually exists: a sprawling, multi-voiced, internally diverse collection of texts written across more than a millennium by dozens of authors in multiple languages and genres, compiled and canonized through a centuries-long process of communal discernment, and read in wildly different ways by wildly different communities for two thousand years.

The first step toward trusting the Bible is to stop expecting it to be something it never claimed to be.

A Library, Not a Book

The word "Bible" comes from the Greek ta biblia — "the books." The plural is not incidental. The Bible is a library: sixty-six books (in the Protestant canon; seventy-three in the Catholic; more in the Orthodox), written by more than forty authors over a span of roughly 1,500 years, in at least three languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek), across multiple continents and cultural contexts. It includes history, law, poetry, prophecy, wisdom literature, gospel narrative, epistolary correspondence, and apocalyptic vision. To read Genesis and Revelation as if they belong to the same genre is like reading a legal brief and a love poem as if they operate by the same rules.

The diversity of the biblical library is not a weakness to be apologized for. It is a feature to be understood. The Bible contains four Gospels, not one, and they do not always agree on the details of the events they narrate. Matthew and Luke give different genealogies for Jesus. Mark ends without resurrection appearances (in the earliest manuscripts). John includes events and discourses that the Synoptic Gospels do not mention. The early church knew this. It did not harmonize the Gospels into a single narrative. It kept all four, side by side, in a deliberate act of theological polyphony. The message was clear: the truth about Jesus requires more than one perspective to tell.

The Old Testament is similarly diverse.
