The Deuteronomistic history (Joshua through Kings) interprets Israel's story through the lens of covenant faithfulness: when Israel obeys God, it prospers; when it disobeys, it suffers. The book of Job dismantles that very framework, presenting a righteous man who suffers catastrophically and whose friends' insistence on the prosperity theology is explicitly condemned by God. Ecclesiastes pushes further, questioning whether the patterns of divine justice are discernible at all: "The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong." The Bible argues with itself. This is a sign of intellectual honesty, not incoherence.

What Inerrancy Means and Does Not Mean

The doctrine of biblical inerrancy, as articulated in the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978), holds that the Bible, in its original manuscripts, is without error in all that it affirms. This is a more careful claim than it is often taken to be. The Chicago Statement itself includes important qualifications: it acknowledges that the Bible uses phenomenological language (the sun "rises"), approximations, and literary conventions; it affirms that genre must be taken into account; it denies that inerrancy requires strict literalism.

The problem is that the popular understanding of inerrancy has little to do with the Chicago Statement. In common usage, "inerrancy" has come to mean something like "every sentence of the Bible is a factual assertion that can be verified by modern standards of accuracy." This is not what the doctrine means, and treating it as such creates problems that the doctrine's careful formulators never intended. When a believer is told that inerrancy means the Bible cannot contain any factual discrepancy, and then discovers that the accounts of Paul's conversion in Acts 9, 22, and 26 differ in their details, the result is not a deeper faith but a crisis of faith — a crisis produced not by the Bible itself but by the expectations placed upon it.

A more robust understanding of biblical authority does not require inerrancy in the popular sense. It requires the conviction that the Bible is the primary and normative witness to God's self-revelation, that it is trustworthy in its central claims about God, humanity, sin, and salvation, and that it functions as the authoritative text of the Christian community for faith and practice. This is the view held by the vast majority of Christian tradition — Catholic, Orthodox, and much of Protestantism — and it does not depend on the absence of every historical or scientific difficulty.

The Transmission Question

A common skeptical argument runs as follows: we do not have the original manuscripts of any biblical text; we have only copies of copies, separated from the originals by decades or centuries; therefore we cannot know what the originals said. This argument has a grain of truth and a mountain of distortion.

The grain of truth: we do not possess the autographs (original manuscripts) of any biblical text. The earliest complete manuscripts of the New Testament date to the fourth century — Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus. The mountain of distortion: the textual evidence for the New Testament is vastly more abundant than for any other ancient text. We have approximately 5,800 Greek manuscripts, 10,000 Latin manuscripts, and thousands of manuscripts in other ancient languages. The earliest fragmentary manuscripts — such as P52, a fragment of John's Gospel — date to within a few decades of the original composition. By comparison, the earliest manuscript of Homer's Iliad dates to roughly 500 years after its composition, and we have fewer than 2,000 manuscripts of it. No classical scholar doubts that we can reconstruct Homer with reasonable accuracy. The textual evidence for the New Testament is orders of magnitude greater.

The field of textual criticism — the scholarly discipline devoted to reconstructing the original text from the available manuscripts — has produced a New Testament text that scholars across the theological spectrum regard as highly reliable. Bruce Metzger, perhaps the greatest textual critic of the twentieth century, estimated that the New Testament text is 99.5 percent certain, and that the remaining variants affect no significant doctrine. Bart Ehrman, Metzger's student and a prominent agnostic scholar, has acknowledged the reliability of the textual tradition even while disagreeing with its theological claims.

The variants that do exist are overwhelmingly minor — spelling differences, word-order changes, the kind of scribal errors one would expect in a hand-copied tradition. The handful of significant variants — the longer ending of Mark, the Johannine Comma (1 John 5:7-8), the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) — are well known, are flagged in every modern translation, and do not affect any central Christian doctrine. The text of the Bible has been transmitted with a fidelity that is remarkable by the standards of the ancient world.

Genre Matters

The single most important skill for reading the Bible honestly is the ability to recognize genre. Poetry is not history. Apocalypse is not prediction. Parable is not journalism. Law code is not systematic theology. When Jesus says, "If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out," he is not prescribing self-mutilation. He is using hyperbole — a recognized rhetorical device — to make a point about the seriousness of moral compromise. When the psalmist writes, "The Lord is my shepherd," he is not making a zoological claim about God's profession. He is using metaphor to express trust in God's provision and care.

The creation accounts in Genesis 1-2 are a case study in the importance of genre. Genesis 1 is a highly structured, liturgical text — six days of creation arranged in two parallel triads (forming and filling), culminating in the Sabbath rest. It reads less like a scientific report and more like a hymn. Genesis 2 tells a different creation story with a different order of events (in Genesis 1, animals are created before humans; in Genesis 2, the man is created before the animals). Reading both as journalistic accounts of the same event creates an immediate contradiction. Reading them as two complementary theological narratives — one emphasizing the cosmic scope of God's creative work, the other emphasizing the intimacy of God's relationship with humanity — dissolves the contradiction and reveals the depth of both texts.

The prophetic literature is not primarily about predicting the future. It is about calling the present to account. When Isaiah says, "Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hates" (Isaiah 1:14), he is not making a prediction. He is delivering a divine indictment of a religious establishment that practices ritual without justice. Reading the prophets as a crystal ball for contemporary geopolitics — as much popular prophecy teaching does — is a fundamental misreading of the genre.

The book of Revelation, or the Apocalypse, is the most misread book in the Bible precisely because its genre is so unfamiliar to modern readers. Apocalyptic literature was a well-established genre in the ancient world, with recognizable conventions: symbolic numbers, cosmic imagery, beasts representing empires, a final confrontation between good and evil. First-century readers would have recognized these conventions instantly. Modern readers, unfamiliar with the genre, tend to read Revelation as a literal prediction of future events — an approach that produces endless speculation and very little understanding.

The Bible the Bible Actually Is

The Bible we actually have is stranger, more honest, and more durable than either the fundamentalist or the skeptic imagines. It contains genealogies that do not match, numbers that do not add up, and laws that later biblical texts modify or set aside. It includes the Song of Solomon, which is an erotic love poem, and Ecclesiastes, which flirts with nihilism. It preserves the story of David — the man after God's own heart — committing adultery, arranging a murder, and being confronted by a prophet who tells him a parable to trick him into pronouncing his own judgment. It does not protect its heroes. It does not sanitize its history. It does not resolve its tensions into a neat systematic theology.

And it has endured. It has survived the Roman Empire's attempt to destroy it, the medieval church's attempt to control it, the Enlightenment's attempt to dismiss it, and the modern church's attempt to domesticate it. It has been translated into more than 700 languages. It has shaped the moral imagination of Western civilization — its concepts of human dignity, justice, care for the vulnerable, and the equality of persons before God have become so deeply embedded in Western thought that even secular people who reject the Bible's authority often hold values that are unintelligible apart from it.

How to Read It Honestly

Reading the Bible honestly means reading it on its own terms. It means paying attention to genre, to historical context, to the literary conventions of the ancient world. It means acknowledging the tensions without flattening them and sitting with the difficulties without pretending they do not exist. It means recognizing that the Bible was written in specific historical contexts by authors who shared the cosmological assumptions of their time — a flat earth, a solid dome over the sky, a three-tiered universe — and that these assumptions are part of the cultural medium through which the theological message was communicated, not part of the message itself.

It also means refusing to read the Bible cynically. The skeptic who approaches the Bible looking only for contradictions and moral failures will find them. But this is a way of reading that refuses to hear what the text is actually saying — refuses to sit with the Sermon on the Mount, with the parable of the prodigal son, with the vision of the new heavens and the new earth, with the relentless biblical insistence that the God of the universe cares about the widow, the orphan, and the stranger. A hermeneutic of suspicion, applied without a corresponding hermeneutic of trust, is not honest reading. It is reading with a predetermined conclusion.

Can you trust the Bible? Not if you mean: can you treat it as a science textbook, a history textbook, or a systematic theology that dropped complete from heaven? No. But if you mean: can you trust it as the primary witness to God's self-revelation, as a text that has been tested by centuries of critical scrutiny and has survived, as the book that still has the power to name what is wrong with the world and point toward what would make it right — then yes. You can trust it. Not because it is simple, but because it is honest. And honest things are worth trusting, even when — especially when — they do not give us everything we wish they would.
excerpt: The Bible is not what most people think it is — defenders and critics alike. It is stranger, more varied, more honest, and more resilient than either the fundamentalist or the skeptic imagines.

title: What Christians Actually Believe About Hell
body:
Few doctrines have caused more damage to the Christian witness than the popular version of hell — the one preached from revival stages and painted on highway billboards, the one that reduces the gospel to a fire-insurance policy and God to a deity whose primary attribute is wrath. And few doctrines have been more poorly understood, even by the people who preach them most loudly. The Christian tradition has never spoken with one voice about hell. It has harbored a range of views, some of them held by the most revered thinkers in the history of the church, and the honest conversation about hell requires knowing what the options actually are.

This is not an argument for any single position. It is a map of the terrain. What you do with the map is between you and God. But you owe it to yourself — and to the people damaged by bad theology — to at least know what the tradition actually contains.

Eternal Conscious Torment: The Majority Tradition

The view most commonly associated with Christianity — and the one that has dominated Western theology since the fifth century — is eternal conscious torment (ECT). On this view, those who die without saving faith in Christ are consigned to hell, where they experience conscious suffering for all eternity. There is no exit. There is no reprieve. The punishment is infinite in duration, regardless of the finite nature of the sins committed.

The theological foundations of this view were laid primarily by Augustine of Hippo (354-430), who argued in The City of God that the punishment of the wicked is eternal in the same sense that the blessedness of the righteous is eternal — both are without end. Augustine's influence on Western Christianity was immense, and his interpretation of hell became, for practical purposes, the default position of both Catholic and Protestant theology.

Jonathan Edwards, in his 1741 sermon "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God," gave the doctrine its most vivid — and most terrifying — expression in the American context. Edwards described sinners dangling over the pit of hell like a spider held over a flame, preserved from falling only by the arbitrary mercy of a God who is under no obligation to sustain them. The sermon was a masterpiece of rhetorical terror, and it shaped American evangelicalism's relationship to hell for centuries.

The biblical case for ECT rests primarily on a handful of texts: Matthew 25:46, where Jesus speaks of "eternal punishment"; Revelation 20:10, which describes the devil being "tormented day and night forever and ever"; and Mark 9:48, where Jesus, quoting Isaiah, describes a place "where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched." Supporters of ECT argue that these texts, taken at face value, teach a punishment that is both conscious and unending.

The philosophical and moral objections to ECT are formidable. The most common objection is the disproportion between the offense and the punishment. How can a finite life of sin — even a life of extraordinary wickedness — merit infinite suffering? If a human judge sentenced a thief to an eternity of torture, we would call that judge a monster. How can we call God just for doing the same? The traditional response — that sin against an infinite God merits infinite punishment — has struck many theologians, including some firmly within the evangelical tradition, as a rationalization rather than an argument.

Annihilationism: Conditional Immortality

Annihilationism, also known as conditional immortality, holds that the unsaved do not suffer eternally but are ultimately destroyed — that the final punishment is not everlasting torment but the cessation of existence. On this view, immortality is not an inherent property of the human soul but a gift of God, granted to the redeemed and withheld from the lost. The wicked are raised, judged, punished proportionally to their sins, and then annihilated. They cease to exist.

The view gained significant attention in the evangelical world when John Stott, one of the most respected evangelical leaders of the twentieth century, cautiously endorsed it in his 1988 dialogue with David Edwards. "I find the concept intolerable," Stott wrote of eternal conscious torment, "and do not understand how people can live with it without either cauterizing their feelings or cracking under the strain." Stott argued that the biblical language of "destruction" and "perishing" should be taken at face value: the lost are destroyed, not preserved in torment.

Edward Fudge, in his exhaustive study The Fire That Consumes (1982, revised 2011), provided the most thorough biblical case for annihilationism. Fudge argued that the Old Testament consistently presents death as the final punishment for sin, not everlasting torment; that the New Testament language of "eternal punishment" refers to a punishment whose results are eternal (permanent destruction), not a punishment whose process is eternal (unending torment); and that the imagery of fire in the Bible is consistently associated with consumption and destruction, not preservation and ongoing pain.

The annihilationist position has gained significant ground in recent decades, particularly among evangelical scholars. Clark Pinnock, John Wenham, and the contributors to the Rethinking Hell project have all argued for some version of conditional immortality. The Evangelical Alliance in the UK, in its 2000 report The Nature of Hell, acknowledged annihilationism as a legitimate evangelical position, while affirming that ECT remained the majority view.

Christian Universalism: The Hope That All Will Be Saved

Christian universalism holds that God's redemptive purposes will ultimately encompass all of creation — that in the end, every human being will be reconciled to God, and hell, whatever it is, will be emptied. This is not the same as the popular caricature of universalism, which suggests that sin does not matter and everyone goes to heaven regardless. Christian universalists take sin with full seriousness. They simply believe that God's grace is more powerful than human rebellion, and that the story does not end until God's love has won every heart.

The tradition is ancient. Origen of Alexandria (c. 184-253), one of the most brilliant minds in the early church, taught apokatastasis — the final restoration of all things, including the eventual salvation of the devil. Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335-395), one of the Cappadocian Fathers and a key architect of Trinitarian theology, held a similar view, arguing that evil is by nature finite and will eventually be consumed by the infinite goodness of God. Both Origen and Gregory stood well within the mainstream of their era; the condemnation of Origen's broader theological system at the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553) was directed at other aspects of his thought, and scholars debate whether apokatastasis itself was formally condemned.

In the twentieth century, Karl Barth's theology left the door open to universalism, though Barth refused to state it as a certainty. Barth insisted that God's election in Christ is an election of all humanity — that in Christ, God has said "Yes" to the whole human race. Whether this "Yes" is ultimately irresistible, Barth would not say. He regarded universalism as a hope that must not be foreclosed, but also as a conclusion that must not be presumed, because to presume it would be to place a limit on God's freedom.

David Bentley Hart, in That All Shall Be Saved (2019), offered the most ambitious recent defense of universalism, arguing that eternal conscious torment is not merely unappealing but logically incoherent — that a God who creates beings he knows will suffer eternally cannot be called good in any meaningful sense of the word. Hart's argument is philosophical, exegetical, and patristic, drawing on the Greek Fathers to claim that universalism is not a modern invention but the deepest current in the earliest Christian tradition.

Purgatory: The Catholic Position

The Catholic doctrine of purgatory offers a fourth framework. On this view, those who die in God's grace but are not yet fully purified undergo a process of purification after death before entering the fullness of heaven. Purgatory is not a "second chance" for the damned; it is a completion of the sanctification that was begun in this life but left unfinished at death. The doctrine was formally defined at the Councils of Florence (1439) and Trent (1563), though its roots extend back to the early church's practice of praying for the dead — a practice that implies the dead are in a state where prayers can benefit them.

The logic of purgatory is, in some respects, straightforward. Most people who die in faith are manifestly not saints. They retain habits of sin, disordered loves, and incomplete transformation. If heaven is the full experience of God's presence, and if the unreformed soul is incapable of experiencing that presence fully, then some process of final purification seems necessary. The Catholic tradition locates this process after death. Many Protestant theologians, while rejecting the formal doctrine, have struggled with the same underlying question: how does a partially sanctified person become fit for the full presence of God?

C.S. Lewis, an Anglican, expressed sympathy for something like purgatory in Letters to Malcolm: "Our souls demand Purgatory, don't they? Would it not break the heart if God said to us, 'It is true, my son, that your breath smells and your rags drip with mud and slime, but we are charitable here and no one will upbraid you with these things, nor draw away from you. Enter into the joy'? Should we not reply, 'With submission, sir, and if there is no objection, I'd rather be cleaned first'?"

The Biblical Data

Part of the difficulty in the hell debate is that the biblical data is less uniform than any of the positions typically admits. The key terms themselves are complex. "Sheol" in the Old Testament is the shadowy abode of the dead — all the dead, righteous and wicked alike — and carries no connotation of punishment. It is the grave, the underworld, the place where the dead exist in a diminished state. "Hades" in the New Testament roughly corresponds to Sheol and similarly does not always carry a punitive sense. "Gehenna," the term most often translated as "hell" in Jesus' teaching, refers to the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem — a place associated with child sacrifice in Israel's history and, by the first century, with the burning of refuse. Whether Jesus intended "Gehenna" as a literal description of an afterlife destination or as a vivid metaphor for the consequences of rejecting God's reign is a matter of ongoing scholarly debate.

The "lake of fire" in Revelation 20 is explicitly identified within the text as "the second death" — language that the annihilationist reads as destruction, the traditionalist reads as eternal torment, and the universalist reads as the death of death itself. The parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31) is often cited as evidence for conscious torment after death, but parables are notoriously poor vehicles for extracting doctrinal propositions — no one argues from the parable of the prodigal son that heaven literally involves a feast with fattened calves.

Why It Matters

The hell debate is not an abstract theological exercise. How you understand hell shapes how you understand God, and how you understand God shapes everything else. If hell is eternal conscious torment, then God is a being who sustains the existence of the damned for the sole purpose of punishing them forever — a being whose justice requires infinite suffering for finite offenses. If hell is annihilation, then God is a being who respects the finality of human choices, even the choice to reject God's love, but does not perpetuate suffering beyond what justice requires. If hell is ultimately emptied, then God is a being whose love is relentless enough to pursue every soul until every soul is won.

Each view has consequences for evangelism, for pastoral care, for the way Christians treat those outside the faith. A Christianity built on the terror of eternal torment will produce a certain kind of convert — one motivated by fear rather than love, one whose relationship with God is fundamentally coercive. A Christianity built on the hope of universal redemption will produce a different kind of community — one less anxious, perhaps, but also less urgent. The stakes are not merely theological. They are human.

What I will not do is tell you which view is correct. What I will do is insist that you know what the options are — that you understand the tradition is broader, more diverse, and more internally contested than the version of hell you were probably taught. The God behind the doctrine matters more than the doctrine itself. And whatever hell turns out to be, the God revealed in Jesus Christ is a God who went to the cross to keep people out of it. That much, at least, is not in dispute.
excerpt: The Christian tradition has never spoken with one voice about hell. The honest conversation requires knowing what the options actually are — and what each one reveals about the God who stands behind it.

title: Science and Faith Are Not at War
body:
The narrative is so deeply embedded in Western culture that it feels like a fact: science and religion have always been at war, and science has been winning. The narrative has its canonical stories — Galileo persecuted by the Inquisition, Darwin demolishing Genesis, Copernicus defying the church — and its implicit moral: as scientific knowledge advances, religious belief retreats, because the two are fundamentally incompatible. One deals in evidence; the other in wishful thinking. One progresses; the other regresses. The choice between them is a choice between reason and superstition.

This narrative is largely false. It is not false because the church has always been friendly to science — it has not. It is false because the relationship between science and faith is far more complex, far more collaborative, and far more interesting than the warfare metaphor allows. The conflict thesis, as historians of science call it, was itself an invention — a nineteenth-century polemical construction that serious historians have spent the last several decades dismantling.

The Conflict Thesis and Its Collapse

The idea that science and religion are inherently at war was popularized by two books: John William Draper's History of the Conflict Between Religion and Science (1874) and Andrew Dickson White's A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom (1896). Both were enormously influential. Both were also deeply misleading. Draper and White had agendas — Draper was an anti-Catholic polemicist, and White was the president of Cornell University, which he had founded as a secular institution and needed to defend against religious critics. Their books were not dispassionate histories. They were advocacy documents dressed in historical clothing.

The conflict thesis has been rejected by virtually every serious historian of science working today. David Lindberg and Ronald Numbers, in their landmark edited volume God and Nature: Historical Essays on the Encounter Between Christianity and Science (1986), demonstrated that the relationship between Christianity and the natural sciences has been characterized far more by complexity, collaboration, and mutual influence than by conflict. John Hedley Brooke's Science and Religion: Some Historical Perspectives (1991) came to the same conclusion. The consensus among historians of science is clear: the warfare metaphor is a myth.

This does not mean there have been no conflicts. There have been real and significant episodes of tension between scientific findings and theological claims. But these episodes have been the exception, not the rule, and even the canonical examples — Galileo, Darwin — are far more complicated than the popular versions suggest.

What Actually Happened with Galileo

The Galileo affair is the founding myth of the conflict narrative: a courageous scientist persecuted by an ignorant church for daring to assert that the earth moves around the sun. The actual history is considerably more tangled.

Galileo Galilei (1564-1642) was a devout Catholic who never abandoned his faith. His heliocentric views, published in Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632), drew on the work of Copernicus — who was himself a Catholic canon, and whose De Revolutionibus (1543) had been dedicated to Pope Paul III. The Copernican system had circulated for decades without provoking significant ecclesiastical opposition. Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, the most prominent theologian of the era, had stated explicitly that if heliocentrism were scientifically demonstrated, the church would need to reinterpret the relevant biblical passages.

What turned the Galileo case from a scientific debate into a confrontation was a combination of personal politics, ecclesiastical power dynamics, and Galileo's own rhetorical missteps. Galileo's Dialogue placed the geocentric arguments in the mouth of a character named Simplicio — a name that could be read as "simpleton" — and Pope Urban VIII, who had previously been Galileo's patron, believed that Simplicio's arguments were a caricature of his own views. The prosecution of Galileo was driven as much by wounded pride and political calculation as by theological conviction. The Inquisition's condemnation was real, and it was wrong. But it was not a case of science versus religion in any straightforward sense. It was a case of institutional power, personal animosity, and theological overreach — a failure of the church to distinguish between the Bible's theological message and the cosmological assumptions of its authors.

Darwin and the Church: The Actual Record

The popular narrative of Darwin's reception is similarly oversimplified. The story usually told goes like this: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, the church reacted with horror, and the famous debate between Thomas Henry Huxley and Bishop Samuel Wilberforce at Oxford in 1860 settled the matter in science's favor. The actual history is far more diverse.

Many Christians — including prominent theologians and clergy — accepted evolution relatively quickly. Asa Gray, the foremost American botanist and a devout Christian, was Darwin's most important ally in the United States and saw no conflict between evolution and faith. Charles Kingsley, an Anglican clergyman and novelist, wrote to Darwin that it was "just as noble a conception of Deity to believe that He created primal forms capable of self-development" as to believe in special creation. B.B. Warfield, the Princeton theologian most associated with the doctrine of biblical inerrancy, accepted a form of theistic evolution — a fact that would astonish many of his modern admirers.

The Huxley-Wilberforce debate, far from being the decisive confrontation of popular memory, was actually a minor event at the time. The story was embellished and mythologized in subsequent decades, largely by Huxley's allies, to serve the narrative of science's triumph over religion. Contemporary accounts of the debate are inconsistent — witnesses disagreed about what was said, who won, and whether the exchange was as dramatic as later versions claimed.

The opposition to Darwin that did exist came not only from religious quarters. Many scientists — including figures like Lord Kelvin, who objected on thermodynamic grounds, and St. George Jackson Mivart, who offered scientific criticisms of natural selection — resisted Darwin's theory on scientific, not religious, grounds. The debate over evolution in the nineteenth century was genuinely complex. The reduction of that complexity to "science versus religion" is a distortion of the historical record.

Christians and the History of Science

The conflict thesis obscures one of the most remarkable features of the history of science: the central role that Christian institutions and Christian thinkers played in the development of the scientific enterprise. The medieval university system — the institutional framework within which modern science emerged — was a creation of the church. The University of Paris, the University of Oxford, the University of Bologna — all were founded under ecclesiastical authority in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The monks and clerics who populated these institutions were not enemies of learning. They were its custodians.

The list of scientists who were devout Christians is not a list of exceptions. It is a catalog of the founders of modern science. Copernicus was a Catholic canon. Galileo remained a Catholic throughout his life. Johannes Kepler described his astronomical work as "thinking God's thoughts after him." Isaac Newton wrote more pages of theology than of physics. Gregor Mendel, the founder of genetics, was an Augustinian friar. Georges Lemaitre, who proposed the Big Bang theory, was a Catholic priest. The assumption that scientific genius and religious belief are incompatible is contradicted by the very history of science itself.

The philosopher Alfred North Whitehead argued in Science and the Modern World (1925) that modern science was made possible by the medieval conviction, rooted in Christian theology, that the universe is rational and ordered — that it operates according to consistent laws because it is the creation of a rational God. This conviction, Whitehead argued, provided the philosophical foundation for the scientific method: the belief that the universe is intelligible, that its patterns can be discovered, and that the human mind is equipped to discover them. Without this conviction, the enterprise of science would have no warrant.

Scientists Who Believe

The claim that serious scientists cannot be serious believers is refuted by the existence of serious scientists who are serious believers. Francis Collins, who led the Human Genome Project and served as director of the National Institutes of Health, is an evangelical Christian who has written extensively about the compatibility of faith and science. John Polkinghorne, a Cambridge particle physicist who became an Anglican priest, developed a sophisticated theology of science that integrates quantum mechanics and trinitarian theology. Jennifer Wiseman, a senior astrophysicist at NASA, has spoken publicly about how her study of the cosmos deepens rather than diminishes her Christian faith.

A 2009 Pew Research Center survey found that 51 percent of scientists believe in God or a higher power. The number is lower than the general population, but it is not negligible — and it demolishes the claim that scientific expertise is incompatible with religious belief. The National Academy of Sciences includes members who are devout Christians, Jews, Muslims, and adherents of other traditions. They do not check their faith at the laboratory door.

Models for the Relationship

If science and faith are not at war, what is their relationship? Several models have been proposed, each with strengths and limitations.

Stephen Jay Gould proposed the NOMA model — Non-Overlapping Magisteria — in his 1999 book Rocks of Ages. On this view, science and religion address fundamentally different questions: science asks how the natural world works; religion asks what it means and how we should live. The two domains do not overlap, and conflict arises only when one trespasses on the other's territory. The NOMA model has the virtue of clarity, but many thinkers — both scientific and theological — find it too neat. If God created the universe, then God's creative action must have some relationship to the universe that science studies. And if science discovers features of the universe that bear on questions of meaning — the fine-tuning of cosmological constants, the emergence of consciousness — then the magisteria do overlap, whether we want them to or not.

The dialogue model, associated with Ian Barbour and others, holds that science and religion address different questions but that their answers interact and can inform each other. Scientific discoveries about the age of the universe, the evolution of life, and the nature of consciousness raise questions that theology has resources to address. Theological convictions about the goodness of creation, the value of human life, and the reality of moral obligation raise questions that science alone cannot answer. The two disciplines are in conversation, not competition.

The integration model goes further, arguing that science and theology can be woven into a single, coherent framework. Teilhard de Chardin, the Jesuit paleontologist, attempted a grand synthesis of evolutionary biology and Christian theology. More recently, scholars associated with the John Templeton Foundation have pursued research at the intersection of science and religion, exploring questions about the nature of consciousness, the fine-tuning of the cosmos, and the evolutionary origins of altruism.

No single model captures the full complexity of the relationship. What all serious models share is the rejection of the warfare metaphor — the recognition that science and faith, whatever their tensions, are not enemies but neighbors, occupying adjacent rooms in the house of human inquiry, and that the conversation between them is one of the most important conversations a thoughtful person can have.

The Questions Science Cannot Answer

The limits of science are not weaknesses. They are the boundaries of a discipline that has defined its domain with admirable precision. Science investigates the natural world through observation, hypothesis, experimentation, and revision. It does this extraordinarily well. But there are questions that the scientific method, by its own design, is not equipped to answer. Why is there something rather than nothing? What grounds moral obligation? Does life have purpose? Is the universe meaningful, or is meaning a human projection onto an indifferent cosmos? What happens when we die?

These are not failed scientific questions waiting for better instruments. They are philosophical and theological questions that require different tools — tools that include reason, tradition, experience, revelation, and the cumulative wisdom of communities that have wrestled with these questions for millennia. The scientist who says "science cannot answer that question" is not confessing a limitation. The scientist is defining a boundary. And the theologian who says "let me bring a different set of tools to the table" is not trespassing on science's territory. The theologian is working in an adjacent field where the soil is different and the methods must be different too.

The deepest mistake of the new atheism — the movement associated with Richard Dawkins, Sam Harris, Christopher Hitchens, and Daniel Dennett — was not its criticism of religion's failures, much of which was deserved. The deepest mistake was its claim that science could replace religion — that empirical investigation could answer every meaningful human question, and that any question science could not answer was therefore not a real question. This is not a scientific claim. It is a philosophical claim — the claim known as scientism — and it is a claim that most philosophers, including many who are atheists, regard as unjustified. Science is magnificent at telling us how the universe works. It has nothing to say about whether the universe matters.

The war between science and faith is not a war that needs to be won. It is a war that never existed — except in the imagination of polemicists on both sides who found it more useful to fight than to think. The actual history is richer, messier, and more hopeful than the myth. And the sooner we leave the myth behind, the sooner we can get on with the real work: asking the deepest questions about the universe with every tool we have — including both the telescope and the prayer.
excerpt: The supposed war between science and religion is not a historical fact but a nineteenth-century invention — and the real history is far more interesting than the myth it replaced.

title: Evolution and Genesis: A Pastor's Guide
body:
No topic in the conversation between faith and culture has been more badly handled than the relationship between evolution and Genesis. It has been turned into a litmus test for orthodoxy, a battleground for culture wars, and a stumbling block that has driven countless thoughtful people away from the church — not because they could not believe in God but because they were told that believing in God required them to reject the overwhelming consensus of modern science. That is a false choice, and the church should stop offering it.

I say this as a pastor, not as a scientist. My training is in theology, not biology. But I have spent enough time in this debate to know that the options are more numerous, more carefully reasoned, and more theologically responsible than most churches acknowledge. The purpose of this essay is not to tell you what to believe about evolution and Genesis. It is to lay out the terrain honestly so that you can make an informed decision — and to insist that the decision is not between faith and science. It is between different ways of holding both.

What Genesis 1-3 Actually Says

The first step in this conversation is to read Genesis 1-3 carefully, on its own terms, in its own context. This is harder than it sounds, because most of us come to Genesis with centuries of interpretive assumptions already in place — assumptions we mistake for the text itself.

Genesis 1 is a carefully structured, symmetrical text. It describes creation in six days arranged in two parallel triads. In days 1-3, God creates the domains: light and darkness, sky and sea, land and vegetation. In days 4-6, God fills the domains: sun and moon and stars (filling the domain of light), birds and fish (filling sky and sea), land animals and humans (filling the land). Day 7 is the Sabbath — God's rest. The structure is architectural, not chronological. It reads like a liturgical hymn, not a laboratory notebook.

When Genesis 1 is read alongside the other creation texts of the ancient Near East — the Babylonian Enuma Elish, the Egyptian creation accounts, the Atrahasis epic — its distinctive theological claims come into sharp focus. Unlike the Babylonian account, in which the world is created from the dismembered body of a slain goddess, Genesis depicts creation as the free, intentional act of a single God who speaks the world into being. Unlike the Mesopotamian accounts, in which humans are created as slaves to serve the gods, Genesis declares humans to be created in the "image of God" — a royal designation in the ancient world, applied in other cultures only to kings. Genesis is making claims about who God is, what humans are, and what creation means. Whether it is also making claims about how many hours the process took is a question the text itself does not obviously answer.

Genesis 2 tells a different creation story with a different sequence. In Genesis 1, the sequence is vegetation, animals, humans (male and female together). In Genesis 2, the sequence is the man, vegetation, animals, the woman. If both chapters are read as chronological accounts of the same events, they contradict each other. The early church fathers — including Origen, Augustine, and Basil — were aware of this, and none of them treated both accounts as straightforward chronological history. Augustine, in The Literal Meaning of Genesis, argued that the "days" of creation might not be ordinary days and that Christians should not make claims about the natural world that would make the faith look foolish to educated pagans. That was in the fifth century.

Young Earth Creationism

Young Earth Creationism (YEC) holds that Genesis 1-2 describes the creation of the universe in six literal twenty-four-hour days, approximately 6,000 to 10,000 years ago. The position is associated with the work of Henry Morris and John Whitcomb, whose The Genesis Flood (1961) launched the modern young-earth movement, and with organizations like Answers in Genesis, the Institute for Creation Research, and the Creation Research Society.

YEC proponents argue that the Hebrew word yom (day), when accompanied by a number and the phrase "evening and morning," always refers to a literal twenty-four-hour day in the Old Testament. They argue that the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11 provide a chronological framework that, when calculated, yields an age for the earth of roughly 6,000 years. They argue that the geological record is better explained by a global flood than by uniformitarian geology, and that the apparent age of the universe — the light from distant stars, the radiometric dating of rocks, the fossil record — is either the result of God creating the universe with the appearance of age or the product of catastrophic geological processes during and after the flood.

The scientific difficulties with YEC are substantial and well-documented. The age of the universe — 13.8 billion years, established by multiple independent lines of evidence including cosmic microwave background radiation, the redshift of distant galaxies, and the abundance of light elements — is not a marginal finding. It is one of the best-established results in all of science. The age of the earth — 4.5 billion years, established by radiometric dating of meteorites and terrestrial rocks — is similarly well-established. The fossil record documents the sequential appearance of life forms over hundreds of millions of years, in a pattern that is consistent with evolutionary theory and inconsistent with the simultaneous creation of all species. To reject these findings requires rejecting not a single scientific claim but the entire framework of modern physics, chemistry, geology, and biology.

This does not mean that people who hold YEC are unintelligent. Many are deeply thoughtful. But the scientific case against a young earth is overwhelming, and the church does itself no favors by pretending otherwise.

Old Earth Creationism

Old Earth Creationism (OEC) accepts the scientific evidence for the age of the universe and the earth while maintaining that God created the major kinds of life through direct, special creative acts. The position takes several forms.

The day-age interpretation reads the "days" of Genesis 1 as long periods of time — eons rather than twenty-four-hour days. The Hebrew word yom can refer to an indefinite period (as in "the day of the Lord"), and proponents argue that this reading is linguistically legitimate and aligns the Genesis sequence roughly with the scientific sequence of cosmic and biological history. Hugh Ross, an astrophysicist and the founder of Reasons to Believe, is the most prominent advocate of this view.

The gap theory posits a long interval between Genesis 1:1 ("In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth") and Genesis 1:2 ("The earth was without form and void"), during which the geological ages unfolded. The six days of creation in Genesis 1:3-31 describe a relatively recent re-creation or restoration of the earth. This view was popular in the nineteenth century but has largely fallen out of favor among both scientists and theologians.

The framework interpretation, developed by Meredith Kline and Henri Blocher, reads the six days of Genesis 1 not as a chronological sequence but as a literary framework — a topical arrangement that presents God's creative work in two parallel triads (forming and filling). On this view, the "days" are a literary device, not a calendar, and the question of how long creation took is simply not a question Genesis is designed to answer.

Evolutionary Creation

Evolutionary creation (also called theistic evolution) accepts the full scientific account of evolution — common descent, natural selection, deep time — while affirming that the entire process is God's chosen method of creation. On this view, God did not create each species individually by direct intervention. God created a universe with the physical laws and initial conditions necessary for life to emerge and evolve, and God sustains and directs the process through natural means. Evolution is not an alternative to divine creation. It is the mechanism of divine creation.

The BioLogos Foundation, founded by Francis Collins, is the most prominent advocate of evolutionary creation. Denis Lamoureux, a professor of science and religion at the University of Alberta, has developed a sophisticated theological framework for the position, arguing that just as God accommodated divine revelation to the scientific understanding of the biblical authors (who assumed a flat earth and a solid dome over the sky), so God accommodated the mechanism of creation to natural processes that science can investigate.

Evolutionary creationists argue that the evidence for common descent is overwhelming: the shared DNA of all living organisms, the nested hierarchy of morphological similarities, the fossil record's documentation of transitional forms, the geographic distribution of species, the vestigial structures that make no sense apart from evolutionary history. They argue that this evidence is not a threat to faith but a source of wonder — that the God who could create a universe capable of generating life, consciousness, and love through the patient unfolding of natural processes is a more impressive God, not a lesser one.

What Is at Stake Theologically

The real theological questions in the evolution debate are not about the age of the earth or the mechanism of speciation. They are about deeper matters: the image of God, the fall, original sin, and the nature of death.

If human beings evolved from earlier primates, what does it mean to say that humans are created in the "image of God"? The answer depends on what the image of God is. If it is a biological feature — a soul implanted in the first human pair at a specific moment in history — then evolutionary continuity with other species poses a challenge. But if the image of God is a relational and vocational category — the capacity to relate to God, to bear God's authority in creation, to exercise stewardship and moral responsibility — then it need not be located in a specific biological event. It can be understood as a divine calling conferred on humanity as humanity emerged into the kind of consciousness that could receive it.

The fall is a more difficult question. If there was no historical Adam and Eve, no single moment of first disobedience in a garden, what do we make of the doctrine of original sin? Several options have been proposed. Some evolutionary creationists argue that Adam and Eve were historical figures — perhaps the first members of a population of early humans whom God called into covenant relationship. Others argue that the fall is a theological description of a universal human condition — the pervasive tendency toward selfishness, idolatry, and violence that characterizes every human society — rather than a historical account of a single event. The apostle Paul's use of Adam in Romans 5 must be taken seriously, but Paul's theological point — that sin and death are universal, and that Christ is the answer to both — does not necessarily depend on a particular theory of human origins.

The question of death before the fall is also significant. If the earth is billions of years old and life has been evolving for hundreds of millions of years, then death — animal death, at a minimum — preceded any human sin. YEC proponents argue that this contradicts Romans 5:12 ("sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin"). But many scholars argue that Paul's reference is to human death, not animal death, and that the natural death of organisms is a feature of a good creation, not a consequence of the fall. Trees shedding leaves, predators consuming prey, organisms completing their life cycles — these are not evils to be explained. They are the normal operations of a living world.

How to Have This Conversation Honestly

The evolution-and-Genesis debate generates more heat than light because both sides often fight for things that are not actually at stake. The young-earth creationist fears that accepting evolution means abandoning the authority of Scripture, the reality of God's creative action, and the theological significance of human beings. These fears are understandable, but they are not warranted. One can affirm the authority of Scripture, the reality of divine creation, and the unique dignity of human beings while accepting the scientific evidence for evolution. The question is not whether God created. The question is how.

The secularist, on the other hand, often assumes that evolution disproves God — that the mechanism of natural selection, once understood, eliminates the need for a Creator. This is a philosophical claim, not a scientific one. Natural selection explains how species change over time. It does not explain why there is a universe capable of producing life in the first place, or why that universe is governed by the kind of mathematical laws that make science possible, or why consciousness emerged from matter, or why human beings experience moral obligation. Evolution is a powerful explanation of biological diversity. It is not a metaphysical system.

The church owes its people better than a false choice between faith and science. It owes them the truth: that the Christian tradition has always contained a diversity of views on how to read Genesis, that the greatest minds in the history of the church did not read Genesis 1 as a science textbook, and that the theological convictions that matter — that God is the Creator, that the universe is not an accident, that human beings bear the image of God and are called to a purpose — can be held with integrity regardless of one's view on the mechanism of creation.

What cannot be held with integrity is the insistence that Christians must choose between their Bibles and their biology textbooks. That insistence is not a defense of the faith. It is an obstacle to it. And it is time the church stopped building obstacles and started building bridges — not by abandoning theological conviction, but by distinguishing conviction from interpretation, and interpretation from the Word of God itself.
excerpt: The debate over evolution and Genesis has generated more heat than light for over a century. The path forward requires understanding what Genesis actually says, what science actually shows, and what is genuinely at stake theologically.

title: What Happened to the Historical Jesus
body:
The question of the historical Jesus is not a question about whether Jesus existed. Virtually no serious historian doubts that a Jewish teacher named Jesus of Nazareth lived in first-century Palestine, was baptized by John the Baptist, gathered followers, and was crucified under Pontius Pilate. These facts are attested not only by the New Testament but by external sources — Josephus, Tacitus, Pliny the Younger — and they are accepted by scholars across the theological spectrum, from devout believers to committed atheists. The question of the historical Jesus is a different and more difficult question: What can we know about Jesus through the methods of historical inquiry alone, and what is the relationship between the Jesus of history and the Christ of faith?

This question has occupied some of the finest minds in Western scholarship for over two centuries. The answers have been varied, contentious, and consequential. They have reshaped theology, challenged the church, and illuminated the Gospels in ways that both believers and skeptics ignore at their peril.

The First Quest: Reimarus to Schweitzer

The quest for the historical Jesus began in the eighteenth century with Hermann Samuel Reimarus, a professor of Oriental languages in Hamburg, who argued that the real Jesus was a failed Jewish revolutionary whose disciples, unable to accept his death, invented the resurrection and the entire theological framework of Christianity. Reimarus's work was published posthumously by Gotthold Ephraim Lessing between 1774 and 1778, and it ignited a firestorm that has never fully subsided.

What followed was the first quest for the historical Jesus — a movement, primarily among German liberal Protestants, that sought to strip away the theological layers added by the early church and recover the "real" Jesus beneath. The assumption was that the real Jesus was a simple moral teacher whose message had been distorted by Paul and the early church into a supernatural religion of incarnation, atonement, and resurrection. The questers produced a series of "lives of Jesus" that, with remarkable consistency, discovered a Jesus who looked remarkably like a nineteenth-century liberal Protestant — rational, ethical, undogmatic, and thoroughly modern.

Albert Schweitzer demolished this enterprise in his landmark work The Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906). Schweitzer demonstrated that the liberal lives of Jesus were exercises in projection — each scholar found in Jesus a reflection of his own ideals. But Schweitzer's own proposal was equally radical: the real Jesus, Schweitzer argued, was a Jewish apocalypticist who believed the kingdom of God was about to arrive in a dramatic, world-ending event. When the end did not come, Jesus threw himself on "the wheel of history" by going to his death, hoping to force God's hand. The kingdom did not come, and Jesus died in despair. Schweitzer's Jesus was not a comfortable figure. He was a stranger — alien, mistaken, and ultimately tragic.

Schweitzer's work effectively ended the first quest. The conclusion was sobering: the attempt to find the historical Jesus behind the Gospels had produced not the historical Jesus but a series of mirrors reflecting the assumptions of the questers.

The New Quest and the Third Quest

After a period of scholarly retreat — Rudolf Bultmann and the form critics argued that the Gospels tell us almost nothing about the historical Jesus and everything about the faith of the early church — a "new quest" was launched in 1953 by Ernst Kasemann, one of Bultmann's own students. Kasemann argued that a complete disconnection between the Jesus of history and the Christ of faith was theologically intolerable: if the church's proclamation about Jesus had no grounding in the actual person and teaching of Jesus, Christianity was built on a fiction.

The new quest developed criteria of historicity — tools for identifying material in the Gospels that likely goes back to the historical Jesus. The criterion of dissimilarity holds that a saying or action attributed to Jesus is more likely original if it is dissimilar to both the Judaism of Jesus' day and the theology of the early church (the reasoning being that the church would not have invented material that served neither its Jewish roots nor its own interests). The criterion of multiple attestation holds that material attested in multiple independent sources is more likely historical. The criterion of embarrassment holds that material that would have been embarrassing to the early church — Jesus' baptism by John (implying Jesus' subordination), his cry of dereliction on the cross, his association with sinners and tax collectors — is more likely traceable to Jesus himself, because the church would not have invented it.

The "third quest," emerging in the 1980s and 1990s, shifted the focus from these atomistic criteria to the larger question of Jesus' place within first-century Judaism. Scholars like E.P. Sanders, N.T. Wright, James D.G. Dunn, and John P. Meier argued that Jesus must be understood as a Jew operating within the social, political, and religious world of Second Temple Judaism. The third quest took the Jewish context seriously, studied the historical evidence with rigor, and produced a range of portraits that, while differing in emphasis, converged on several key points.

What Virtually All Historians Agree On

E.P. Sanders, in his influential work Jesus and Judaism (1985), identified a set of facts about Jesus that are accepted by virtually all historians, regardless of their theological commitments. These "almost indisputable facts" include: Jesus was baptized by John the Baptist. He was a Galilean who preached and healed. He called disciples and spoke of there being twelve. He confined his activity to Israel. He engaged in a controversy about the temple. He was crucified outside Jerusalem by the Roman authorities. His disciples continued as an identifiable movement after his death. Some Jews persecuted parts of the new movement.

To these, most historians would add: Jesus taught primarily in parables and aphorisms. He proclaimed the kingdom of God as central to his message. He associated with people on the margins of Jewish society — sinners, tax collectors, the poor. He was known as a healer and exorcist (whether one attributes these to supernatural power, psychosomatic healing, or legend, the reputation itself is historically certain). He clashed with some of the religious authorities of his day, particularly over matters of purity, Sabbath observance, and the temple.

These facts are established on the same grounds as other facts of ancient history — multiple attestation, contextual plausibility, and the presence of material that the early church would have been unlikely to invent. They are not articles of faith. They are conclusions of historical inquiry, accepted by scholars who disagree about virtually everything else.

The Resurrection: What Can History Say?

The resurrection of Jesus is the point at which the historical method reaches its limit — not because the evidence is lacking but because the event, if it occurred, transcends the categories that historical method is equipped to handle.

The historical data surrounding the resurrection are well-established. Almost all scholars — including skeptics like Bart Ehrman and Gerd Ludemann — accept the following: Jesus was crucified and buried. His tomb was found empty shortly after his death (the empty tomb is disputed by some scholars, but the majority position, including among non-Christian historians, is that the tomb was indeed empty). The disciples had experiences they interpreted as encounters with the risen Jesus. These experiences transformed them from a demoralized group of fugitives into a movement willing to die for the proclamation that Jesus had been raised from the dead. The church emerged in Jerusalem, the very city where Jesus had been publicly executed, within weeks of his death — a fact that is difficult to explain if the body was still in the tomb.

N.T. Wright, in his massive The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003), argued that the bodily resurrection of Jesus is the best historical explanation for the convergence of these data. Wright's case rests on two central claims: first, that the early Christian belief in resurrection was a radical mutation within Jewish resurrection belief — the Jews expected a general resurrection at the end of history, not the resurrection of a single individual in the middle of history — and that this mutation requires an adequate cause; second, that no alternative explanation (hallucination, legend, cognitive dissonance) adequately accounts for the empty tomb, the post-mortem appearances, and the explosive emergence of the church.

Bart Ehrman, in contrast, argues that the historian cannot invoke the supernatural as an explanation. "The historian has no access to miracles," Ehrman writes. Historical method, by definition, deals in probabilities, and the probability of any naturalistic explanation — however implausible — is always higher than the probability of a miracle. This is not an empirical finding but a methodological assumption: the historian, qua historian, cannot say "God raised Jesus from the dead," because that claim lies outside the scope of historical method.

The honest assessment is that history can establish that something extraordinary happened — that the disciples were genuinely convinced they had encountered the risen Jesus, that this conviction transformed their lives and launched a movement, and that the alternative explanations all have significant weaknesses. Whether that "something" was a bodily resurrection, a series of visionary experiences, or something else entirely is a question that history alone cannot answer. It is a question that requires a judgment — a judgment informed by history but not determined by it.

Jesus in Scholarly Debate

The third quest has produced multiple portraits of Jesus, each emphasizing different aspects of the evidence. Sanders emphasized Jesus as an eschatological prophet who expected the imminent restoration of Israel. Marcus Borg presented Jesus as a Spirit-filled sage and social prophet. John Dominic Crossan depicted Jesus as a Mediterranean Jewish peasant whose program was one of radical social egalitarianism. N.T. Wright portrayed Jesus as the one who believed himself to be the embodiment of Israel's God, returning to Zion to establish his kingdom. Dale Allison has recently argued that Jesus was a Jewish apocalypticist who genuinely expected the end of the world — and was wrong about its timing.

These portraits are not all equally persuasive, but their diversity illustrates an important point: the historical evidence is rich enough to sustain multiple interpretations. The Jesus of history is not a figure who can be reduced to a single category. He was a teacher, but his teaching was bound up with claims about the kingdom of God that were more than ethical instruction. He was a healer, but his healings were signs of the kingdom, not merely acts of compassion. He was a prophet, but he spoke and acted as one with an authority that exceeded the prophetic tradition. He was a Jew, rooted in the Scripture and traditions of Israel, but he related to that tradition with a freedom that scandalized some of his contemporaries.

Why the Historical Jesus Matters

The historical Jesus matters for faith because Christianity is a historical religion. It makes claims not about timeless truths but about events that happened in space and time — claims that can be investigated, tested, and debated. If Jesus was not a real person who really lived, really taught, and really died, then Christianity is a fiction. If the resurrection did not happen — if the body is still in the ground — then, as Paul wrote, "our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14). Christianity stakes everything on the claim that something happened, and historical inquiry is one of the tools we have for evaluating that claim.

But the historical Jesus is not enough by himself. History can establish that Jesus existed, that he taught and healed, that he was crucified, and that his followers were convinced he had been raised. History cannot establish that he was the incarnate Son of God, that his death was an atoning sacrifice, or that his resurrection was the firstfruits of the new creation. These are theological claims that go beyond what historical method can adjudicate. They require a response — not just an assessment of evidence but a decision about what the evidence means, a willingness to trust, a readiness to follow.

The historical Jesus matters because he keeps the church honest. He prevents Christianity from becoming a purely spiritual religion disconnected from the real world — a religion of ideas without a body, of doctrines without a life. The Jesus who sweated in the Galilean sun, who ate with sinners, who wept at a friend's tomb, who overturned tables in the temple, who cried out in anguish on the cross — that Jesus is not a theological abstraction. He is a person. And the Christian claim is not merely that he existed but that he is alive, and that everything depends on what you do with him.

That is not a historical conclusion. It is an invitation. History brings you to the threshold. What you do at the threshold is between you and the one who stands on the other side of it.
excerpt: The quest for the historical Jesus has occupied scholars for over two centuries. What they have found — and what they cannot find — matters for everyone who takes the question of Jesus seriously.

title: Miracles: Do They Still Happen?
body:
The word "miracle" carries more baggage than almost any other word in the religious vocabulary. For the skeptic, it conjures images of credulous peasants, faith healers, and the suspension of rational thought. For the believer, it conjures images of divine power breaking into the natural order — parted seas, empty tombs, water turned to wine. Both images are distortions, and the honest conversation about miracles requires setting both aside long enough to ask the real question: Is the universe a closed system in which nothing can occur that is not determined by prior natural causes, or is it open to the action of a reality beyond itself?

That is a philosophical question, not an empirical one. No experiment can determine whether the universe is open or closed. No measurement can detect the presence or absence of a God who acts. The question of miracles, at its deepest level, is a question about the nature of reality itself — and answering it requires philosophy and theology, not just science.

Hume's Argument and Its Problems

The most famous argument against miracles was advanced by David Hume in section 10 of his An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748). Hume defined a miracle as a violation of a law of nature and argued that the evidence against any miracle must always outweigh the evidence in its favor. The reasoning goes like this: a law of nature is established by uniform experience — the sun has always risen, the dead have always stayed dead, water has always flowed downhill. Testimony that a miracle has occurred must be weighed against this uniform experience. Since the regularity of nature is supported by the entire weight of human observation, while testimony for a miracle is always limited and fallible, it is always more rational to reject the testimony than to accept the miracle.

Hume's argument is elegant, but it has been challenged on several grounds. First, Hume's definition of miracle as a "violation" of natural law assumes a particular understanding of natural law — the Newtonian understanding, in which laws of nature are exceptionless regularities. But this understanding has been complicated by developments in physics. Quantum mechanics has introduced genuine indeterminacy into the foundations of physical reality. The laws of physics, as currently understood, are statistical generalizations, not iron decrees. This does not prove that miracles occur, but it undermines the assumption that the universe is a deterministic machine in which exceptions are logically impossible.

Second, Hume's argument is circular. He argues that we should reject testimony for miracles because uniform experience testifies against them. But "uniform experience" already assumes that miracles have not occurred. If a miracle has occurred, then experience is not uniform. Hume's argument works only if the conclusion is already assumed — that is, only if we already know that miracles do not happen. As the philosopher John Earman argued in Hume's Abject Failure (2000), Hume's argument is not the decisive refutation of miracles it is often taken to be.

Third, Hume's argument proves too much. If we should always prefer the more probable explanation — if testimony can never be strong enough to overcome the prior improbability of an event — then we should reject any sufficiently improbable historical event, including many that are well-attested. The emergence of life from non-living matter is extraordinarily improbable. The specific sequence of events that produced the universe in its current form is extraordinarily improbable. Yet these events occurred. Prior improbability, by itself, does not make an event non-actual.

The Biblical Category: Signs, Not Violations

The biblical understanding of miracles is different from the modern philosophical debate in important ways. The Bible does not use the concept of "violation of natural law," for the simple reason that the concept of natural law, as a fixed, autonomous system of regularities, did not exist in the ancient world. The biblical authors did not think of the universe as a machine that God occasionally overrides. They thought of it as God's creation, sustained moment by moment by God's will, in which God is free to act in ordinary and extraordinary ways.

The primary biblical category for what we call miracles is "signs" — events that point beyond themselves to the reality and character of God. When Jesus turns water into wine at Cana, the Gospel of John calls it a "sign" that "revealed his glory" (John 2:11). The point of the miracle is not the violation of chemistry. The point is what the act reveals about who Jesus is and what God is doing through him. When Jesus heals the blind man in John 9, the theological focus is not on the restoration of physical sight but on the metaphor of sight and blindness — the capacity to see what God is doing in the world.

This is not to say that the biblical authors did not believe the events actually occurred. They manifestly did. But the significance of the events, for the biblical writers, was not that they broke the rules. The significance was what they communicated. A miracle, in the biblical understanding, is not God cheating at his own game. It is God communicating through his own creation in a way that catches our attention.

The Cessationist Position

Within Christianity, the cessationist position holds that the miraculous gifts of the Spirit — healing, prophecy, tongues, and other extraordinary manifestations — ceased with the death of the apostles or with the completion of the New Testament canon. The argument, most fully developed by B.B. Warfield in Counterfeit Miracles (1918), holds that miracles served a specific purpose: to confirm the apostles as God's authorized messengers and to validate the truth of the gospel during the foundational period of the church. Once the canon was complete and the apostolic witness was established, the confirming purpose of miracles was fulfilled, and the miraculous gifts ceased.

Cessationism has been the dominant position in Reformed and dispensationalist theology. It is grounded in a particular reading of 1 Corinthians 13:10 ("when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away"), interpreted as a reference to the completed canon of Scripture. But this interpretation is disputed. Many scholars argue that "the perfect" refers not to the canon but to the return of Christ — a reading that would undermine the cessationist argument.

The Continuationist Position

The continuationist position holds that the gifts of the Spirit have continued throughout church history and remain operative today. This is the position of Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity, which represents the fastest-growing segment of global Christianity — an estimated 600 million adherents and growing. Continuationists argue that neither the New Testament nor church history supports the cessationist claim. The book of Acts does not present miracles as restricted to the apostles — Stephen, Philip, and Ananias all perform miraculous acts, and none of them are apostles. Paul's lists of spiritual gifts in 1 Corinthians 12 and Romans 12 are addressed to ordinary congregations, not to apostles, and contain no suggestion that the gifts are temporary.

Church history, continuationists argue, provides a continuous stream of miracle reports, from the early church fathers (Irenaeus, Augustine, and Gregory the Great all attested to miraculous occurrences) through the medieval period to the modern era. The cessationist claim that miracles ceased with the apostles requires ignoring or explaining away an enormous body of historical testimony.

The Evidence

Craig Keener, a New Testament scholar at Asbury Theological Seminary, published a two-volume work, Miracles: The Credibility of the New Testament Accounts (2011), that represents the most comprehensive scholarly examination of miracle claims in the modern era. Keener documented hundreds of cases of reported miraculous healings from around the world — cases attested by medical professionals, confirmed by medical records, and reported by credible witnesses. His cases include the healing of the blind, the deaf, and the paralyzed, as well as cases of recovery from medically terminal conditions.

Keener does not claim that every reported miracle is genuine. He acknowledges the reality of fraud, exaggeration, and misattribution. What he does claim is that the sheer volume of testimony — from diverse cultures, across multiple continents, attested by educated and uneducated witnesses alike — cannot be dismissed as the product of credulity or psychological manipulation. The Western academy's dismissal of miracle claims, Keener argues, is itself a cultural bias — a product of Enlightenment rationalism that assumes in advance what it claims to have demonstrated: that miracles do not occur.

Candy Gunther Brown, a professor of religious studies at Indiana University, conducted empirical studies of healing prayer, published in the Southern Medical Journal (2010), that documented statistically significant improvements in hearing and vision among subjects who received prayer. The studies were peer-reviewed and met the standards of medical research. They do not prove that God healed anyone — the improvements could, in principle, be attributed to psychosomatic factors, placebo effects, or other naturalistic explanations. But they do demonstrate that the effects of prayer are measurable and not merely imagined.

The Hardest Question: Why Not Everyone?

Any honest discussion of miracles must confront the hardest question head-on: if God heals some people, why not all? If miracles occur, they occur selectively — and the selectivity is, for many, the most devastating argument against them. The parent who prayed desperately for a dying child and received silence does not need a theology of miracles. They need an honest acknowledgment that the distribution of miraculous healing, if it occurs at all, is not fair — not fair by any standard of fairness that human beings can comprehend.

This is the pastoral reality that any theology of miracles must reckon with. The prosperity gospel — the claim that sufficient faith guarantees healing — is not merely bad theology. It is cruelty dressed in religious language. It tells the person who was not healed that the problem is their faith, adding spiritual guilt to physical suffering. It is, as the theologian Jurgen Moltmann observed, a theology that works for the healthy and the wealthy and has nothing to say to anyone else.

The honest answer is that we do not know why some prayers appear to be answered and others do not. Any claim to understand the pattern is a claim to understand the mind of God, and that is a claim that exceeds human competence. What can be said — what must be said — is that the God revealed in Jesus Christ is a God who heals and a God who suffers, and that these two truths must be held together. The same Jesus who healed the blind man also wept at the tomb of Lazarus. The same Jesus who raised the dead also died. The Christian hope is not that God will spare us from suffering. It is that God is present in the suffering, and that suffering is not the final word.

The Difference Between Demanding Proof and Remaining Open

The honest position on miracles is neither credulity nor closed-mindedness. It is openness — a willingness to evaluate claims on their merits, to take testimony seriously without accepting it uncritically, and to resist the temptation to decide in advance what is and is not possible.

The demand for proof before believing is understandable. But it can become its own form of closed-mindedness — a commitment to a particular metaphysical framework (naturalism, the closed universe) that is held with the same dogmatic certainty that the critic attributes to the believer. The person who says "miracles are impossible" is not making a scientific statement. They are making a philosophical commitment — a commitment that the universe is the kind of place in which certain things cannot happen. That commitment may be correct. But it is a commitment, not a conclusion of evidence.
