David, the man after God's own heart, wrote psalms of such raw psychological distress that any contemporary therapist would recognize the symptoms of clinical depression. "My bones wasted away through my groaning all day long," he writes in Psalm 32. "I am weary with my moaning; every night I flood my bed with tears," he writes in Psalm 6. "Why are you cast down, O my soul? Why are you in turmoil within me?" he asks in Psalm 42 — a question that names, with remarkable psychological precision, the experience of depression as a state that the sufferer can observe but not control.

Elijah, after his greatest prophetic victory on Mount Carmel, collapsed into a depression so severe that he asked God to take his life. "It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life," he said in 1 Kings 19. God's response is instructive. God did not rebuke Elijah for lack of faith. God did not deliver a sermon on the sin of despair. God sent an angel with food and water and told Elijah to sleep. God addressed the physical needs of the prophet's body before addressing the spiritual needs of his soul. The first act of divine care for a depressed man was not a Bible study. It was a meal and a nap.

Jeremiah, the weeping prophet, expressed such sustained anguish that his writings have given the English language the word "jeremiad." "Cursed be the day on which I was born," he wrote in Jeremiah 20:14 — a statement that, in a contemporary church context, would likely prompt a referral to the pastor rather than inclusion in the canon of Scripture. Job sat in ashes and cursed the day of his birth. Jonah asked God to kill him. The psalmist in Psalm 88 — the darkest psalm in the Psalter — ends without resolution, without comfort, without the expected turn to hope. "Darkness is my closest friend," it concludes. The Bible includes that psalm. The church should learn from its inclusion.

The biblical witness does not treat mental anguish as a moral failing. It treats it as a human reality — one that can coexist with deep faith, prophetic calling, and intimate relationship with God. The church's insistence on treating mental illness as a spiritual deficiency is not a biblical position. It is a betrayal of the Bible's own testimony.

The God who sent an angel with bread for a suicidal prophet did not ask Elijah to pray harder. The church should take the hint.

Trauma-Informed Ministry

Trauma-informed ministry begins with a simple recognition: a significant number of the people sitting in church pews on any given Sunday are carrying the effects of traumatic experiences — abuse, neglect, violence, loss, abandonment, betrayal — that shape how they hear the gospel, how they experience community, and how they relate to God. A church that is not aware of this reality will inadvertently retraumatize the people it is trying to help.

Consider the standard evangelical altar call. A preacher asks people to come forward, publicly, in front of the entire congregation, to confess their brokenness and surrender to God. For many people, this is a meaningful and genuine spiritual experience. For a survivor of sexual abuse — for whom public vulnerability was precisely the mechanism of their violation — this invitation may trigger a trauma response. The church, without knowing it, has reenacted the dynamics of the survivor's abuse in a spiritual register.

Trauma-informed ministry does not abandon the gospel. It delivers the gospel with awareness of how it will be received by wounded people. It trains pastors and lay leaders to recognize the signs of trauma. It creates multiple pathways for response that do not require public vulnerability. It ensures that counseling ministries are staffed by people with actual training, not merely good intentions. It maintains clear boundaries around confidentiality, physical contact, and the use of authority. It recognizes that spiritual care and clinical care are partners, not competitors, and it builds relationships with licensed mental health professionals to whom it can refer people whose needs exceed its competence.

This is not a capitulation to secular psychology. It is an application of the biblical mandate to love one's neighbor — a mandate that requires caring enough about the neighbor's actual experience to learn how to help without doing harm.

Becoming Places of Healing

The church has the potential to be one of the most powerful resources for mental health in American life. It has what no clinical practice can offer: a sustained community of care that extends beyond the fifty-minute therapeutic hour, a framework of meaning that addresses the existential dimensions of suffering, rituals and practices that orient the sufferer toward hope without demanding premature resolution, and a theological tradition that insists — against every culture of toxic positivity — that suffering is real, that lament is faithful, and that God is present in the darkness.

To realize this potential, the church must first do no harm. It must stop treating mental illness as a spiritual failing. It must stop offering spiritual solutions to clinical problems. It must stop stigmatizing therapy, medication, and professional mental health care. It must stop pretending that prayer and Bible study are sufficient responses to clinical depression, anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, PTSD, and the full spectrum of mental health conditions that affect its members.

Then it must take positive steps. Train pastoral staff in mental health first aid. Build relationships with licensed therapists and counselors in the community. Create support groups for people living with mental illness and their families. Preach honestly about mental health — not as a special topic for a designated Sunday but as an integrated dimension of the church's ongoing pastoral care. Normalize the language of mental health in the same way the church has normalized the language of physical health. When someone says, "I am seeing a therapist," the response should be the same as when someone says, "I am seeing a doctor": support, not suspicion.

The church that tells a depressed person to pray harder is not exercising spiritual authority. It is exercising spiritual malpractice. And the most faithful thing it can do — the thing most consistent with the example of a God who sent bread to a suicidal prophet and let the darkest psalm stand in the canon without resolution — is to sit with the suffering, take it seriously, and offer every resource available to address it. Spiritual and clinical. Prayer and treatment. Community and competence. The whole response for the whole person.

That is not a compromise of faith. It is faith doing what faith is for.
excerpt: The church that tells a depressed person to pray harder is not offering spiritual counsel. It is practicing spiritual malpractice. And the Bible it claims to follow knows better.

title: Toxic Masculinity in the Pulpit
body:
In 2006, Mark Driscoll stood before a conference of pastors and declared that the problem with the American church was that it had become too feminine. The church needed men, he argued — real men, tough men, men who would fight and lead and dominate. He mocked pastors who were gentle, who wept, who preferred diplomacy to confrontation. He described Jesus as a cage fighter, an alpha male, a warrior who would return at the end of days to deliver divine violence. The message was clear: godly manhood was aggressive, confrontational, and unapologetically dominant. Anything else was weakness. Anything else was feminization. Anything else was failure.

Driscoll was not an outlier. He was the loudest voice in a movement that had been building for decades — a movement that defined masculinity in terms of power, authority, and control, and that located these qualities at the center of God's design for men. John Eldredge's Wild at Heart, published in 2001 and eventually selling over four million copies, told men that they were designed to be warriors, adventurers, and rescuers — and that the modern church, with its emphasis on gentleness, servanthood, and emotional vulnerability, had stolen their masculine identity. The Council on Biblical Manhood and Womanhood, founded in 1987, codified a vision of gender in which male leadership and female submission were presented as the eternal, unchangeable order of creation.

The result was a theology of masculinity that bore almost no resemblance to the man at the center of the Christian story. It looked, instead, remarkably like the cultural ideal of the American alpha male — competitive, dominant, emotionally controlled, sexually aggressive — dressed in theological clothing and marketed as God's original design.

The Driscoll Playbook

Mark Driscoll built Mars Hill Church in Seattle from a handful of people meeting in a living room to over fourteen thousand weekly attendees in fifteen years. His appeal was concentrated among young men — a demographic that most churches struggled to reach. He succeeded by offering them a Christianity that affirmed the version of masculinity they already held: aggressive, competitive, uncompromising, and contemptuous of softness in any form.

Driscoll's preaching was laced with the language of domination. He publicly humiliated men he considered insufficiently masculine. He described stay-at-home fathers as failures. He joked about men who displayed emotion. He wielded theological authority as a weapon, framing disagreement with his leadership as rebellion against God. Former elders and staff members have described a culture of intimidation, bullying, and spiritual coercion in which Driscoll's word was effectively law and dissent was treated as disloyalty.

The Mars Hill experiment ended in 2014, when the accumulated weight of Driscoll's behavior — plagiarism, financial impropriety, bullying, abuse of authority — finally exceeded what the institution could sustain. The church dissolved. Its campuses closed. Thousands of members were scattered, many of them deeply wounded by an experience they had been told was biblical Christianity.

But Driscoll did not disappear. He moved to Arizona and planted a new church, which grew rapidly. The market for his version of masculinity had not diminished. It had, if anything, expanded — fueled by a broader cultural anxiety about masculinity that Driscoll was positioned to exploit. The pattern repeated itself, with new allegations of authoritarian leadership, staff abuse, and institutional control emerging from the new church. The product had not changed. It did not need to. The demand was still there.

The Warrior-Poet Myth

Eldredge's Wild at Heart offered a softer version of the same essential message. Men, Eldredge argued, are hardwired for three things: a battle to fight, an adventure to live, and a beauty to rescue. These desires are not cultural constructions but divine implants — the fingerprints of God on the male soul. The modern church, Eldredge argued, had domesticated men, turning them into "really nice guys" who had lost touch with their primal masculine energy.

The appeal is understandable. Many men in the church do feel that their experience is not reflected in the prevailing culture of evangelical Christianity — a culture that often emphasizes emotional expression, relational intimacy, and gentle compliance in ways that feel foreign to their lived experience of masculinity. Eldredge gave these men permission to be something other than domesticated — to embrace risk, physicality, and strength as features, not bugs, of their masculine design.

The problem is not the affirmation of masculine energy per se. The problem is the definition of masculine energy that Eldredge assumes. The warrior-poet framework draws its vision of manhood not from the life of Christ but from romantic mythology, Hollywood action narratives, and Jungian archetypes. The "battle" is framed in terms of conquest and competition. The "adventure" is framed in terms of individual heroism. The "beauty" is framed in terms of rescue — positioning women as objects to be saved rather than agents in their own right. The entire framework is self-referential: it centers male experience, male desire, and male self-actualization. The other — whether woman, neighbor, or God — exists primarily as a mirror for the man's heroic arc.

Jesus does not appear in this framework except as an afterthought — a divine endorsement of the masculine ideal the author has already constructed. And the Jesus who does appear is selectively edited: the Jesus who overturned tables makes the cut, but the Jesus who washed feet does not. The Jesus who confronted the Pharisees makes the cut, but the Jesus who wept at Lazarus's tomb is treated as an anomaly rather than a revelation.

What Biblical Manhood Actually Looks Like

The New Testament presents a vision of manhood that is, by the standards of both first-century Mediterranean culture and twenty-first-century American culture, profoundly countercultural. It does not affirm the alpha-male ideal. It crucifies it.

Jesus wept. Publicly. At the tomb of a friend. In a culture where male tears were a sign of weakness, Jesus wept without apology, without explanation, without the macho caveat that he was only crying because he was about to do something powerful. He wept because his friend was dead and grief was the appropriate response to death. The Son of God modeled emotional vulnerability as an expression of strength, not a lapse from it.

Jesus washed feet. The act of a slave — the lowest act of service in the ancient household — performed by the one who held all authority. He knelt before his disciples, took off his outer garment, and did the work that no self-respecting man would do. And when Peter objected — when Peter displayed the masculine instinct to refuse the humiliation of being served — Jesus told him that unless he accepted it, he had no part in the kingdom. The kingdom's definition of greatness was not power exercised over others but service rendered to others. "The greatest among you shall be your servant," Jesus said. He was not speaking metaphorically.

Jesus refused violence. In the Garden of Gethsemane, when Peter drew a sword to defend him, Jesus told him to put it away. "Those who live by the sword will die by the sword." He submitted to arrest, trial, torture, and execution without resistance — not because he lacked power but because the kingdom he embodied operated on fundamentally different terms than the kingdoms of the world. The cross is not a warrior's victory. It is a servant's sacrifice. And it is the central symbol of the faith that the toxic masculinity movement claims to represent.

Paul's vision of manhood is consistent with Jesus' example. The fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control — reads like a deliberate inversion of the warrior-male ideal. Gentleness is listed as a spiritual virtue, not a feminine weakness. Self-control is valued over aggression. Patience is prized over decisive action. The man shaped by the Spirit looks nothing like the man shaped by the Driscoll playbook. He looks, instead, like someone whose strength is expressed in service, whose authority is exercised in humility, and whose courage is demonstrated not in domination but in vulnerability.

The church does not need more alpha males. It needs more men willing to do what Jesus did: kneel, serve, weep, and absorb the world's violence rather than return it.

The Damage Done

The toxic masculinity movement in the church has caused damage in every direction. It has damaged women, who have been told that their role is to submit, support, and admire — and that resistance to male authority is resistance to God. Women in churches shaped by this theology report feeling invisible, silenced, and instrumentalized — valued for their compliance rather than their gifts, their beauty rather than their wisdom, their willingness to serve male vision rather than their capacity to lead in their own right.

It has damaged men, who have been given a vision of manhood that is impossible to sustain without constant performance and self-suppression. Men who do not fit the alpha-male template — men who are gentle, artistic, emotionally expressive, contemplative — are made to feel that their masculinity is deficient, that they are not the men God designed them to be. The suicide rate among men, the epidemic of male loneliness, the crisis of male emotional illiteracy — these are not unrelated to a cultural and religious framework that tells men their value lies in dominance and their vulnerability is weakness.

It has damaged families, where the theology of male headship has been used to justify patterns of control, emotional abuse, and domestic violence. Not every complementarian household is abusive. But a theology that locates final authority in the husband and frames wifely submission as a divine mandate provides structural cover for abuse when it occurs. The wife who questions her husband's authority can be told she is disobeying God. The husband who controls his wife can frame his control as spiritual leadership. The children who grow up in these households learn that power is gendered, that authority flows in one direction, and that the strongest person in the room is, by definition, the one God has placed in charge.

It has damaged the church's witness. A church that preaches a gospel of sacrificial love while modeling a culture of masculine domination is not merely inconsistent. It is unintelligible. The watching world sees the contradiction even when the church does not. And the watching world draws the obvious conclusion: the church's gospel is not powerful enough to transform its own culture.

Healthy Masculinity in Pastoral Leadership

Healthy masculinity in the pulpit does not require the abandonment of strength, courage, or conviction. It requires the redefinition of these qualities in light of the gospel rather than in light of cultural mythology.

Strength, in the gospel, is the capacity to bear the weight of another's suffering without flinching — not the capacity to impose one's will. Courage is the willingness to be vulnerable, to admit error, to name one's own sin before naming others' — not the willingness to dominate a room. Conviction is fidelity to the truth even when the truth is costly — not the rhetorical force to shout down disagreement.

A pastor who leads with healthy masculinity creates space for others rather than filling it himself. He listens more than he speaks. He asks questions rather than issuing pronouncements. He shares power rather than hoarding it. He admits what he does not know. He models emotional honesty — not the performed vulnerability of the confessional sermon illustration but the genuine, unscripted honesty of a man who has learned that his authority does not depend on his perfection.

He holds his authority lightly, knowing that it belongs to God, not to him. He exercises discipline when necessary — but with grief, not satisfaction. He confronts sin — but his own first. He leads — but toward the cross, not toward the throne.

This is not weakness. It is the hardest kind of strength. The strength to serve rather than dominate. The strength to absorb rather than inflict. The strength to follow a Savior who demonstrated, in the most definitive way possible, that the way up is down, the way to power is through service, and the way to life is through death.

The church that grasps this will not need to manufacture masculine energy or market warrior theology. It will have something far more compelling: men who look like Jesus. And that — not aggression, not domination, not the swagger of the celebrity pastor — is what the world has never seen enough of and has always, whether it knows it or not, been waiting for.
excerpt: The church that confuses aggression with authority and domination with leadership has not recovered biblical manhood. It has baptized the very thing the gospel came to crucify.

title: Colonialism and Missions
body:
On mission Sundays in American churches, the story is always the same. Brave missionaries cross oceans and jungles to bring the gospel to people who have never heard it. The emphasis is on sacrifice, heroism, and the life-altering power of the Christian message. Slides show smiling children. Testimonies recount dramatic conversions. The offering plate circulates with a special appeal for the unreached. It is a stirring narrative. It is also, in its selective telling, a profoundly dishonest one.

The parts we do not tell on mission Sundays are the parts that matter most for understanding why the word "missionary" carries, in much of the non-Western world, connotations not of love but of destruction. The history of Christian missions is inseparable from the history of European colonialism. The gospel traveled in the holds of slave ships, in the baggage trains of conquering armies, in the administrative apparatus of colonial governments that used Christianity as a tool of cultural subjugation. This does not mean that every missionary was a colonialist, or that every conversion was coerced, or that the gospel itself is reducible to its colonial carriers. But it means that any honest reckoning with the history of Christian missions must contend with the entanglement of the gospel with empire — an entanglement that was not incidental but structural, not accidental but theological.

The Doctrine of Discovery

In 1452, Pope Nicholas V issued the papal bull Dum Diversas, authorizing King Alfonso V of Portugal to "invade, search out, capture, vanquish, and subdue" all non-Christians, to reduce them to perpetual slavery, and to take their possessions and lands. In 1493, Pope Alexander VI issued Inter Caetera, granting Spain sovereignty over the lands Columbus had "discovered" in the Western Hemisphere. These documents — collectively known as the Doctrine of Discovery — provided the theological foundation for European colonialism. They established the principle that Christian nations had a divinely sanctioned right to claim sovereignty over non-Christian lands and peoples.

The Doctrine of Discovery was not a marginal theological opinion. It was official church teaching, ratified by papal authority and implemented by Christian governments across Europe. It provided the legal and theological basis for the conquest of the Americas, the colonization of Africa and Asia, the displacement and destruction of indigenous peoples on every continent. It was cited in U.S. Supreme Court decisions — notably Johnson v. McIntosh (1823) — as the foundation of American property law. Its effects are not historical curiosities. They are structural features of the world we inhabit.

The theological logic of the Doctrine of Discovery rested on a simple premise: non-Christian peoples were, by virtue of their unbelief, less than fully human and therefore incapable of legitimate sovereignty over their own lands and lives. The gospel was not offered as an invitation but wielded as a justification — a theological mechanism for transferring the wealth, land, and autonomy of non-Christian peoples to Christian ones. The cross was not separate from the conquest. It was the conquest's authorization.

Residential Schools and Forced Conversion

The residential school system — implemented in the United States, Canada, Australia, and other settler-colonial states — represents one of the most devastating intersections of Christianity and colonialism. In Canada alone, over 150,000 indigenous children were removed from their families and placed in church-run residential schools between the 1880s and the 1990s. The schools were operated by Catholic, Anglican, United, and Presbyterian churches with government funding and government sanction. Their explicit purpose, in the words of one Canadian official, was to "kill the Indian in the child."

Children were forbidden to speak their languages, practice their spiritual traditions, or maintain contact with their families. They were given Christian names, forced to attend Christian worship, and punished — often severely — for any expression of their indigenous identity. Physical abuse, sexual abuse, malnutrition, and medical neglect were widespread. Thousands of children died in the schools. Many were buried in unmarked graves. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, which spent six years documenting the system's history, called it "cultural genocide."

The churches that operated these schools did so in the sincere belief that they were saving souls. This sincerity does not mitigate the harm. It deepens it. The damage was done not by people who cynically exploited Christianity for colonial purposes but by people who genuinely believed that the destruction of indigenous culture was a necessary condition for indigenous salvation. The theology was the problem. A theology that cannot distinguish between conversion and cultural destruction, between the gospel and the erasure of identity, between salvation and assimilation is a theology that has lost its way so completely that its sincerity makes it more dangerous, not less.

The pattern extends far beyond North America. In Australia, the Stolen Generations — Aboriginal children forcibly removed from their families and placed in church-run institutions — suffered similar abuses. In Africa, missionaries frequently served as advance agents for colonial governments, establishing schools and hospitals that, however beneficial in their immediate effects, functioned within a colonial framework that undermined indigenous social structures, political systems, and spiritual traditions. In Latin America, the Spanish encomienda system granted colonizers the right to indigenous labor in exchange for Christian instruction — a system that amounted, in practice, to enslavement under a theological veneer.

The Indigenous Christian Response

The relationship between indigenous peoples and Christianity is not, however, a simple story of victimization. Indigenous Christians have, from the beginning, engaged the gospel on their own terms — accepting what resonated with their traditions, rejecting what was merely colonial, and creating forms of Christian faith that are rooted in indigenous soil rather than transplanted from European greenhouses.

Liberation theology — born in Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s — emerged from the experience of colonized peoples who read the Bible and found in it not the justification for their oppression but the resources for their liberation. Gustavo Gutierrez, the Peruvian theologian who gave the movement its name, argued that the God of the Bible is a God who takes the side of the poor, the oppressed, and the marginalized — not the side of their oppressors, however Christian those oppressors may claim to be. The Exodus narrative, the prophetic tradition, the Magnificat of Mary, the Sermon on the Mount — all of these point toward a God whose justice flows downward, toward the bottom, toward the people the powerful have forgotten.

Richard Twiss, a Lakota/Sicangu member of the Rosebud Sioux tribe and a Christian theologian, spent his life articulating an indigenous Christian theology that refused the colonial binary — the assumption that becoming Christian required ceasing to be indigenous. Twiss argued that indigenous cultural forms — drumming, dance, ceremony, artistic expression — could be legitimate vehicles for Christian worship, just as European cultural forms — organ music, Gothic architecture, clerical vestments — had always been. The gospel, he insisted, is translatable into every culture precisely because it belongs to none of them. The colonial error was not the introduction of the gospel to indigenous peoples but the insistence that the gospel could only be received in European packaging.

In Africa, the independent church movement — churches founded and led by Africans, free from European missionary control — has produced some of the most vibrant and creative expressions of Christianity in the world. These churches draw on African cultural resources — communal worship, ancestor awareness, healing practices, oral tradition — in ways that European missionaries would not have sanctioned. They represent not a departure from Christianity but a decolonization of it — a refusal to accept the colonial premise that African culture is incompatible with Christian faith.

The gospel does not require the destruction of culture. It requires the transformation of culture. And the people best equipped to lead that transformation are the people whose culture it is — not the foreigners who arrive with the answers already written.

How to Do Missions Without Colonialism

The colonial model of missions was built on a set of assumptions that the church must name and reject. The assumption that the missionary brings God to a place where God is absent — as if the Creator of all things had no presence among the peoples he created before the missionary arrived. The assumption that Western culture is the natural container for the gospel — as if the faith born in Palestine, shaped by Greek philosophy, preserved by Middle Eastern monks, and carried to Europe by North African theologians was inherently European. The assumption that the missionary's role is to teach and the indigenous person's role is to learn — as if the encounter between the gospel and a new culture were a one-way transmission rather than a mutual discovery.

Partnership models of mission begin with a different set of assumptions. They assume that God is already at work in every culture and that the missionary's first task is not to speak but to listen — to discern what God has been doing before the missionary arrived. They assume that the indigenous community is not a passive recipient of the gospel but an active participant in its interpretation and embodiment. They assume that the gospel will take forms in the new culture that the missionary could not have predicted and may not recognize — and that this is not a failure of the mission but its success.

Concrete practices follow from these assumptions. Short-term mission trips, as commonly practiced, should be radically reconceived. The typical short-term trip — in which a group of American teenagers spends a week painting an orphanage, taking selfies with local children, and returning home with a story about how the experience "changed their perspective" — is, at best, a form of spiritual tourism. At worst, it reinforces the colonial dynamic: wealthy outsiders arrive, perform charity, extract emotional benefit, and leave. The local community is not transformed. The visitors are not formed. And a great deal of money that could have funded local workers has been spent on airfare.

Long-term mission work, when it is done well, looks like partnership. It means working under indigenous leadership rather than over it. It means funding local organizations rather than building parallel structures. It means learning the language, the culture, the history, and the theological categories of the community being served — not as a prerequisite for preaching but as a form of respect for the people being encountered. It means being willing to receive as well as give, to learn as well as teach, to be changed as well as to change.

It means, ultimately, doing what the incarnation itself demonstrates: entering another's world on their terms, not your own. God did not send the gospel from a distance. God entered human culture, took on human flesh, spoke a human language, ate human food, lived within the constraints of a particular time and place. The incarnation is the model for all Christian mission: not the imposition of one culture on another but the translation of the gospel into the idiom of the community it encounters.

The church cannot undo the damage of colonial missions. The children who died in residential schools cannot be brought back. The cultures that were destroyed cannot be fully recovered. The trust that was violated cannot be easily rebuilt. But the church can tell the truth about what happened. It can repent of the theological errors that made it possible. It can commit to forms of mission that honor the dignity, agency, and cultural integrity of the communities it serves. And it can listen — genuinely, humbly, without defensiveness — to the voices of those who bear the scars of its history.

That listening is not optional. It is the beginning of the repentance the church owes to the peoples it harmed in Christ's name. And it is the only foundation on which a genuinely Christian practice of mission can be rebuilt — a practice that carries the cross without the sword, that offers the gospel without demanding the surrender of identity, and that trusts the Spirit to do what missionaries, in their colonial confidence, always believed only they could do: bring the good news to life in soil that is not their own.
excerpt: The cross arrived in the colonies alongside the sword. The church has spent centuries celebrating the gospel's spread while refusing to examine the wreckage it left behind. That refusal is itself a theological failure.

title: What Christians Can Learn From Judaism
body:
Jesus was Jewish. This statement is so obvious that it should not need saying, and so consistently ignored in its implications that it cannot be said often enough. Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day. He was presented at the temple according to the law of Moses. He attended synagogue. He observed the feasts. He wore tzitzit. He debated Torah with rabbis. He quoted the Psalms from the cross. The prayer he taught his disciples — the Lord's Prayer — is structured on Jewish liturgical patterns. The meal he shared on his last night — the Last Supper — was a Passover seder. The faith that Christians call their own was born inside Judaism, shaped by Jewish categories, expressed in Jewish idiom, and proclaimed by Jewish apostles to a world that had no framework for understanding it apart from the Jewish story of God, creation, covenant, and redemption.

And yet, within a few centuries, Christianity had not merely distinguished itself from Judaism but defined itself against it. The synagogue became the enemy. The Torah became the old dispensation, superseded and surpassed. The people of Israel became the people who had rejected their own Messiah — a rejection that, in the hands of Christian theologians from John Chrysostom to Martin Luther, justified centuries of persecution, forced conversion, ghettoization, and, in its most catastrophic expression, the theological soil in which the Holocaust took root.

The recovery of Christianity's Jewish roots is not a matter of interfaith politeness. It is a matter of theological survival. A Christianity severed from Judaism is a Christianity that has lost access to the intellectual, spiritual, and moral resources of its own foundation. And the things that Judaism preserves — things that Christianity has largely forgotten — are precisely the things that the contemporary church most desperately needs.

Torah Study as a Way of Life

In Judaism, the study of Torah is not preparation for something else. It is the thing itself. The Talmud Torah — the study of Torah — is considered one of the highest forms of worship, an act of devotion that is its own reward. The Talmud teaches that the study of Torah is equal to all the other commandments combined. This is not because Judaism is a religion of the intellect rather than the heart. It is because Judaism understands that the intellect and the heart are not separable — that the rigorous, disciplined engagement with a sacred text is itself a form of encounter with the God who gave it.

The contrast with contemporary evangelical Christianity is stark. In much of American Christianity, the Bible is a resource to be mined for principles, a sourcebook for sermon illustrations, a collection of promises to be claimed. It is rarely studied with the kind of sustained, rigorous, communal attention that characterizes Jewish Torah study. The average evangelical sermon extracts a verse, derives an application, and moves on. The text is instrumental — a means to an end, not an end in itself. The depth, complexity, and internal tensions of the text are smoothed over in the service of a tidy takeaway.

Jewish Torah study operates on entirely different assumptions. The text is inexhaustible. Every word, every letter, every apparent contradiction is significant. The purpose of study is not to resolve the text but to inhabit it — to live inside its questions, to sit with its tensions, to discover that the same passage yields different meanings at different stages of life. The rabbinical tradition encourages multiple interpretations of the same text, holding them in creative tension rather than resolving them into a single correct reading. The Talmud records minority opinions alongside majority ones, preserving dissent as part of the tradition rather than erasing it.

Christians who adopted this posture toward Scripture would find their reading immeasurably enriched. They would discover that the Bible is not a flat, self-evident manual of propositions but a living text that resists easy consumption and rewards sustained, patient, communal engagement. They would learn to sit with difficulty rather than resolving it prematurely. They would recover the ancient Christian practice of lectio divina — slow, meditative reading that allows the text to read the reader — which is, in its essential posture, closer to Jewish Torah study than to the evangelical quiet time.

Shabbat and the Discipline of Rest

The Jewish Sabbath — Shabbat — is not a day off. It is a day of resistance. In a world organized around productivity, efficiency, and the relentless accumulation of more, Shabbat declares that the world does not depend on human effort. It will continue without our work. God does not require our productivity. The command to rest is not a concession to human weakness but an assertion of divine sovereignty: the world belongs to God, not to us, and our refusal to stop working is not diligence but idolatry — the worship of our own indispensability.

Abraham Joshua Heschel, in The Sabbath, described Shabbat as a "palace in time" — a sacred architecture built not in space but in the rhythms of the week. Six days belong to the world of things. The seventh belongs to the world of meaning. On Shabbat, the observant Jew does not merely refrain from work. She enters a different mode of being — one oriented not toward doing but toward being, not toward producing but toward receiving, not toward mastering the world but toward delighting in it.

Christianity has, for the most part, lost the Sabbath. The Protestant tradition, in its anxiety about legalism, jettisoned Sabbath observance along with other aspects of the Torah that it deemed no longer binding. What replaced it — the "Lord's Day" of Sunday worship — retained the communal gathering but lost the comprehensive rest. Contemporary American Christians work on Sundays, shop on Sundays, check email on Sundays. The day has been absorbed into the culture of productivity that Shabbat was designed to resist.

The recovery of Sabbath — not as a legalistic obligation but as a spiritual discipline, a weekly act of resistance against the tyranny of productivity — would address one of the deepest pathologies of contemporary Christian life. The epidemic of pastoral burnout, the culture of overwork in ministry, the inability of Christians to distinguish their worth from their output — these are, at root, Sabbath problems. They are the symptoms of a community that has forgotten how to stop.

Questioning as Worship

In the Christian tradition, doubt is generally treated as a problem to be solved — a spiritual deficiency that needs correction, a phase to be moved through on the way to certainty. In Judaism, questioning is not a phase. It is a practice. It is, in a profound sense, worship itself.

The rabbinical tradition is built on argument. The Talmud — the central text of rabbinic Judaism — is structured as a record of debates among the rabbis, with competing interpretations set side by side, often without resolution. The tradition does not merely tolerate disagreement. It enshrines it. The minority opinion is preserved not because it might someday become the majority but because the act of wrestling with the text — of pushing against it, questioning it, arguing with it — is itself a form of faithfulness.

This posture extends to the relationship with God. Abraham argues with God over the fate of Sodom. Moses argues with God over the fate of Israel. Job argues with God over the meaning of suffering. Jacob wrestles with God physically and is renamed Israel — a name that means, literally, "one who wrestles with God." The tradition derived from these stories does not treat wrestling with God as a sign of weak faith. It treats it as the defining characteristic of the people of God.

The church that cannot make room for doubt, argument, and unresolved questioning is not more faithful than the rabbinical tradition. It is less honest. It has confused certainty with faith, compliance with devotion, and the absence of questions with the presence of God. A faith that cannot survive questioning was never strong enough to be called faith in the first place. Judaism knows this. Christianity keeps forgetting it.

Supersessionism: The Error That Shaped Everything

Supersessionism — the theological claim that the church has replaced Israel as the people of God, that the new covenant has rendered the old covenant obsolete, that Christianity has superseded Judaism — is the root theological error from which nearly all Christian anti-Judaism flows.

The claim has a long history. The Epistle of Barnabas, written in the early second century, argued that the Jews never properly understood their own Scriptures and that the covenant belongs exclusively to Christians. Justin Martyr, writing around 155 CE, told Trypho the Jew that "the Scriptures are not yours, but ours." John Chrysostom preached sermons against the Jews of such vitriol that they were used to justify persecution for over a millennium. Augustine developed the "witness doctrine," arguing that Jews were preserved by divine providence not as bearers of a living covenant but as witnesses to Christian truth — their degraded state serving as proof that God had transferred his favor to the church.

The theological consequences of supersessionism have been catastrophic. If the church has replaced Israel, then Jewish existence is theologically unnecessary. If the old covenant is obsolete, then Judaism is an anachronism — a religion that should have ended when Christianity began. If the Jews rejected their own Messiah, then they bear a collective guilt that justifies their marginalization, persecution, and worse. The line from supersessionist theology to the pogroms of medieval Europe to the ghettos of early modern Europe to the ovens of Auschwitz is not straight — history is never that simple — but it is traceable. The theological soil was prepared by the church. Others planted the seeds and reaped the harvest. But the soil was ours.

Paul, in Romans 9-11, explicitly rejects supersessionism. "Did God reject his people? By no means," he writes. "God's gifts and his call are irrevocable." The olive tree metaphor in Romans 11 is unmistakable: Gentile Christians are branches grafted into an existing tree — the tree of Israel. They do not replace the tree. They do not supersede it. They are guests in someone else's story. "Do not be arrogant toward the branches," Paul warns. "You do not support the root; the root supports you."

The church largely ignored Paul's warning. It was arrogant toward the branches. And the consequences of that arrogance — theological, moral, and historical — are still being reckoned with.

Dialogue Without Conversion Pressure

Honest interfaith dialogue between Christians and Jews requires Christians to abandon the assumption that the dialogue's purpose is to bring Jews to Christ. This is not a concession to pluralism or a surrender of Christian conviction. It is a recognition that the relationship between Christianity and Judaism is unique among all interfaith relationships and cannot be forced into the standard missionary paradigm.

Judaism is not a religion that has failed to hear the gospel. It is the religion that gave birth to the gospel. The Jewish people are not an unreached people group. They are the original covenant community from which Christianity emerged. To treat Judaism as simply one more religion to be evangelized is to misunderstand both Judaism and Christianity's relationship to it.

Dialogue between Christians and Jews, at its best, is a recovery of family relationship — a conversation between siblings who share a parent, a library, and a story, even though they have told the story differently for two thousand years. Such dialogue requires Christians to listen to Jewish self-understanding on its own terms, not through the filter of Christian categories. It requires Christians to take seriously the possibility that God's covenant with Israel remains operative — that Judaism is not an empty shell awaiting Christian fulfillment but a living tradition with its own integrity, its own relationship with God, and its own gifts to offer the world.

This does not require Christians to abandon their own convictions about Christ. It requires them to hold those convictions with the humility appropriate to a tradition that has spent two millennia getting its relationship with its parent tradition catastrophically wrong. The church that approaches Judaism with anything less than deep humility, genuine curiosity, and a willingness to learn has not yet reckoned with its own history. And until it does, it has nothing worth saying.
excerpt: Christianity emerged from Judaism and then spent two millennia pretending it had outgrown its parent. The cost of that pretension has been theological impoverishment, moral blindness, and a faith unmoored from the tradition Jesus himself practiced.

title: What Christians Can Learn From Islam
body:
In the popular imagination of Western Christianity, Islam occupies the space reserved for the threat — the civilizational rival, the theological adversary, the religion that replaced Christian persuasion with the sword. The centuries of conflict — the Crusades, the Ottoman wars, the contemporary specter of terrorism — have deposited a residue of fear and hostility so thick that most Western Christians cannot think about Islam without thinking through it. The faith practiced by nearly two billion people, rooted in the same Abrahamic soil as Christianity, oriented toward the same God, honoring many of the same figures — Abraham, Moses, Mary, Jesus — is reduced, in the Christian imagination, to a caricature: violent, oppressive, monolithic, and fundamentally incompatible with Christian truth.

This caricature serves no one. It does not serve Christians, who remain ignorant of a tradition that has much to teach them. It does not serve Muslims, who are perpetually misrepresented by the people who claim to follow a God of truth. And it does not serve the God who, Christians confess, is sovereign over all peoples and all traditions — a God whose work in the world is not confined to the boundaries of Christianity, however uncomfortable that truth may be.

Learning from Islam does not require the abandonment of Christian convictions. It requires the intellectual honesty to recognize that God may have deposited truths in other traditions that Christians have neglected in their own — and the spiritual humility to receive those truths as gifts rather than threats.

The Five Pillars and the Discipline of Submission

The Five Pillars of Islam — the shahada (declaration of faith), salat (prayer five times daily), zakat (almsgiving), sawm (fasting during Ramadan), and hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca) — constitute a comprehensive framework of spiritual discipline that shapes every dimension of a Muslim's life. They are not optional. They are not suggestions. They are the non-negotiable architecture of a life oriented toward God.

The contrast with much of contemporary Christianity is instructive. The average American Christian attends church sporadically, prays inconsistently, gives modestly, fasts rarely or never, and undertakes no form of pilgrimage. The spiritual disciplines that the Christian tradition has historically valued — regular prayer, fasting, almsgiving, pilgrimage — exist in theory but have largely evaporated in practice. The Muslim who prays five times a day, facing Mecca, interrupting whatever else is happening to kneel before God, is practicing a level of spiritual discipline that most Christians admire in the abstract and avoid in practice.

The word "Islam" itself means "submission" — voluntary submission to the will of God. This is not a concept foreign to Christianity. Jesus in Gethsemane prayed, "Not my will, but yours be done." Paul wrote of presenting one's body as a "living sacrifice." The entire monastic tradition — from the Desert Fathers to Benedict to Francis — is built on the principle that the spiritual life requires the disciplined subordination of the self to God. But in much of contemporary Christianity, submission has been replaced by preference, discipline by comfort, and the costly demands of following God by the therapeutic language of personal fulfillment. Islam's uncompromising emphasis on submission — on the daily, embodied, non-negotiable practice of orienting one's entire life toward God — is a rebuke that Christians should receive with gratitude rather than resentment.

Justice as a Non-Negotiable

The Islamic emphasis on justice — adl — runs through every dimension of the tradition. The Quran identifies justice as one of God's essential attributes and one of the community's essential obligations. Zakat — the third pillar — is not charity in the Christian sense of a voluntary act of generosity. It is an obligation: a fixed percentage of one's wealth, distributed annually to those in need. The right of the poor to a share of the wealthy person's resources is not a matter of the wealthy person's discretion. It is a matter of divine command.

This understanding of economic justice is deeply consonant with the biblical prophetic tradition. Amos, Isaiah, Micah, and the other Hebrew prophets thundered against economic exploitation and demanded structural justice for the poor — not as a supplement to worship but as a precondition for it. "I hate, I despise your religious festivals," God says through Amos. "But let justice roll on like a river." The prophetic tradition insists that piety without justice is not merely incomplete. It is offensive to God.

Christianity has largely domesticated this tradition, treating generosity as a personal virtue rather than a structural obligation. The tithe, where it is practiced, is voluntary. Giving is framed as a response to blessing rather than a requirement of justice. The radical economic vision of the early church — "they held all things in common" — has been reduced to a historical curiosity. Islam's insistence that economic justice is not optional, not a matter of personal preference, not separable from the life of faith, recovers a dimension of the prophetic tradition that Christianity has allowed to atrophy.

Common Ground

The common ground between Christianity and Islam is more substantial than either tradition typically acknowledges. Both are monotheistic — both confess one God, creator of all things, sovereign over history, judge of all people. Both trace their lineage to Abraham. Both honor the Hebrew prophets. Both affirm the virgin birth of Jesus. The Quran speaks of Jesus (Isa) with profound reverence — as a prophet, as the Messiah, as one born of the Spirit of God, as a worker of miracles. Muslims do not accept the divinity of Christ or the doctrine of the Trinity, but the Jesus of the Quran is not a marginal figure. He is one of the most honored prophets in the Islamic tradition.

Both traditions share a moral seriousness that is increasingly rare in the secular West. Both insist that human life has meaning, that moral choices have consequences, that the universe is not indifferent to how we live. Both reject the nihilism and consumerism that characterize late-modern Western culture. Both maintain that worship — the orientation of the whole person toward God — is the highest human activity. Both affirm the reality of the afterlife, the certainty of judgment, and the importance of living in light of eternity.

These commonalities do not erase the differences, which are real and significant. The Christian confession of the Trinity, the divinity of Christ, and the atoning work of the cross are claims that Islam explicitly rejects. The Islamic understanding of revelation — that the Quran is the literal, uncreated word of God, dictated verbatim to Muhammad — differs fundamentally from the Christian understanding of Scripture as divinely inspired but humanly mediated. These differences matter. They should not be papered over in the name of false harmony.

But the differences should not be weaponized, either. The fact that Christians and Muslims disagree about the nature of Christ does not mean they have nothing to say to each other about the nature of God, the demands of justice, the practice of prayer, or the meaning of human existence. Honest interfaith dialogue lives in the tension between genuine commonality and genuine difference — refusing to collapse either into the other.

What Honest Dialogue Looks Like

Honest interfaith dialogue is not a debate to be won. It is a conversation to be entered. It begins with the willingness to listen to the other tradition on its own terms — not through the filter of one's own categories, not in search of ammunition for apologetic arguments, but with genuine curiosity about how the other sees God, understands the world, and practices faithfulness.

For Christians, this means setting aside the caricatures. Islam is not monolithic. It contains within it a vast diversity of traditions — Sunni and Shia, Sufi mysticism and Salafi rigorism, the philosophical tradition of al-Farabi, Ibn Sina, and Ibn Rushd, the poetic tradition of Rumi and Hafiz, the legal traditions of the four Sunni schools and the Ja'fari school of Shia jurisprudence. Reducing this richness to a single image — the terrorist, the oppressor, the civilizational threat — is not merely unfair. It is intellectually lazy. And intellectual laziness is a poor foundation for the pursuit of truth that both traditions claim to value.

Dialogue also requires Christians to reckon with their own tradition's failures toward the Muslim world. The Crusades were not defensive operations launched to protect Christendom from aggression. They were wars of conquest, marked by massacre, plunder, and the slaughter of civilians. The sack of Jerusalem in 1099, in which Crusaders waded through blood in the streets and murdered Muslims and Jews indiscriminately, is a stain on Christian history that no amount of revisionism can erase. The colonial subjugation of the Muslim world in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries — justified, in part, by Christian civilizational pretensions — has left wounds that are still open. Christians who enter dialogue with Muslims without acknowledging this history are not ready for honest conversation.

The goal of dialogue is not agreement. It is understanding — the kind of understanding that allows two people who disagree profoundly about ultimate questions to recognize each other as fellow seekers of the God who, both traditions confess, is greater than any human understanding of him. That recognition does not require the surrender of conviction. It requires the expansion of imagination — the willingness to consider that God's truth may be larger than any single tradition's apprehension of it, and that the encounter with the other may reveal dimensions of one's own faith that were previously invisible.

The Christian who takes Islam seriously — who reads the Quran with attention, who listens to Muslim prayers with respect, who learns the names of God that Islam preserves and Christianity has forgotten — will not become less Christian. She will become a more humble, more curious, and more honest Christian. And humility, curiosity, and honesty are not threats to faith. They are among faith's finest fruits.
excerpt: Islam is the faith Christians know least and fear most. That fear has produced ignorance, and that ignorance has impoverished both traditions. The common ground between them is deeper than either side typically admits.

title: What Christians Can Learn From Buddhism
body:
In 1968, Thomas Merton — Trappist monk, contemplative writer, and one of the most influential spiritual voices of the twentieth century — traveled to Asia to meet with Buddhist monks and teachers. In Bangkok, he delivered a lecture to a conference of monastics. He spoke of the convergences between Christian and Buddhist contemplative practice — the shared commitment to silence, simplicity, and the disciplined emptying of the self. He spoke of what Christians could learn from Buddhism without abandoning their own tradition. Later that day, Merton died — electrocuted by a faulty fan in his hotel room, in circumstances that remain somewhat mysterious. He was fifty-three years old.

Merton's Asian journey was not a departure from his Christian faith. It was a deepening of it. He had spent twenty-seven years in a Trappist monastery, living under a rule of silence, prayer, and manual labor. He had written over sixty books on Christian spirituality, theology, and contemplative practice. He was, by any measure, one of the most deeply rooted Christians of his century. And it was precisely the depth of his rootedness that gave him the freedom to engage Buddhism without fear — to recognize in another tradition the same realities he had encountered in his own, expressed in different language and practiced through different forms.

Merton's example points to a truth that the Western church has been slow to grasp: Christianity and Buddhism, despite their profound metaphysical differences, share a remarkable convergence in their contemplative practices, their diagnosis of the human condition, and their prescriptions for spiritual transformation. The church that dismisses Buddhism as a pagan philosophy or an incompatible worldview is not protecting its faith. It is impoverishing it.

Mindfulness and the Christian Contemplative Tradition

Mindfulness — the practice of sustained, nonjudgmental attention to the present moment — has entered Western culture primarily through Buddhism. It has been secularized, commercialized, and stripped of its spiritual context to the point where it is now marketed as a productivity tool, a stress-reduction technique, and a corporate wellness strategy. This domestication has made many Christians suspicious of it — and understandably so.

But mindfulness did not originate as a secular self-help technique. In Buddhism, it is one of the core practices of the Eightfold Path — samma sati, or right mindfulness — a disciplined form of attention that enables the practitioner to see reality clearly, without the distortions of craving, aversion, and delusion. It is a spiritual discipline, not a lifestyle hack.

And the Christian tradition has its own version of it — though most contemporary Christians have never heard of it. The Desert Fathers and Mothers of the third and fourth centuries practiced nepsis — a Greek term meaning "watchfulness" or "vigilance" — which is, in its essential posture, strikingly similar to Buddhist mindfulness. Nepsis is the practice of sustained attention to one's own inner life — to the movements of thought, desire, and emotion — in order to discern the presence and action of God. The practitioner learns to observe without reacting, to notice without grasping, to be present to what is happening rather than lost in what has happened or what might happen.

The Cloud of Unknowing, a fourteenth-century English mystical text, instructs the reader to let go of all thoughts, images, and concepts — even thoughts of God — in order to encounter God in the darkness beyond thought. Meister Eckhart spoke of Gelassenheit — "releasement" or "letting be" — the practice of releasing attachment to ideas, possessions, and even spiritual experiences in order to receive God in pure nakedness of spirit. John of the Cross described the noche oscura — the dark night of the soul — in which God withdraws all consolation and sensible experience, stripping the soul of its attachments so that it can be united with God in pure faith.

These are not borrowed ideas. They are indigenous to the Christian tradition. But they have been marginalized — pushed to the edges of Christian practice by a tradition that prizes intellectual certainty, verbal expression, and emotional experience over the silent, imageless encounter with God that the contemplatives describe. Buddhism's emphasis on the discipline of attention, the letting go of mental clutter, and the practice of presence can help Christians recover what their own tradition already contains but has largely forgotten.

Suffering: The First Noble Truth and the Way of the Cross

The First Noble Truth of Buddhism — dukkha, often translated as "suffering" but more accurately rendered as "unsatisfactoriness" or "pervasive dissatisfaction" — is the recognition that human existence is characterized by a fundamental inability to find lasting satisfaction in any conditioned thing. Pleasure fades. Possessions decay. Relationships end. The self that seeks permanence in an impermanent world is perpetually frustrated. This is not pessimism. It is diagnosis. And the diagnosis must be made accurately before any treatment can be effective.

Christianity, at its best, shares this diagnosis. The book of Ecclesiastes — "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity" — reads like a Hebrew anticipation of the First Noble Truth. Augustine's restless heart, which "finds no rest until it rests in God," identifies the same fundamental dissatisfaction with creaturely existence that Buddhism names as dukkha. Paul's groaning creation in Romans 8, which "waits with eager longing" for its liberation, describes a world in which suffering is not an aberration but a pervasive condition awaiting redemption.

But much of contemporary Christianity has lost this honesty about suffering. The prosperity gospel promises that faith produces material blessing. The therapeutic gospel promises that faith produces emotional comfort. The triumphalist gospel promises that faith produces victory. All three are refusals to sit with the First Noble Truth — refusals to acknowledge that suffering is not an interruption of normal life but a constitutive feature of it. Buddhism's unblinking gaze at the reality of suffering can help Christians recover the honesty that their own tradition demands but their contemporary practice often avoids.

Attachment, Desire, and What the Desert Fathers Already Knew

The Second Noble Truth of Buddhism identifies the cause of suffering as tanha — craving, attachment, clinging. We suffer because we grasp at things that cannot be held — pleasure, status, security, life itself. The solution, in the Buddhist framework, is not the acquisition of the desired object but the release of the desire itself. Freedom comes not from getting what you want but from ceasing to be controlled by wanting.

The Desert Fathers called this apatheia — not apathy in the modern sense but freedom from the tyranny of the passions. Evagrius Ponticus, a fourth-century desert monk, catalogued the "eight thoughts" — later condensed into the seven deadly sins — that entrap the soul: gluttony, lust, avarice, sadness, anger, acedia (spiritual lethargy), vainglory, and pride. His analysis of how these thoughts arise, how they gain power over the mind, and how they can be released through disciplined attention and practice is remarkably similar to Buddhist psychology. The Desert Fathers were doing, in their own theological framework, what Buddhist monks had been doing for centuries: observing the mechanics of desire and developing practices for its liberation.

John of the Cross made the same point in a different register. "To come to possess all, desire the possession of nothing," he wrote. "To come to be all, desire to be nothing." This is not nihilism. It is the recognition that attachment — even attachment to spiritual goods — becomes an obstacle when it substitutes the gift for the Giver. The soul that clings to its experience of God has mistaken the experience for God and must be stripped of even that consolation in order to receive God directly.

Contemporary Christianity, particularly in its American expressions, has become a religion of attachment — attachment to outcomes, attachment to experiences, attachment to the conviction that God's primary job is to give us what we want. Buddhism's ancient, rigorous analysis of attachment and its consequences can help Christians recognize the spiritual trap they are in — and recover the resources within their own tradition for getting out of it.

Merton's Dialogue

Merton's engagement with Buddhism was not syncretism — the blending of two traditions into a third thing that is neither. It was dialogue — the genuine encounter between two traditions, each with its own integrity, in which both are illuminated without either being compromised. Merton remained a Christian. He remained a monk. He remained committed to Christ, the Trinity, the Eucharist, and the full architecture of Christian faith. But he recognized that Buddhist practice — its discipline of attention, its honesty about suffering, its analysis of attachment, its commitment to compassion — illuminated dimensions of his own tradition that he might not have seen without the encounter.

"I think we have now reached a stage of religious maturity at which it may be possible for someone to remain perfectly faithful to a Christian and Western monastic commitment," Merton wrote, "and yet to learn in depth from, say, a Buddhist discipline and experience." This is not the language of capitulation. It is the language of confidence — the confidence of a man whose faith was deep enough to encounter the other without being threatened by the encounter.

The fear that learning from Buddhism will dilute Christian faith reveals not the strength of that faith but its fragility. A Christianity so insecure that it cannot engage another tradition without losing its own identity is a Christianity that does not trust its own foundations. The deepest Christians in history — the Desert Fathers, the mystics, the contemplatives — have always been the most open to truth wherever it is found, because they knew that all truth, in the end, comes from the God they served.

Learning Without Syncretism

The distinction between learning and syncretism is not difficult to maintain, though it requires intellectual discipline. Syncretism collapses the differences between traditions, producing a vague spirituality that belongs to none of them. Learning preserves the differences while allowing each tradition to illuminate the other. A Christian can adopt the practice of sitting meditation — attention to breath, release of discursive thought, sustained presence — without adopting Buddhist metaphysics. A Christian can learn from the Buddhist analysis of attachment without abandoning the Christian doctrine of creation's goodness. A Christian can appreciate the Four Noble Truths as a profound diagnosis of the human condition without accepting that the solution is nirvana rather than resurrection.

The key is rootedness. The Christian who learns from Buddhism must be deeply enough rooted in her own tradition to know what she is receiving and what she is not — to distinguish between a practice that deepens her faith and an idea that contradicts it. Merton could engage Buddhism because he had spent twenty-seven years in a monastery. He knew who he was. He knew what he believed. He knew the difference between a gift to be received and a claim to be rejected.

The church that recovers its own contemplative tradition — the Desert Fathers, the mystics, the practice of silence and simplicity and sustained attention — will find that it needs to borrow less from Buddhism than it feared, because the resources were already there. But the encounter with Buddhism may be precisely what catalyzes the recovery. Sometimes you do not see what your own tradition contains until someone from another tradition shows it to you. That is not a threat to Christian faith. It is one of the ways faith grows.
excerpt: The contemplative traditions of Christianity and Buddhism have been carrying on a quiet conversation for centuries. The church has much to gain from listening more carefully to what the Buddhists have long practiced.

title: What Christians Can Learn From Indigenous Spirituality
body:
In the opening chapters of Genesis, God places the first humans in a garden and gives them a task: tend it. The Hebrew word is shamar — to keep, to guard, to watch over. The human relationship to the earth, in the Bible's own framing, is not ownership but stewardship. Not dominion in the sense of domination but care in the sense of guardianship. The earth belongs to God. Humans are its caretakers, charged with preserving what they have been given.

This theology is clear in the text. It is almost entirely absent from the practice of Western Christianity. The Christian West — shaped by the Enlightenment, the Industrial Revolution, and the capitalist logic of extraction and consumption — has treated the earth not as a garden to be tended but as a resource to be exploited. Forests have been clear-cut, rivers poisoned, species driven to extinction, and the climate itself destabilized — all within cultures that claimed the Bible as their foundational text. The disconnect between the theology and the practice is staggering.

Indigenous spiritual traditions, across the globe and across their enormous diversity, have preserved what Western Christianity forgot: that the earth is sacred, that humans are part of the creation rather than above it, that the land has a voice and the creatures have a dignity that human ambition does not override. The church that destroyed these traditions in the name of evangelization silenced the very voices that were saying what the Bible itself says. The irony is painful. The cost is incalculable.

Creation Care: What the West Forgot

Indigenous traditions understand the human relationship to the earth in terms that Western Christianity, for all its theological resources, has largely failed to practice. The Lakota concept of Mitakuye Oyasin — "all my relatives" — expresses a relational understanding of the created order in which humans, animals, plants, rivers, mountains, and the earth itself are bound together in a web of kinship. This is not animism in the crude sense that Western missionaries attributed to it — the worship of natural objects. It is a sophisticated ecological theology that recognizes what the Bible affirms and Western practice denies: that creation is a community, not a commodity.

The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Thanksgiving Address — recited at the opening of gatherings — names and thanks every element of the created order: the earth, the waters, the fish, the plants, the trees, the animals, the birds, the winds, the sun, the moon, the stars. It is a liturgy of gratitude that takes twenty minutes to recite because it refuses to take any element of creation for granted. It names each gift individually, acknowledges its contribution to the whole, and expresses the community's dependence on and gratitude for what has been given.

Compare this with the average Christian prayer before a meal — a perfunctory few seconds that names God as the source of blessing but says nothing about the earth that produced the food, the animals that gave their lives, the water that nourished the crops, or the human labor that brought the meal to the table. The Haudenosaunee Thanksgiving Address practices, in concrete liturgical form, the theology of creation care that the Bible teaches but the church has reduced to an abstraction.

Wendell Berry — a Christian farmer, poet, and essayist — has spent a lifetime arguing that the church's failure of creation care is not a peripheral issue but a theological crisis. "The ecological teaching of the Bible is simply inescapable," he writes. "God made the world because He wanted it made. He thinks the world is good, and He loves it. It is His world; He has never relinquished title to it." A theology that treats the earth as disposable, Berry argues, has not understood the God who made it. Indigenous traditions that treat the earth as sacred have understood something that the Christian West, for all its theological sophistication, has not.

Community Over Individualism

Western Christianity, particularly in its Protestant and evangelical forms, has become radically individualized. Salvation is a personal decision. Faith is a private relationship with God. The spiritual life is conceived primarily in individual terms: my quiet time, my prayer life, my relationship with Jesus. The community exists to support the individual's spiritual formation, not the other way around.

Indigenous traditions operate on fundamentally different assumptions. The individual exists within and through the community. Identity is communal before it is personal. Decisions are made collectively. Spiritual practices are communal practices. The self is understood not as an autonomous agent pursuing its own spiritual goals but as a node in a web of relationships — with other humans, with ancestors, with the land, with the spirit world — that constitute the self's identity and meaning.

This communal orientation is not foreign to Christianity. It is, in fact, deeply biblical. The New Testament's dominant metaphor for the church is the body — a single organism composed of interdependent members, none of which can say to the others, "I have no need of you." The early church held all things in common. The Hebrew concept of corporate identity — in which the individual is constituted by the community rather than the community by individuals — runs through the entire Old Testament. The Western turn toward individualism is not a biblical development. It is an Enlightenment development that Christianity absorbed uncritically.

Indigenous traditions can help the church recover what the Enlightenment displaced: the understanding that the spiritual life is inherently communal, that the self is formed in relationship, and that the radical individualism of contemporary Christianity is not a feature of the faith but a distortion of it.

The Sacred in the Ordinary

One of the most significant features of indigenous spiritual traditions is the refusal to separate the sacred from the ordinary. There is no division between the spiritual and the material, the holy and the everyday, the place where God is present and the place where God is not. The entire created order is pervaded with spiritual significance. A meal is a ceremony. A walk is a meditation. The land is not the backdrop for spiritual life. It is the medium of spiritual life.

Christianity, in its Western form, has been deeply shaped by the Greek dualism that separates matter and spirit — a dualism that is foreign to the Hebrew worldview in which Christianity is rooted. The sacred has been confined to sacred spaces (churches), sacred times (Sundays), sacred activities (worship), and sacred personnel (clergy). The ordinary — work, eating, walking, planting, resting — has been relegated to the secular, the non-spiritual, the domain of the merely material.

Indigenous traditions know better. And so, it should be noted, does the Bible. The Psalms find God in the mountains, the seas, the storms, and the stars. The incarnation — God becoming flesh, dwelling among us — is the ultimate refusal of the sacred-secular divide. A God who became a carpenter, ate meals with sinners, touched lepers, and washed feet has declared, in the most definitive way possible, that the ordinary is the dwelling place of the holy.

The recovery of this understanding — the recognition that God is present not only in the sanctuary but in the field, not only in the sermon but in the silence, not only in the church building but in the created order that surrounds and sustains it — is one of the most important gifts indigenous spirituality has to offer the Christian tradition. It is also one of the most faithful, because it recovers what the Bible teaches and the church has lost.

The Damage Done in Christ's Name

Any honest engagement between Christianity and indigenous spirituality must begin with an acknowledgment of the damage the church has done. The destruction of indigenous spiritual traditions was not an unfortunate side effect of well-intentioned mission work. It was a deliberate strategy, theologically justified and institutionally implemented. Missionaries and colonial administrators classified indigenous spiritual practices as paganism, devil worship, or superstition — and then systematically destroyed them. Ceremonies were banned. Sacred sites were desecrated. Spiritual leaders were imprisoned or killed. Children were removed from their families and placed in institutions designed to erase their cultural and spiritual identity.

The theological justification for this destruction rested on assumptions that the church must now name and repudiate. The assumption that God was entirely absent from indigenous traditions before the missionaries arrived. The assumption that indigenous spiritual practices were uniformly demonic. The assumption that cultural destruction was a necessary precondition for spiritual salvation. These assumptions are not merely wrong. They are blasphemous — attributing to God the absence of the very creative and sustaining work that Scripture says God performs among all peoples and in all creation.

Richard Twiss and Indigenous Christian Theology

Richard Twiss spent his life demonstrating that it was possible to be both fully indigenous and fully Christian — that the forced choice between the two was a colonial imposition, not a theological necessity. A member of the Rosebud Sioux tribe and an ordained minister, Twiss advocated for indigenous expressions of Christian worship that drew on native cultural forms — drumming, dance, regalia, ceremony — as legitimate vehicles for encountering the Christian God.

Twiss's work was controversial within both indigenous and Christian communities. Some indigenous people viewed him as a collaborator with the religion that had destroyed their ancestors' traditions. Some Christians viewed his incorporation of indigenous cultural forms as syncretism — the blending of Christianity with paganism. Twiss rejected both critiques. He argued that the gospel has always been translated into cultural forms — from the Greek philosophy of the early councils to the Gothic architecture of medieval Europe to the contemporary worship music of American evangelicalism — and that indigenous cultural forms deserve the same dignity and recognition as any other.

"Why is it," Twiss asked, "that an Italian painting of Jesus is considered sacred art, but a Lakota painting of Jesus is considered syncretism?" The question exposes the colonial double standard at the heart of Western Christianity's relationship with indigenous culture.
